prompt: Some friends are having a conversation about how boring things have gotten ... in the middle of a comically dramatic / dangerous / or otherwise intense scene .
content:
**The Dragon in the Cheesecake Factory**

At 3:17 p.m., the fire-breathing dragon burst through the wall of the Cheesecake Factory. This was not, according to Jonah, the most interesting thing to happen to him all week.

“Honestly,” he said, ducking a jet of flame, “I feel like things have gotten kind of boring.”

Alex, pinned behind an overturned dessert cart, threw a bread roll at the dragon’s snout. “Boring? We’re being attacked by a dragon in a mall.”

“I mean socially,” Jonah said. “Like, every Friday it’s the same. Someone suggests a bar. Someone else says it’s too loud. We end up at my place watching a cooking show. Last week we watched a man in Ohio make a sourdough starter. For forty minutes.”

The dragon roared. Its tail smashed a display of cheesecake, sending New York slices through the air like shrapnel. Priya caught one and took a bite. “This is good. Also, you’re not wrong. Our group chat has been dead since August. The last message was your mom’s birthday.”

“That was a group chat?” Jonah said. He rolled under a table as the dragon’s claws shredded the tablecloth. “I thought that was just a calendar thing.”

“See?” Priya said, chewing. “We need hobbies. Something new. Maybe pottery.”

Alex reloaded the flare gun he’d found in the security office. “We are in a literal dragon attack. We have hobbies.”

“Emergency hobbies don’t count,” Jonah said. “I mean, like, a Tuesday night thing. A book club. Or axe throwing.”

The dragon inhaled. The air shimmered. Alex grabbed both of them by the collars and yanked them behind the bar. Flame washed over the espresso machines, which exploded in a fragrant hiss of burnt coffee. Somewhere, a fire alarm played the first four notes of a cheerful jingle on a loop.

“We could do axe throwing,” Alex admitted, “but I feel like everyone’s tired by seven-thirty. That’s the real problem. We’re not boring; we’re tired.”

“Both can be true,” Priya said. She popped up and flung a cheesecake at the dragon. It hit the beast’s eye. It blinked, confused and mildly sticky. “Also, we never do anything spontaneous. Remember when we used to just drive somewhere? Now everything needs a poll and three reminders.”

Jonah nodded. “I miss spontaneity.”

The dragon smashed the bar into splinters. They ran. The mall’s central escalator had stopped, which was probably for the best because the dragon was now breathing fire up the down escalator. They sprinted past a closed Claire’s and a kiosk selling phone cases that said *I’m Not Arguing, I’m Just Explaining.*

“Tuesday,” Alex said, panting. “We could do Tuesdays. Cheap movie night.”

“Movies are passive,” Jonah said. “We need active. But not, like, hiking active. Maybe archery.”

“We’re being chased by a dragon,” Priya said. “We’re doing archery. With a flare gun.”

“That’s not archery.”

“Close enough.”

They burst through the mall’s emergency exit into the loading dock, where the dragon’s wing clipped a lamppost and sent it spinning like a bottle. Alex aimed the flare gun, missed, and hit a stack of cardboard boxes that immediately caught fire. The dragon turned toward the fire, delighted, as if someone had brought it a snack.

“Oh, great,” Alex said. “Now it has a side dish.”

“See, this is what I mean,” Jonah said, slumping against a dumpster. “This is the most exciting thing that’s happened in months, and even now we’re talking about how boring we are. We’re in a rut.”

Priya sat next to him. “We’re in a loading dock, behind a burning mall, while a dragon eats cardboard. This is not a rut. This is a low point.”

“Ruts can be low points.”

The dragon belched a small, satisfied flame and turned back to them. Alex grabbed a discarded shopping cart and shoved it toward the beast. The dragon sniffed it, then ate the cart in one crunch. It chewed thoughtfully. Its expression shifted from murderous to mildly interested to what could only be described as disappointed. It spat out a wheel.

“We need to get to the car,” Alex said.

“The car is on the other side of the loading dock,” Priya said.

“Then we need a distraction.”

“I have one,” Jonah said. He stood up, cupped his hands around his mouth, and shouted at the dragon: “Hey! Do you ever feel like every weekend is the same?”

The dragon paused. It tilted its head. It did not speak, but its posture suggested that it, too, had been wondering whether life had become a series of interchangeable Saturdays.

“Exactly,” Jonah said. “So here’s the plan. We’re going to run to that car. You’re going to chase us. It’ll be spontaneous. It’ll be exciting. And then, next week, we’re all going to try something new. Even you.”

The dragon snorted a plume of smoke. It seemed to consider this.

“Was that a yes?” Alex whispered.

The dragon lunged. They ran. It was, Jonah had to admit, not boring.

Later, crammed in Priya’s sedan with the windows down and the dragon’s wingbeats fading behind them, Alex said, “So. Tuesday.”

“Tuesday,” Priya agreed. “But nothing that requires buying special shoes.”

“Agreed,” Jonah said. “We’ll figure it out in the group chat.”

“Don’t say group chat,” Priya said. “It’s dead.”

“Then we’ll revive it,” Alex said. “With a poll.”

Jonah groaned. But he was smiling.

The car swerved onto the highway. Behind them, the mall parking lot glowed orange. The dragon, they later learned, had eaten the rest of the cheesecake and then flown away, apparently bored.

prompt: The time of Armageddon is soon . All the gods of various pantheons congregate to debate on why their end of the world should happen . While squabbling among each other , a god that was never worshiped speaks its mind .
content:
# The God of the Almost

The time of Armageddon was soon.

It had been soon for a very long while, in the way that the last hour of a party is soon, and everyone knows it but no one wants to be the first to leave. The gods had gathered on the Concourse of Last Things, a flat black plain polished from the crust of a dead star. Banners of forgotten temples snapped in a wind that smelled of incense and ozone. Every pantheon had sent representatives. Some came in glory. Some came in borrowed bodies. Some came only as a rumor of thunder.

They had been arguing for three hundred years.

“Ragnarok,” said Odin, striking the ground with Gungnir, “is the only honest ending. Even the gods die. It teaches courage.”

“It teaches that your wolf has poor table manners,” said Zeus. “My flood had moral clarity. And a boat.”

“Your flood was derivative,” said Ra. “The sun has been insulted long enough. Apophis will swallow it, and the world will return to the cool silence of Nun.”

“All things dissolve in me,” said Shiva, mildly, as if discussing the weather. “The dance is already happening. Your apocalypses are local feuds.”

“The fifth sun must fall,” said Quetzalcoatl, feathers ruffling. “The earth will shudder and devour itself. It is written in jade and blood.”

“Mine has a great serpent,” said Ra.

“Mine has a great serpent too,” said Quetzalcoatl.

“Mine has accounting,” said a thin god from a minor bureaucracy, and was ignored.

They squabbled over worshipper counts and last rites. They accused one another of plagiarism. Odin claimed the Christian apocalypse had stolen the idea of a final battle. Zeus pointed out that nearly everyone had stolen the flood. Ra said the sun going out was classic, and if it wasn’t broke, don’t fix it. Anansi, who had come because he could not resist a meeting, stole the minutes twice and sold them back once.

At the back of the Concourse, unnoticed, stood a god with no name.

It had no temple. It had no priests. It had no myth that anyone bothered to tell around a fire. It was not the god of death or war or harvest or love. It was the god of the almost: the prayer that died in the throat, the hand that almost reached out, the person who looked at the sky and said nothing. It was the kindness done in secret. It was the apology never spoken. It was the chance to stop that was not taken. It existed because the world is full of things that are never claimed, and something has to keep them.

No one had ever worshiped it. No one had ever cursed it, either. It simply stood there in a coat made of unsent letters and listened.

Finally, it spoke.

“I have never been worshiped.”

The hall did not fall silent at once. Gods are slow to notice quiet things. But the voice was strange—made of all the swallowed prayers, all the stopped confessions—and it carried. One by one, the pantheons turned.

Zeus squinted. “Who let you in?”

“No one,” said the god. “That is rather the point.”

“You have no cult,” said Odin. “No chosen people. No final battle.”

“No apocalypse,” it agreed. “And that is why I would like to speak.”

Shiva smiled, which was not necessarily reassuring. “Speak, then, little maybe.”

The god of the almost looked around the table at the assembled makers of endings. “You have spent three hundred years arguing over whose ending is truest. Odin says his is brave. Zeus says his is moral. Ra says his is inevitable. Shiva says his is already happening. You have argued over whose followers deserve to be saved, whose rituals are correct, whose monsters are the most impressive. But none of you have asked the world.”

“The world does not vote,” said Ra.

“No,” said the god. “It has never been allowed to.”

It stepped forward. No one stopped it. It had no worshippers to offend, no temples to defend, no prophecy to fulfill. It was, in a way, the freest thing in the room.

“I am the god of the people who never prayed to you,” it said. “The ones who looked at the sky and felt nothing. The ones who were told their grief was too small for a god. The ones who lived and died without a single ceremony. The ones who almost believed, and then didn’t. The ones who were saved by a stranger and did not know who to thank. I have no ending written for me. No one ever thought I was important enough to destroy.”

A murmur went through the pantheons. Some sounded offended. Some sounded ashamed.

“You want to know why your end of the world should happen?” the god continued. “Because you are afraid. You are afraid that no one will tell your stories anymore. You are afraid that the last temple will close and the last prayer will go unanswered. You are afraid of being forgotten. So you have decided to end everything, because an ending is at least a kind of attention.”

“Careful,” said Odin, low.

“I am being careful,” said the god. “I am the only one here who is. You are all compromised. You owe your worshippers endings. You owe them floods and fires and final battles. I owe no one anything. I am the god of the people who never asked you for anything. And they are the majority. They will be ended without a ceremony. They will not be counted in your songs. They are the ones you keep leaving out of the last day.”

Quetzalcoatl shifted his feathers. “And what would you have us do?”

The god of the almost considered the question as if it were a small, frightened animal.

“If you must have an Armageddon,” it said, “let it be this: the end of gods who need the world to end to prove they mattered. Let the sky stay up. Let the dead star keep its silence. Let the world continue without your permission. The only true end is the end of needing to be right.”

For a moment, no one spoke. The cosmic machinery behind the Concourse—the great clock of last things, the loom of fates, the ledger of ends—whirred and clicked. It had been built to process a single apocalypse. It had forms for fire and flood and wolf and serpent and earthquake. It had no form for “none.”

“You cannot vote,” said Zeus at last. “You have no worshippers.”

“That is why my vote counts,” said the god. “I am the only one here who does not need you to remember me.”

It raised its hand. There was no lightning. No thunder. No choir. Just a small, quiet motion, like a hand closing around nothing.

“I vote for none,” it said.

The great clock stopped. The loom snagged. The ledger of ends found no page with that word on it, and so the end could not be filed.

The gods argued for another hour, then another day, then another century. But the machinery would not turn. An apocalypse requires a claimant. It requires someone to say, “This is the true end, and it is mine.” And the only claimant willing to speak for the unworshipped, the uncounted, the almost, had said no.

Eventually, the pantheons began to leave. Odin went first, grumbling about wasted time. Zeus left in a shower of sparks and wounded dignity. Ra set the sun on a low flame and went home. Shiva danced once, briefly, and then was gone. Anansi stole the last page of the minutes and vanished.

Amaterasu, who had said little all along, paused before the forgotten god. She did not bow. She simply nodded, once, as one light to another.

Then the Concourse was empty.

The god of the almost stood alone on the dead star, in its coat of unsent letters. The time of Armageddon had passed. It had not been defeated. It had simply been forgotten—which was, perhaps, the one thing it had always known how to survive.

And the world went on. Messy, unfinished, full of people who looked at the sky and said nothing. The god of the almost returned to its small work: sitting beside a hospital bed, standing in the pause before a confession, waiting in the silence after a disaster. It was never worshiped. But every now and then, someone said “thank you” to no one in particular, and the god of the almost heard, and smiled, and whispered back:

“Not yet.”

prompt: Write a good fight scene .
content:
The rain fell in sheets, turning the neon-drenched alley into a blurred watercolor of violence. Kael stood at the far end, the hood of his worn coat pulled low, the rain tracing cold fingers down his neck. He wasn’t hiding. He was waiting.

The man who stepped out from the deeper shadows was a mountain given life. His name was Garrick, and his reputation was a litany of broken bones and shattered lives. He was a head taller than Kael and twice as wide, a slab of muscle and malice clad in a reinforced leather jacket that creaked with his movements.

“You’re a hard man to find, Kael,” Garrick’s voice was a low rumble, like rocks grinding together.

“Not really,” Kael replied, his own voice quiet. “I’m just a good listener.” He’d heard Garrick was looking for him, and he’d chosen this place. A dead end. No witnesses, no escape routes for either of them.

Garrick cracked his knuckles, a sound like snapping twigs. “The boss wants what you took. Give it back, and I’ll make it quick.”

Kael’s eyes, the color of a stormy sea, never left Garrick’s. “I don’t have it.”

“Then you’re no use to me,” Garrick said, and lunged.

For a man his size, his speed was terrifying. He closed the distance in two ground-eating strides, a massive fist swinging like a wrecking ball aimed at Kael’s head. It was a blow meant to end a fight before it began.

Kael didn’t try to block it. He dropped, his body folding with a fluid grace, the fist whistling through the space his head had occupied a heartbeat before. Using the momentum, Kael pivoted on his heel, his leg sweeping out in a low arc. The kick connected with the back of Garrick’s knee. It was like striking a concrete pillar. The big man stumbled, a flicker of surprise in his piggish eyes, but he didn’t go down.

Garrick snarled, backhanding with a fist the size of a ham. Kael threw his forearms up to guard, but the force was staggering. The impact drove him back, his boots skidding on the wet asphalt, sending a shockwave of pain up his arms. He tasted blood from a split lip.

The first exchange was over. The first lesson was learned: don’t trade blows with the mountain.

Garrick grinned, a predator’s smile. He advanced again, more cautiously this time, his hands up in a boxer’s guard. He threw a jab, then a cross. Kael weaved and bobbed, slipping the punches by inches. The air crackled with the force of Garrick’s missed strikes. He was a force of nature, but a predictable one. His style was all power, all forward pressure.

Kael needed to be a different kind of animal.

He feinted left, then darted right, landing a sharp kick to Garrick’s thigh. It was like kicking a tree trunk. Garrick grunted, more annoyed than hurt, and answered with a looping hook. Kael ducked under it, driving a stiff elbow into Garrick’s ribs. It was a solid hit, but it felt like he’d just elbowed a leather-bound drum. Garrick barely flinched.

The big man grabbed for him, his hands like shovels. Kael twisted away, but Garrick was faster than he looked. He caught a handful of Kael’s coat, yanking him off balance. A knee, harder than a sledgehammer, slammed into Kael’s stomach.

The world exploded into white-hot agony. All the air left his lungs in a silent scream. He doubled over, and a hammer-fist came down on his back, driving him to his knees in a puddle of oily water. He could feel the grit of the pavement against his cheek, the taste of copper and regret filling his mouth.

“You’re quick, kid,” Garrick’s voice boomed from above. “I’ll give you that. But you can’t win a war of attrition with an army.”

He was right. Another hit like that, and it was over. Kael’s vision swam. He saw Garrick’s boot pull back for a kick that would shatter his ribs. It was the finality of the move that saved him. Garrick was committing to it, putting his whole weight behind it.

Kael didn’t try to get up. He rolled.

The boot slammed into the pavement where his chest had been, spider-webbing the asphalt. The shock must have gone right up Garrick’s leg. He roared in frustration and pain, momentarily off balance.

It was the opening Kael needed.

He surged upward from the ground, not with a punch, but with his entire body. He drove his shoulder into Garrick’s midriff, wrapping his arms around the giant’s waist. He wasn’t trying to knock him over; he was trying to anchor himself. He drove his head up, connecting with Garrick’s chin in a savage headbutt.

Garrick staggered back, his head snapping up. For the first time, there was real pain in his eyes. His grip on Kael loosened.

Kael didn’t let go. He held on, raining short, brutal elbow strikes into Garrick’s face and neck, using his smaller frame to its advantage, denying the bigger man the leverage for a full swing. It was ugly, close-quarters, and desperate. It was fighting dirty, and it was the only way.

Garrick roared, grabbing Kael by the hair and trying to pry him off. He succeeded, throwing Kael backward. Kael stumbled, his back hitting the brick wall of the alley.

Garrick charged, a bull seeing red. A massive, wide-swinging haymaker came at Kael’s head, a punch that would have decapitated a lesser man.

Kael didn’t dodge. He ducked, letting the fist slam into the brick wall with a sickening crunch of knuckles. Garrick screamed, a sound of pure, primal rage and pain. His hand was a ruined mess.

Now. It was his only chance.

Kael exploded forward. He wasn’t thinking anymore, his body a vessel for months of training and fury. He drove a knee into Garrick’s injured hand, a short, sharp blow that made the giant gasp. Then, as Garrick’s body curled protectively, Kael launched a blistering combination.

A jab to the eye. A right cross to the already-broken nose. A left hook to the jaw. Each blow was precise, aimed at the vulnerable points he’d cataloged in the first few seconds of the fight. A liver shot that folded Garrick over. A knee to the face that snapped his head back.

Garrick, for all his power, was a house with a faulty foundation. Kael was a sledgehammer, tapping at the cracks.

The big man was swaying now, his eyes glassy, his breath a wet, ragged rattle. His hands were down. He was done.

Kael stepped in with one final, cold purpose. He put his entire weight behind a final right hook, pivoting his hips, his fist a piston of bone and will. It caught Garrick flush on the temple.

The mountain finally fell.

Garrick crumpled, a controlled demolition, his body hitting the ground with a heavy, final splash. The rain continued to fall, washing the blood from the asphalt, drumming a soft rhythm on the fallen giant’s leather jacket.

Kael stood over him, chest heaving, every nerve on fire. His knuckles were raw, blood mingling with the rain. He spat a glob of red onto the ground and looked down at the man who was supposed to be an army.

He was just a man. A big, brutal man. But a man.

Kael turned and walked away, his silhouette melding into the rain and the neon glow. He was still a hard man to find. But now Garrick knew where he was. He was the one walking away.

prompt: Death comes to collect someone and ends up falling in love with them .
content:
# The Last Jar of Honey

Death arrived at Maren Halsey’s orchard at 4:17 p.m. on a Tuesday, exactly as the ledger said.

She was in the apiary, veiled and gloved, humming to a hive. She did not turn around. “You’re early,” she said.

“I am never early.”

“Then I’m late.” She lifted her veil. Her face was pale, tired around the eyes, but her gaze was the color of wild honey. “Kettle’s on. I have three jars to finish before I’m ready.”

Death had collected saints and soldiers, liars and lovers. He had never been invited to tea. He should have refused. But she walked toward the cottage, and he followed.

Inside, she poured two cups and set one before him. “I know why you’re here,” she said. “The doctors gave me six months. I got eight. I consider that a win.”

He said nothing. The ledger in his coat pocket had her name written in careful black script: *Maren Halsey, beekeeper, thirty-four.*

“I’m not afraid,” she said, though her hands trembled a little around her cup. “I just hate unfinished things.” She nodded toward the table, where three jars stood beside a book of recipes. “Sit.”

He sat. He had no weight in most worlds, but her chair held him.

She talked about bees. How a hive survives winter by eating summer. How workers die when they sting. How the queen is not really in charge at all. Death listened. He usually arrived at the final sentence of a life. He had never heard the whole story.

She laughed at her own joke about the spring a swarm had filled the village chapel with honey, and something inside him turned over, like a key in a lock long rusted.

The next evening, he came back. “Paperwork,” he said.

“Paperwork,” she repeated. “You’re a terrible liar.”

He helped her carry jars. He stood in the orchard while bees landed on his hands and did not sting. “They know,” she said. “Bees always know what’s coming.”

By the third day, he loved her. It was impossible and absurd. He was a function, not a man. But she made him feel like a man. He wanted to hear her laugh. He wanted to pour her tea. He wanted to be the last thing she saw, and he hated himself for it.

On the fourth evening, she was weaker. She sat by the window with a blanket around her shoulders. “You haven’t taken me,” she said. “Why?”

“I don’t know.”

She smiled. “You do.”

He knelt beside her. “If I take you, I lose you. If I don’t, you suffer. I am not supposed to love. It is not in the ledger.”

Maren touched his face. Her hand was warm. “I love you too,” she said. “Which is why you have to take me now, while I can still say it.”

He shook his head. “I can’t.”

“You can,” she said. “Do it gently. And don’t go away.”

So Death did the hardest thing he had ever done. He gathered her in his arms—not as a collector, but as a lover. He felt her last breath against his neck. He lifted her soul out of her body, bright as a lantern. The orchard hummed. The bees rose in a golden cloud.

At the threshold between worlds, Maren stopped. “You’re not coming?”

“I’m Death,” he said. “I cannot.”

She took his hand. “Then stop.”

And because he loved her, he did. He set down the ledger. He let the office of Death fall from his shoulders like a heavy coat. Somewhere, a new collector picked up the book. The bees settled. The orchard grew quiet.

Maren smiled. “Come on,” she said. “I know a place with better tea.”

They walked into the light together.

And for the first time in the history of endings, Death was not the last to leave. He was late, because he had stopped to fall in love.

content:
# The Names We Carry

On the transport to Vey, Corporal Kael Renn read his orders three times.

**SPECIAL DIVISION INFANTRY, NECROMANCER CLASS.**

Below that, in smaller type: *Attach to 4th Line Squad, Bridge Defense. Authorized to reclaim fallen personnel under field command. Not authorized to retain personal effects. Not authorized to ask questions.*

The man across from him, Sergeant Voss, had a face like a brick that had seen too many walls fall on it. He looked Kael over, noted the chalk-white stitching on his coat and the bone-handled knife at his belt, and grunted.

“So you’re the corpse-wrangler.”

“Reclamation specialist,” Kael said.

“Right.” Voss jerked a thumb at the others. “That’s Miri, Dane, and Oz. Oz is our medic. Try not to make his job harder by dying in a way that lets you reanimate yourself. I’ve read the regs. It’s technically possible and absolutely nobody wants to see it.”

Private Miri leaned forward. She was young enough that her helmet looked borrowed. “Can you raise animals?”

“Only if they died recently and owed the Crown money,” Kael said.

Dane snorted. Oz didn’t laugh. Oz had the tired eyes of a man who had already seen what a necromancer could do to a battlefield and had decided he preferred ordinary corpses.

They reached Vey at dusk. The city was burning in that slow, patient way that meant it had been burning for days. Saint Orra Bridge spanned the black river at the eastern edge, and beneath it the evacuation convoy crawled like a line of ants carrying their own weight in fear. The Chorus was coming. The enemy always came in waves—pale, wire-mouthed things that had once been people and now moved like one animal wearing too many bodies. When they died, their corpses sometimes got up again on their own. The Special Division had a solution for that.

Kael was the solution.

He showed the squad his left forearm. Names were written there in ash ink, from wrist to elbow. Some were faded. Some were fresh.

“Rule one,” he said. “I don’t raise anyone who asked not to be raised. Rule two: if I raise you, you follow your last order until you fall again. Rule three: don’t ask what it costs.”

“What does it cost?” Miri asked.

Kael didn’t answer. He rolled his sleeve down.

The first wave hit at 0340.

The Chorus came out of the smoke in a loose crescent, shrieking without voices. Voss put them in a fighting withdrawal across the bridge. Rifles cracked. Miri fired until her barrel glowed. Dane lobbed grenades over the concrete barrier. Oz dragged a screaming soldier behind cover and got to work with steady hands.

Kael stood apart, chalk in one hand, knife in the other. He was not there to shoot. He was there to wait.

The first dead was a Chorus fighter, skinny and broken at the bottom of the barricade. Kael crouched, pressed two fingers to its forehead, and spoke its true name. He didn’t know how he knew it. That was the class. The dead told you their names if you listened right.

The corpse shuddered. Its eyes went wet and glassy. It stood.

“Hold the left line,” Kael said.

It walked forward, picked up a fallen rifle, and emptied it into the Chorus before a second wave tore it apart. Kael felt the cost like a tooth pulled from the back of his skull. A memory went with it—something small, blue, a kitchen window. He didn’t know whose kitchen. He wrote the Chorus fighter’s name on his arm anyway, because the dead deserved to be carried even if he couldn’t remember why.

By dawn, the squad was down to half.

Miri died first.

A Chorus thing came over the barrier and drove a bayonet through her throat. She made a wet sound, tried to say something, and then her eyes went still. Voss stared at her for one second. Then he looked at Kael.

“Can you?”

“She didn’t say no,” Kael said.

He hated himself for that. He knelt, pressed his fingers to her forehead, and said her name. Miri rose. The wound in her throat gaped, but her hands were steady on her rifle. For a moment—just a moment—her face turned toward Kael like she was trying to remember him too.

“Miri,” he said. “Cover the east side.”

She nodded. Then she turned and killed six Chorus before a grenade took her legs out from under her. She kept firing from the ground until her body stopped responding.

Kael lost the memory of his mother’s kitchen. Not the window. Something else. He didn’t know what he’d lost until it was gone, and that was the worst part.

Oz died at noon. Dane died at 1310. Kael raised them both because Voss asked and because the bridge was still full of civilians and because there was no one else left to hold the line. Oz came back with his medic bag still on his shoulder and stitched up a living soldier with dead hands. Dane came back laughing, though no sound came out, and charged the Chorus with a knife in each fist.

Kael forgot his first snowfall. He forgot his favorite song. He forgot the face of a woman he thought might have been his sister. He wrote the squad’s names on his arm in careful letters.

At 1500, the evacuation horn sounded. The last convoy was across. Voss had a hole in his side and a detonator in his hand. The bridge charges were wired. All they had to do was blow them.

“Get to the far side,” Voss said. His voice was wet. “I’ll cover you.”

“You can’t cover anything,” Kael said.

“I know.” Voss looked at the detonator. “But I can push the button. You raise me, I walk over there, I push it. That’s an order.”

“You’ll be dead.”

“That’s what the class is for, isn’t it?”

Kael wanted to argue. He wanted to say that there was a difference between using the dead and using *this* dead. But Voss was already bleeding out, and the Chorus was coming over the barricade in a gray tide, and the names on Kael’s arm were getting heavier by the minute.

Voss died at 1503. Kael said his name at 1504.

The sergeant rose with his jaw set and his eyes like dirty water. He took the detonator. He walked toward the charge box at the center of the bridge, and the Chorus swarmed him, and he kept walking. Kael watched him press the button.

The bridge went up in a white flash.

Kael woke in a field hospital three days later. His ears rang. His arm was bandaged. A clerk sat beside the cot with a clipboard and a bored expression.

“Name?”

Kael opened his mouth. Nothing came out.

The clerk waited. Then he sighed and tapped the pen against the clipboard. “Corporal. Your name.”

Kael looked down at his left forearm. The bandage covered most of it, but the names were still there, inked in ash and dried blood. He read them aloud.

“Voss. Miri. Dane. Oz.”

The clerk wrote it down. “That’s four. I need yours.”

Kael stared at the clipboard. He tried to reach for something—a kitchen window, a first snowfall, a song, a woman’s face—but there was nothing there. Just names. Just the dead, carried on his skin like a map.

Then he saw the last line, small and crooked, written near his wrist in his own hand.

*Kael Renn.*

“Kael Renn,” he said.

The clerk stamped the form. “Clear for duty. Special Division Infantry, Necromancer Class. New squad assembles at 0600.”

Kael lay back and closed his eyes. Somewhere outside, the war went on. Somewhere outside, the dead were waiting.

He would carry their names. Someone had to.

{prompt}
prompt: For as long as you can remember , you can hear background music appropriate to the situation you 're in . While going to the grocery store one day , you hear what sounds like the most generic JRPG battle theme you 've ever heard .
content:
# Battle Hymn of the Grocery Store

For as long as I can remember, my life has come with a soundtrack.

Not the cool kind, where I stride through fog while a synthwave bassline follows me. More like the universe hired a very literal intern to score my existence. Elevator rides got soft jazz. Awkward family dinners got a single, mournful cello. The one time I developed a crush on my mail carrier, the universe played something that sounded suspiciously like a romantic montage from a toothpaste commercial.

I’d learned to live with it. Mostly.

Then came the Tuesday I went to FreshMart for milk, eggs, and the good cereal that was on sale.

The automatic doors had barely hissed open when my usual background music—a pleasant, forgettable marimba loop—cut out. There was a moment of silence. Then a snare roll. A brass fanfare. A synth arpeggio that sounded like it had been generated by a computer that had only ever heard the phrase “generic JRPG battle theme” and was very proud of itself.

I stopped dead in the entrance.

No one else reacted. A man in a windbreaker selected a cantaloupe with the solemnity of a bomb technician. A toddler screamed for string cheese. The music kept looping: *da-da-da-DAAA, da-da-da-DAAA*, with a wimpy little heroic melody over the top.

I knew what this meant. The universe only played battle music when there was a battle. I once heard a tense boss theme during a dentist appointment, and the dentist found three cavities. I heard a victory fanfare after passing my driving test. I heard a sad violin when I opened a credit card statement. The system was consistent. The system was also very dramatic.

I texted my friend Mara: *Am I about to fight something?*

She replied: *Don’t buy the discounted sushi.*

Helpful.

I grabbed a cart. The music added a bassline. I went to dairy. The music added a danger sting when I passed the eggs. I checked behind the yogurt. Nothing. I went to frozen foods. The theme doubled in tempo. I gripped my shopping list like it was a sword.

Then I reached produce.

The music swelled. A cymbal crashed. I looked up and saw it: a spider.

Not a huge spider. Not a fantasy spider with eight glowing eyes and a health bar. A small, brown, leggy spider, descending from a bunch of organic bananas like it was being lowered into a boss arena. It was positioned directly over the only bananas I needed. My heart did a battle transition. My brain helpfully brought up a menu: *Attack. Magic. Item. Flee.*

I had no magic. My item was a single damp hand wipe. Flee was tempting, but the spider was between me and breakfast.

I grabbed a produce bag. It crinkled. The spider shifted one leg. The music shifted into a minor key. I knew what that meant: enemy turn.

I froze. The spider did nothing. The music looped impatiently. I realized the enemy turn was just me standing there like an idiot while a banana spider considered its options.

I grabbed a baguette from the bakery display next to me. Not to hit the spider—I’m not a monster—but to use as a distance tool. In JRPG terms, I had equipped a long sword. The spider remained unimpressed.

A produce clerk rounded the corner. His name tag said DEVON. The music did not change, but a second melody joined in, like a helper NPC arriving with a heal spell.

I pointed. “Spider,” I whispered, as if it could hear me.

Devon looked at the bananas. Then at me, holding a baguette like a warrior. “Oh, yeah. He’s been back there all morning.”

The battle theme swelled. I had discovered the boss’s name: *He*.

Devon didn’t seem worried. He grabbed a paper towel and a plastic cup, coaxed the spider inside with the calm of a man who had done this a hundred times, and carried it outside. The music held one final chord, then erupted into a four-note victory fanfare.

I expected a level-up screen. Instead, a woman asked me to move my cart.

I put the baguette back. I bought the bananas. I forgot the milk.

At checkout, the victory fanfare faded into the soft, polite jazz of a successful shopping trip. I felt heroic. I had faced the beast and survived. Then my phone buzzed. Mara had texted: *Did you defeat the grocery goblin?*

I typed back: *I leveled up in produce.*

The automatic doors opened, and a cheerful end-credits theme started—rising flutes, gentle strings, the whole “you saved the world” package. I walked to my car feeling great.

Then I realized I’d left my reusable bags in the cart. The music cut to a sad trombone.

I went back inside. The battle theme started again.

I looked around. There was another spider.

It was going to be a long campaign.

{prompt}
prompt: You have been kidnapped by a cult that holds a famous novel as its sacred text . The cult 's leader explains what lies in store for you .
content:
The first thing I registered was the smell. It wasn't damp or musty, as I might have expected from a cult's basement. It was the smell of salt and old paper, a dry, briny scent like a library built inside a ship. I was tied to a wooden chair, the ropes biting into my wrists, the grain of the wood pressing into my back. A single, naked bulb hung overhead, casting a jaundiced light on a room lined with bookshelves. They were all filled with the same book. Hundreds of identical copies of *Moby-Dick*.

My head throbbed. The last thing I remembered was leaving the university library after a late night of research. A sharp pain at the back of my neck. Then nothing.

The heavy door to my left groaned open, and a man entered. He wasn't what I pictured when I thought of a cult leader. No wild eyes or flowing robes. He was a man in his late fifties, perhaps, with a neat gray beard and a tweed jacket with leather elbow patches. He looked like a professor of literature, which, in a way, I suppose he was.

"Ah, you're awake," he said, his voice calm, almost gentle. He pulled up a simple wooden stool and sat before me, his hands clasped loosely in his lap. "I apologize for the headache. Silas is not always as gentle as he could be. He's a harpooner, you see. A man of direct action."

He smiled, a thin, knowing smile that didn't reach his pale blue eyes. "My name is Ahab."

I stared at him, my mind racing. "Ahab? Like...?"

He chuckled softly. "A chosen name, of course. We all take names from the Book when we are called. It helps us remember our purpose. I am the steward of this congregation, the First Nantucketer. And you, my friend, have been brought here for a very special purpose."

My throat was dry as dust. "Where am I? What do you want?"

"You are aboard the *Pequod*," he said, gesturing to the room around us. "And what we want... well, that's a more complex question. It's about what the *Book* demands of us. You see, we are not a cult. We are a crew. And the novel you see around you is not merely a text. It is scripture. It is the map of the human soul."

He stood and walked to a shelf, running a finger lovingly along the spine of a book. "Most people read it as a story of obsession, of a man battling a whale. They are children, playing at the water's edge. They miss the truth. The Whale, you see, is not just a whale. It is the ineffable, the unknowable, the great and terrible truth of the universe. It is God. Or, if you prefer, the Devil. It is the blank, white wall of existence that stares back at us."

He turned back to me. "And Ahab, our namesake, he was not a madman. He was the first true theologian. He understood that the only way to confront the divine is through an act of absolute, all-consuming defiance. The pursuit is the prayer. The obsession is the worship."

He paused, letting his words settle in the stale air. "We, the crew of this final *Pequod*, have dedicated our lives to the Book and its teachings. We seek our own White Whale. Our own ultimate truth. But every ritual requires a sacrifice. A witness. A... Queequeg."

His eyes fell on me, and for the first time, a shiver of genuine terror crawled up my spine. "You are a scholar of literature, are you not? You wrote a paper on the symbolism of the chase in the American novel. We have read it. It was... adequate. But a scholar is not a believer. You have studied the map, but you have never sailed the ocean."

He walked to a small table I hadn't noticed before, upon which lay a pristine copy of *Moby-Dick*, a heavy-looking logbook, and a curious collection of items: a small pot of black ink, a quill pen, and a bone-handled knife. The blade gleamed in the low light.

"The ritual is this," Ahab said, his voice dropping to a conspiratorial murmur. "You have one night to compose your own final chapter. Your own harpoon to hurl at the world. You will write your testament, a confession of your own futile chase, your own search for meaning in a meaningless cosmos. You will pour your soul onto the page for us to study, to learn from. We call it the 'Extract of a Testament'."

He picked up the knife, turning it so the light danced on its edge. "And at dawn, when the first light touches the sea, we will read your words. And then, with this blade, the one that will carve your confession from your corporeal form, we will ensure you understand the finality of the chase. To truly see the Whale, one cannot survive the encounter. Ishmael survived to tell the tale, but he was not the one who faced the beast. He was merely the epilogue."

Panic seized me, cold and sharp. "You're insane. You can't do this. People will look for me."

Ahab smiled his thin, sad smile again. "Of course they will. But the sea is vast, and the *Pequod* is very good at disappearing. Your disappearance will be a mystery, a lost ship on the vast ocean of human events. It will be... poetic."

He placed the knife carefully back on the table, next to the inkpot. "So, you see your task. Your purpose. You are not a victim. You are an instrument of our faith. You are Jonah, swallowed not by a whale, but by a story. Now, you must write your own way out. Or rather," he corrected himself, "you must write your own ending."

He gestured towards the table. "You have until dawn. The ink is a special blend. It will not fade. Make your words worthy of the Book. Make your obsession pure."

He turned and walked towards the door. Silas, a hulking brute of a man with a face like a slab of granite, stepped into the doorway, blocking my only exit. Ahab paused, his hand on the doorframe.

"One last thing," he said, looking back over his shoulder. "There is no key in this room. The door is solid oak. The walls are stone. But if you listen closely," he leaned his head, as if listening to the stones themselves, "you can hear the creak of the timbers. The sigh of the wind in the rigging. The ship is always moving. The chase is always on. Welcome aboard."

The door closed with a dull, final thud. The lock clicked into place. The only sounds left were the hum of the single lightbulb and the frantic, drumming beat of my own heart. I looked at the blank logbook, the quill, the knife. The ghost of a smile, thin and sharp and desperate, touched my own lips. I leaned forward, as far as the ropes would allow. I had a story to write. My own great, terrible, final chapter.

prompt: Terrestrial humans , as depicted by beings on other planets .
content:
# The Earthling Room

On the planet Oth, in the Museum of Received Things, the new exhibit had drawn a crowd from six star systems. The sign above the entrance read:

**TERRESTRIAL HUMANS: A RECONSTRUCTION, BASED ON 312 YEARS OF LEAKED BROADCASTS.**

Curator Ssara clicked her mandibles in satisfaction. She had spent forty-seven cycles assembling the model. It stood behind a glass wall: a tall, soft-bodied creature with two arms, two legs, and a surprisingly small amount of fur. Its skin was a pale synthetic beige. Its mouth was fixed in what the broadcasts suggested was a “friendly baring of bones.” In one hand, the model clutched a black rectangle. In the other, a leash.

At the end of the leash was a small, four-legged predator.

“Question,” said a gelatinous visitor from the moons of Vex. “Which one is the terrestrial human?”

“The tall one,” said Ssara. “Probably.”

“And the small predator?”

“That is a dog. We believe the dog is the dominant species. In every broadcast, humans follow dogs, carry their waste, and speak to them in high-pitched tones. The humans appear to be servants. Some scholars argue the dogs are gods.”

The visitor rippled thoughtfully. “And the black rectangle?”

“A parasitic organism. It attaches to the human hand and feeds on attention. The humans stare into it constantly. They speak to it as though it contains the souls of their ancestors. Occasionally, it makes a sound like a bird, and the human stops walking.”

A child from a methane-breathing species pressed against the glass. “Why does it show its teeth?”

“That is a smile,” Ssara said. “It is a signal of peace. We think. There is another signal, called a ‘scream,’ which is also a signal of peace, but louder.”

The child’s eye-stalks quivered. “Do they have emotions?”

Ssara hesitated. “The broadcasts suggest yes. They leak water from their eyes when sad. They also leak water when happy. Sometimes they leak water while watching other humans pretend to be sad. It is a complex cooling system.”

The exhibit continued. There were dioramas of human rituals. In one, a human sat in a small room, surrounded by glowing rectangles, pressing the same button over and over. The label read: **WORK: A FORM OF RITUAL SUFFERING, POSSIBLY RELIGIOUS.**

In another, a human stood before a mirror and took a picture of itself. The label read: **SOUL-CAPTURE: THE HUMAN ATTEMPTS TO PRESERVE ITS LIKENESS FOR THE GHOST-CHORUS.**

In a third, a human ate a meal while watching another human eat a meal on a screen. The label read: **COMMENSALITY BY PROXY.**

The visitors were delighted. They took notes. They argued about whether humans were dangerous, absurd, or sacred. A representative from the warlike Krellan Imperium suggested that the exhibit proved humans were too chaotic to be left alone. A poet from the Andromeda Reach insisted that any species capable of inventing both the laugh track and the nuclear weapon was clearly tragic.

Ssara listened. She had heard it all before. The problem was that no one had ever actually met a terrestrial human. The broadcasts were old. The signals were tangled. For all anyone knew, the humans had already erased themselves or evolved into something that no longer needed doors.

Then, midway through the afternoon, the museum’s deep-space receiver began to sing.

It was a new signal. Not a leak. A directed transmission. It came from the third planet of a small yellow star. The room went silent as the translation resolved.

A voice. Young. Slightly nervous.

“Hello? Is anyone out there? My teacher says we should say hello. We don’t know if anyone is listening. We’re humans. From Earth. We’re sorry about the advertisements. Please don’t judge us by our advertisements.”

The crowd stared at the speaker. The model human stared back, its plastic smile unwavering.

The child from the methane-breathing species whispered, “They know we’re watching?”

Ssara looked at the black rectangle in the model’s hand. She looked at the leash. She looked at the label that said **FRIENDLY BARING OF BONES.**

She reached out and switched off the exhibit’s laugh track.

“No,” she said quietly. “They only hoped we were.”

The next morning, the Museum of Received Things reopened the Earthling Room. The model remained, but the labels had changed. The dog was no longer labeled **DOMINANT SPECIES.** The black rectangle was no longer labeled **PARASITE.** The smile was no longer labeled **FRIENDLY BARING OF BONES.**

At the center of the room, where the dioramas had been, there was now a single chair facing a screen. The screen played the new message on a loop. A small sign beneath it read:

**TERRESTRIAL HUMANS: A SPECIES THAT DEPICTS ITSELF CONSTANTLY, AND HOPES SOMEONE OUT THERE IS WATCHING.**

**WE ARE.**

Ssara stood by the door as the first visitors arrived. The methane child came back, tugging at its parent’s tentacle. It stared at the empty chair for a long moment.

“Are they going to send another message?” it asked.

Ssara clicked her mandibles softly. “I think so.”

“Will it be accurate?”

“No,” she said. “But it will be theirs.”

{prompt}
prompt: In a world where simulations have become the norm , it gets increasingly difficult to tell the difference between simulation and reality . You 've just met the girl of your dreams , literally . Only thing is you ca n't tell if she 's real or a figment if the simulation .
content:
# Dream Logic

The tram stop was supposed to be a dead zone. No ad overlays, no status halos, no weather tags. Just a concrete bench, a flickering schedule, and rain that may or may not have been real. I stood under the awning, watching my HUD count down the minutes to my next shift, when she stepped out of the crowd.

I knew her.

Not in the way you know a face from the news, or a stranger from a recurring train car. I knew the exact tilt of her chin. The silver ring on her thumb. The small scar through one eyebrow that I had once traced with my mouth in a dream two nights ago, in a sleep-sim so detailed I’d woken up tasting rain.

She looked at me. “You’re the guy who dreams about me.”

My heart did something stupid. “What?”

“Sorry.” She smiled, and it was the same smile from the dream, the one that made the simulated sun feel warmer. “That was weird. It’s just—you looked at me like you recognized me.”

“I do,” I said.

Her name was Mara. She said it like it was a secret. She had no overlay, no floating ID, no social credit ticker. In a city where most people paid extra to have their breakfast annotated, she was aggressively unlabelled. That should have been a clue. It could have meant she was real. Or it could have meant she was a clean render, a black-market companion sim with all the metadata scrubbed off.

“You’re staring,” she said.

“I’m running a check,” I lied.

“On what?”

“Whether you’re a figment of my subconscious.”

She didn’t laugh. That was the first thing that made me nervous. Simulations always laughed at the right time. Real people sometimes didn’t.

We walked because neither of us had anywhere to be. The rain stopped on schedule at 4:15, and the streetlights came on with a soft chime. Every few blocks, my HUD pinged with reality-confidence scores: 87.4%, 91.2%, 89.9%. The numbers meant nothing. A good full-dive could fool the calibration patches. A great one could fool the patch that checked the calibration patch.

“Do you ever wonder if you’re the simulation?” Mara asked.

We were standing outside a bookshop that sold only physical paper, which was either a luxury or a trap. I looked at her. “No.”

“Liar.”

“Okay, sometimes. But I have memories. I have a job. I have a scar on my knee from when I was nine.”

“Simulations have scars,” she said. “They just come with backstories.”

I wanted to ask how she knew I dreamed about her. I wanted to ask why she had the same scar. I wanted to ask if she was an advertisement, a therapy construct, a leaked asset from my own sleep archive. Instead I asked, “What’s your earliest memory?”

She thought about it. “Being carried through a house that smelled like oranges. Someone was singing off-key. I couldn’t see their face.”

The answer was too specific. Too human. Or exactly specific enough to be written by an algorithm that knew I liked oranges.

We went to a null café three blocks down, a place with a Faraday cage built into the walls and a certificate on the door claiming 99.98% simulation-free. Inside, the menu was printed on paper. The chairs were uncomfortable. The coffee tasted like burnt water.

“This is real,” I said, tapping the table.

“Is it?” She wrapped her hands around her cup. “The certificate could be rendered. The discomfort could be a feature. The burned coffee could be a very committed designer.”

“You’re not helping.”

“I’m not trying to.”

We sat in silence. My HUD offered me a diagnostic: *Local Reality Confidence: 94.6%. Anomaly detected in companion identity verification.*

“I have an app,” I said. “It can tell.”

Mara looked at me for a long moment. Then she reached across the table and pressed two fingers to my temple, right where the HUD projected behind my eyes. “Can it tell you what you want?”

“Yes.”

“No, it can’t.” She withdrew her hand. “No one can. That’s the whole problem, isn’t it? You can check the world a hundred times a day and still wake up in a sim. You can fall in love in a null room and find out the null room was rented by a marketing firm.”

“That’s dark.”

“That’s Tuesday.”

I laughed. It felt real. She felt real. The coffee was terrible in a way that felt earnestly, clumsily real.

We left the café and walked until the city thinned out into service alleys and old tram lines. She told me about her sister, a dog she’d had as a child, a job she’d quit last year. I told her about my dreams. Not the ones where I met her—the other ones. The ones where I woke up and couldn’t tell if I’d been asleep. She listened without trying to fix it.

At the end of the line, she stopped under a broken streetlight. The rain had started again, or maybe it had never stopped. My HUD flickered.

*Reality confidence: 61.2%.*

“Mara,” I said. “If I asked you to prove you were real, what would you do?”

She took my hand. Her fingers were cold. “I’d ask you the same thing.”

“I don’t know if I’m real.”

“Neither do I.” She smiled, and it was the smile from the dream, but it was also just hers. “So we’re even.”

I could have run the check. I could have scanned her, flagged her, called a verification service, ruined the whole fragile thing before it had a chance to become a memory. For a second, I wanted to. The uncertainty was a splinter under my skin. But then she squeezed my hand, and the city hummed around us like a server farm, and I decided not to know.

“Blind mode?” I asked.

“Blind mode,” she said.

I switched off my HUD. The world lost its labels. No scores, no timers, no reality-confidence. Just rain, a broken streetlight, and a girl with a scar through her eyebrow, holding my hand like it was an anchor.

Behind her, the tram arrived. It had no driver, and its windows reflected nothing at all.

I didn’t look too closely. I just stepped on.

prompt: You meet the man you could have been , and found that you do n't like him .
content:
**Counterfactual**

I met the man I could have been in a Cracker Barrel outside Toledo, of all places. I was driving home for my father’s bypass, and he was standing by the hostess stand with a buzzer in his hand, wearing a navy quarter-zip and the exact expression I make when I think no one is watching. Same face. Same crooked left eyebrow. Same scar on the thumb from a lawnmower blade. He looked at me and smiled in a way I recognized from mirrors.

“You took the scholarship,” he said.

“I did.”

“I didn’t.”

That was enough. We sat down together.

He ordered sweet tea, meatloaf, no substitutions. I ordered coffee. He told me his name was Daniel, same as mine. He had stayed. He had taken over Dad’s HVAC business when Dad’s back went out. He had married Mara. Three kids. A house on the lake. Season tickets. He told me all of it the way a man reads a profit-and-loss sheet: bottom line first, details if necessary.

He asked about my life. I told him Chicago, copywriting, a small apartment, no kids, a divorce that had been over for three years and still showed up in my dreams. He nodded sympathetically, but his eyes were bright with something that looked like satisfaction.

“So you write ads,” he said.

“Copy, mostly. Some essays.”

“Must be nice, not having real responsibilities.”

I laughed. “I have responsibilities.”

He waved his hand. “I mean people. A family. A business. You can eat cereal for dinner and no one cares.”

“True.”

He said it was a shame I never came back. There was a lot of money in HVAC. He could use a guy like me. “You always were good with words,” he said. “You could sell a furnace to a snowman.” He laughed too loud. A woman at the next table looked over. He didn’t notice, or didn’t care.

I asked about Mara. He said she was fine. Then he said, “She got fat after the third one. But she’s a good mother.” He said it without malice, which was worse. Like he was describing a truck he’d gotten his money’s worth out of. I remembered Mara at eighteen, laughing with her whole body, drawing little stars on my Converse with a Sharpie. I remembered how close I’d come to staying for her. I didn’t like the way he talked about her.

He asked if I was seeing anyone. I said no, not really.

He said, “You know what your problem is? You always think there’s something better around the corner. That’s why you’re forty and alone.”

“I’m thirty-eight.”

“Same thing.”

He checked his phone. A notification from a ring camera. He showed me a video of his son shooting a basketball in a driveway. “That’s my boy,” he said. “Good jump shot. I’m gonna get him a trainer.” Then he added, “Not like you and me. We had to figure it out ourselves.”

I wanted to say: We are not the same. But we were, in the face, in the voice, in the way we both tapped our fingers when we waited. I could see exactly how he had become what he was. He had stayed because staying was easier. He had taken the business because taking it was expected. He had married Mara because she was there, and because it looked good, and because he didn’t know what else to do. Then he had spent twenty years telling himself it was a choice. Maybe it was. But he had made a small life and called it the only real one.

He asked if I was happy. I started to answer, but he kept talking.

“I mean, really happy. Not just busy. I see guys like you in the city, running on that treadmill. You think you’re free, but you’re just alone in a nice apartment with a plant you can’t keep alive.”

“I have two plants.”

He laughed. “There you go. That’s your problem. You make jokes.”

I didn’t like him. It wasn’t because he was successful. I didn’t mind that. It wasn’t because he had a family and I didn’t. I wasn’t sure I wanted one. It was because he was so certain. He had no questions left. He had closed every door inside himself and painted over them. He was a man who had confused comfort with wisdom.

And the worst part was, I could feel the shape of him inside me. That same urge to be right, to be settled, to stop asking. I could have become him so easily. I could have stayed. I could have taken the business. I could have married Mara and learned to talk about her like a used truck. I could have called my fear of the unknown “responsibility” and my smallness “contentment.”

We finished our food. He paid for both meals before I could. “Let me,” he said. “You can get it next time you’re in town.” He said “next time” like it was a promise and a threat.

We walked out together. In the parking lot, he shook my hand. His grip was dry and strong. “Good to see you, Danny,” he said. “Don’t be a stranger.”

I watched him get into a silver pickup with a decal on the back window: a little stick-figure family, a flag, a cross, a fish. He pulled out and drove toward the highway, in the direction of the life I hadn’t chosen.

I stood there for a long time.

When I got into my rental car, I called my sister. She asked if I was okay. I said yes. I didn’t tell her about the man. I didn’t know how. I just said, “I’m on my way.”

Then I sat in the car and looked at my hands. Same scar on the thumb. Same fingers. I put the car in reverse and backed out of the parking spot.

For the first time in years, I was glad to be going back to my messy, uncertain, unproven life. It was mine.

prompt: You caused the home team to lose the big game due to an absurd chain reaction that started from your seat in the crowd . No one knows exactly what happened except for you .
content:
The box score says the Port Avalon Comets lost Game 7 of the Coastal League Championship, 4–3, on a two-run homer in the top of the ninth. The box score is accurate. It is also a coward.

Here is what actually happened.

I was in Section 118, Row 12, Seat 9, holding a soft pretzel the size of a steering wheel and a tiny plastic packet of mustard. The Comets were up 3–2. There were two outs. The opponent’s batter hit a lazy, harmless pop fly to left field—the kind of ball a Little Leaguer catches while thinking about lunch. Danny Cruz, our left fielder, drifted under it. The whole stadium stood up. I stood up too, and because I was nervous, I squeezed the mustard packet.

It shot out of my fingers like a greased watermelon and skittered down the concrete steps.

That was the beginning.

The packet slid under the heel of a man in a “Gravity Is a Theory” T-shirt who was carrying two beers, a tray of nachos, and a foam finger roughly the size of a canoe. He stepped on it, his foot went out from under him, and he grabbed the nearest thing to save himself: an usher holding a tub of popcorn meant for the mascot. Popcorn went up like a geyser. A seagull—because there is always a seagull—dove into the popcorn. A woman in front of me shrieked and flung her souvenir mini-bat. The mini-bat cartwheeled down the aisle, through a gate some kid had propped open with his shoe, and bounced onto the warning track.

Danny Cruz saw the bat at the last second. He did a little hop to avoid it and kicked it into the on-deck circle. The on-deck bat boy flinched and dropped the cooler he was carrying. A neon-blue sports drink bottle rolled onto the grass, spun in a half-circle, and stopped exactly where Danny planted his left foot.

He stepped on it. His leg went sideways. He windmilled. The ball hit the heel of his glove, popped straight up, and fell out.

The batter was safe. The runner on first advanced. The next pitch left the park.

Final score: 4–3.

Bottom of the ninth, we went down in order. The stadium made the sound a stadium makes when it has been punched in the stomach.

Afterward, everyone had a theory. The announcers blamed the wind. The grounds crew got yelled at for leaving a bottle on the field. The vendor who dropped the cooler was fired. The seagull became a meme. The league reviewed the replay and concluded that Danny Cruz had “experienced an unfortunate loss of footing due to foreign debris.”

No one connected the mustard packet. It had been kicked under Row 10, stepped on twice, and carried into the men’s restroom, where it was last seen by a janitor who thought it was just another piece of trash.

But I know. I sat there with mustard on my thumb, my pretzel going cold in my lap, and I understood exactly what I had done.

I could have shouted. I could have waved. I could have run down the steps and thrown myself over the mustard packet like a hero in a war movie.

Instead, I whispered, “No no no no no,” and watched the Comets lose the pennant because I couldn’t hold on to a condiment.

prompt: The most beautiful woman in the world
content:
# The Most Beautiful Woman in the World

They crowned Beatrice on a Tuesday, though she hadn't entered any contest. The title arrived by certified mail, along with a sash, a crystal statuette, and a letter explaining that a consortium of mathematicians, cosmetic surgeons, and art historians had spent seven years developing an algorithm to determine objective human beauty. Beatrice had scored 99.8 out of a possible 100. The remaining 0.2 points were “reserved for the divine.”

She put the sash in a drawer. She put the statuette on a shelf, facing the wall.

By Friday, her face was everywhere. A paparazzo had climbed the fire escape of her apartment building and photographed her through the kitchen window, eating cereal in her bathrobe. The image went viral. Commentators analyzed her jawline, her symmetry, the precise ratio of her eyes to her cheekbones. A brand offered her a million dollars to endorse a toothpaste. A plastic surgeon wrote an op-ed arguing that her existence proved the tyranny of genetics. A philosopher on a late-night talk show said, “We have finally answered the question, ‘What is beauty?’ She is a woman in a bathrobe, eating cereal.”

Beatrice stopped eating cereal. She stopped leaving her apartment. She ordered groceries delivered and left them outside the door until the delivery person was gone. She grew thin. The algorithm had not accounted for that. The consortium issued a statement: “Beauty is not diminished by circumstance. The title is permanent.”

She moved to a cabin in the northern woods, where the nearest town had a population of eighty-two and no cell service. She wore a hood when she went for supplies. The townspeople, who had heard rumors, were polite but distant. They didn’t stare. They didn’t ask for selfies. They asked if she wanted extra eggs.

For two years, she was almost happy. She learned to split wood. She learned to bake bread. She learned that silence has a texture, like unbleached linen. She forgot what it felt like to be looked at.

Then a man named Elias arrived. He was a sculptor, gaunt and gray-bearded, with a white cane and a guide dog named Homer. He knocked on her door on a snowy evening and said, “I know who you are. I don’t care. I want to sculpt your face.”

“Why?” she asked.

“Because I’ve been asked to create a bust of ‘the most beautiful woman in the world’ for a museum in the city. I’ve refused three times. But I’m dying. This is my last commission. I need the money to pay for my dog’s hip surgery.”

Beatrice laughed. It was the first time she had laughed in months. “You’re blackmailing me with a dog?”

“He’s a very good dog.”

She let him in. Homer curled up by the fire. Elias sat across from her, his cane resting against his knee. He explained that he had been blind since birth. He had never seen a face. He sculpted by touch, by the geography of bone and cartilage, by the stories people told him about themselves. He had sculpted kings and beggars, and he had learned that a face is not a shape. It is a history.

“I will need to touch your face,” he said. “Every day for a month. I will not ask you to describe yourself. I will not let anyone photograph you. I will tell the museum that the sitting is private. They will have to wait.”

She agreed.

The first session was strange. He placed his fingertips on her forehead, her temples, the bridge of her nose. He traced the hollows under her eyes. He pressed gently on her jaw. He was silent for a long time. Then he said, “You have a face that has been touched by very few people.”

She flinched. “What does that mean?”

“It means you don’t blink when someone looks at you. You’ve learned to be still. Like an animal in the woods. You think stillness will make you invisible.”

She didn’t answer.

Over the next weeks, they talked. He told her about his childhood, about the shapes of his mother’s hands, about the first sculpture he ever made—a lump of clay that he had loved like a child. She told him about the algorithm, the sash, the statuette facing the wall. She told him about the paparazzi, the cereal, the philosopher. She told him things she had never told anyone, because no one had ever asked.

He touched her face every day. Sometimes he lingered on her cheek. Sometimes he laughed and said, “You’re frowning. I can feel it. Stop thinking about the algorithm.” Sometimes he said nothing at all, and she found the silence companionable.

At the end of the month, the clay bust was finished. He covered it with a cloth and said, “You can look now.”

She lifted the cloth. The sculpture was not a woman with perfect symmetry or a golden ratio. It was a woman with her eyes closed. Her mouth was slightly open, as if she was about to say something. There were faint lines at the corners of her eyes. Her hair was messy. She looked tired. She looked like someone who had been loved.

“That’s not me,” Beatrice said.

“It is,” Elias said. “It’s the you I felt. The you who laughs at bad jokes. The you who cries at the end of movies and then denies it. The you who splits wood like she’s punishing the wood.”

Beatrice touched the clay cheek. It was warm from the fire.

The museum unveiled the bust three months later. The public was outraged. This was not the most beautiful woman in the world. This was a plain woman with a crooked nose and a mole on her chin. The consortium issued a statement calling the sculpture “a tragic misunderstanding of objective beauty.” The tabloids ran headlines: “THE FACE OF FRAUD.” Elias’s commission was canceled. He didn’t care. He had already paid for Homer’s hip surgery, and Homer was now chasing squirrels in the yard.

Beatrice didn’t care either. She had moved into Elias’s cabin, which was larger than hers, and she had started teaching the local children how to bake bread. The townspeople still didn’t stare. They asked for extra eggs.

One day, a journalist tracked her down. The woman had flown in from the city, rented a car, and driven three hours on dirt roads. She found Beatrice in the garden, kneeling in the dirt, her hair tied back with a piece of twine. The journalist held out a recorder. “Can I ask you a question?”

Beatrice brushed the soil from her hands. “Sure.”

“What does it feel like to be the most beautiful woman in the world?”

Beatrice looked at the cabin, where Elias was arguing with Homer about whether the dog was allowed on the couch. She looked at the bread cooling on the windowsill. She looked at her own hands, which were calloused and stained.

“I wouldn’t know,” she said. “I’ve never seen her.”

content:
**The Match**

I met her on the night the old textile mill went up.

I was standing across the street with a paper cup of coffee, watching the smoke curl into the dark like a black ribbon. She appeared beside me without a sound, smelling faintly of gasoline and peppermint.

“Beautiful, isn’t it?” she said.

I should have walked away. Instead, I offered her my coat. Her name was Vera. She carried a matchbook from the Starlight Hotel, which had burned down years ago. I knew because I collected such things—matchbooks from places that no longer existed. She noticed me noticing.

“You’re one of those,” she said.

“What?”

“A watcher.”

She struck a match, lit a cigarette, and let the flame burn down to her fingers before shaking it out. I felt something turn over in my chest. I was a quiet man, a night auditor at a motel, with a drawer full of lighters I never used. She was the first person who saw the fire in me.

We spent three weeks together. She took me to abandoned places—a drive-in theater with a cracked screen, a church with a broken steeple, a warehouse full of mannequins missing hands. She never started fires while I was there. She just talked about them.

“Fire is honest,” she said. “It doesn’t lie about what it wants.”

I asked her if she set the mill. She smiled and didn’t answer. I should have called the police. I didn’t.

Then came the blackout. The city went dark, and she showed up at my door with a bottle of cheap wine and a box of matches.

“Tonight,” she said, “we’re going to make something beautiful.”

I knew what she meant. I told her no. She laughed.

“You don’t say no to this. You’ve been waiting your whole life to say yes.”

She was right. That was the terrible part.

We drove to the edge of the city, to an empty housing development that had been half-built and then abandoned. She had a plan. She always had a plan. I was supposed to be the lookout while she did the rest. But when she handed me the match, I couldn’t move. Not because I was good. Because I wanted to watch her more than I wanted to watch the fire.

She saw it in my face. She stepped close, pressed the match into my palm, and closed my fingers around it.

“Some men just want to watch the world burn,” she said, “and darling, you’re the match.”

Then she kissed me and walked away.

I stood there for a long time. The match was damp from my sweat. I could hear sirens in the distance, or maybe it was blood in my ears. I thought about the drawer of lighters, the years of smoke in my dreams, the way I’d always felt like a house waiting for a spark. I struck the match. It flared, small and orange. I held it up to the wind.

Then I blew it out.

I never saw Vera again. The development burned anyway, two nights later. They blamed faulty wiring. I went back to the motel. I still keep the drawer. But these days, when I smell smoke, I don’t think about the fire. I think about her, standing in the dark, telling me I was the match.

Some men just want to watch the world burn. I wanted to watch her. That was worse.

prompt: Universal real-time language translation seamlessly unites countries , cultures , and families together . It 's breakfast time , and for the first time ever - the translator is down . Your spouse and your children are unintelligble .
content:
**Unsubtitled**

For the first time in recorded memory, the translation service failed at 7:03 a.m. I know the time because my earpiece woke me with a dry click and a flat voice: TRANSLATION OFFLINE—GLOBAL OUTAGE.

My wife, Mira, was already in the kitchen. She turned from the stove and said something in Tagalog. It was lovely—rising and falling, warm as steam. I understood none of it.

“Good morning,” I tried. She frowned, pointed at my ear, then hers. I shrugged. She spoke again, slower, as if volume were the problem. Through the doorway came our children, eight and six, arguing in the two languages they used with friends and grandparents. My son’s words were a bright, fast stream of Mandarin; my daughter answered in something quick and bright that might have been Portuguese. They looked at me, waiting for arbitration. I heard only music and no meaning.

I rebooted the hub. I restarted the app. I held my earpiece up to the window like a fool. The screen said ETA UNKNOWN. The news feed said the same. For the first time ever, the world had gone quiet in every language at once.

Breakfast became charades. Mira pointed at the kettle. I poured coffee. She pointed harder. The kids pointed at cereal, milk, the toaster. My son held up two fingers; I gave him two pancakes. My daughter drew a sun in the air, then a bowl; I gave her yogurt. Mira laughed—the same laugh as always, no translation needed—and I felt my chest loosen.

But then she said something soft and serious, and I didn’t know. Her hand found my wrist. I realized I was afraid. Not of her, but of how much I’d outsourced to a machine. I didn’t know how to say “I’m sorry” in her language. I didn’t know if she was asking for the salt or telling me she loved me.

My daughter climbed down, found a marker, and drew a heart, a coffee cup, and all four of us holding hands. Mira wrote a word beneath the heart. I couldn’t read it. She tapped her chest, then mine. I understood anyway.

At 8:12, the earpieces chirped back to life. The kitchen filled with clean, familiar English. “You gave me coffee when I wanted tea,” Mira said, fond and exasperated. The kids’ voices split into instant sense. It was easy again. It was also a little sad.

I took out my earpiece. “Five more minutes,” I said. Mira didn’t need translation to know what I meant. She took hers out too. The kids followed. We ate burnt toast in the old, hard, human language of hands and eyes and syrup on our fingers. I pointed to the word she’d written. She said it slowly. I repeated it wrong. She smiled and said it again.

It meant *home*. I’m still learning how to say it.

prompt: Description of your favourite meal
content:
## The Blue Pot

The blue enamel pot had a chip on its lip the size of a thumbnail, and my mother refused to replace it. “That’s where the flavor gets out,” she would say, which made no sense and was also true.

I was standing in her kitchen after eleven years away, holding that pot. The apartment smelled of old paper and lemon cleaner. My mother sat at the table with a cardigan buttoned wrong, watching me like I was a repairman who had arrived without instructions. She had forgotten my name twice that morning and called me “dear” four times. I had come home because the nursing aide said the forgetting had quickened.

“I’m making adobo,” I said.

She blinked. “With the blue pot?”

“With the blue pot.”

That was the first sentence she had offered me all day that sounded like her.

My favorite meal has always been my mother’s chicken adobo with garlic fried rice, a runny fried egg on top, sliced tomatoes on the side, and sweet pickled papaya from a jar she saved for Sundays. The chicken braises in soy sauce, vinegar, whole peppercorns, bay leaves, and enough garlic to keep vampires and skeptics away. The sauce reduces until it is dark and glossy, sharp with vinegar but round with fat. The rice is leftover rice, fried in the same pan with chopped garlic until the edges turn crisp and gold. The egg is a fever dream of a yolk, broken over the rice so everything turns yellow. It is not a fancy meal. It is the meal I would choose if I had one dinner left on earth.

I chopped garlic while the chicken browned. My mother watched my hands. “More garlic,” she said.

“I already put in a whole head.”

“More.”

I put in another three cloves. She nodded, satisfied.

The vinegar went in last, and the kitchen filled with that stinging, bright smell that used to mean Saturday afternoon, and homework finished, and my father still alive, humming off-key in the other room. I waited for the sauce to reduce. I fried the rice. I flipped the egg and failed to keep the yolk intact, which my mother would have scolded me for once. Now she just looked at the plate I set before her.

“It’s your favorite,” I said, though I had meant it was mine.

She stared at the chicken, the dark sauce, the egg bleeding into the rice. She picked up her fork. She took a bite.

For a long moment, nothing happened. Then her eyes went wet, not sad-wet but surprised-wet, like someone finding a letter in a coat pocket they hadn’t worn in years.

“You didn’t burn the garlic,” she said.

I laughed. “I almost did.”

“You always almost do.”

We ate. She ate slowly, but she ate all of it. The kitchen clock ticked. Rain started against the window, soft and steady. I told her about the apartment I rented in another city, about my job, about the plant I had kept alive for three years. She listened and maybe understood some of it. When I finished, she pushed her empty plate away.

“You know what makes it good?” she asked.

“The blue pot.”

“No,” she said, with the particular scorn of a woman who had never once been wrong about food. “The vinegar at the end. You have to let it bite.”

I wrote that down on the back of an envelope, though I already knew it. Then I washed the pot, dried it, and put it back on the shelf with its chipped lip facing the wall, where she wouldn’t see it and worry.

The next morning, she called me by my name.

It was not a miracle. It was just a good day. But I made the adobo again anyway, with more garlic, and when the vinegar hit the hot pan, I breathed it in like medicine.
