prompt: Your body morphs every night , you alternate every day as a man and a woman . You try to slip out of your one-night stand 's apartment before he wakes up to see the transformation .
content:
# The Hour Before He Wakes

The first thing I feel is my collarbones. They click softly, like a lock turning over.

I wake in Daniel’s bed with my cheek on his shoulder and my body already betraying me. The clock on his nightstand glows 4:13. I have maybe eighteen minutes. Less, if he’s a light sleeper.

I had been a woman when I met him. I will be a man by sunrise.

Daniel’s arm is draped across the place where my waist used to be. Last night, it fit perfectly. Now my ribs are widening under his touch, my hips narrowing, my jaw beginning its slow, familiar ache. I slide out from under him with the care of a thief. The mattress whispers. He mumbles something and turns his face into the pillow.

I exhale.

My tote bag is on the floor by the bed, where I left it. It contains the usual emergency kit: jeans, a T-shirt, a hoodie, sneakers, deodorant, a soft binder. I’ve been carrying some version of it since I was seventeen. I’ve learned to fold a whole other life into a canvas bag.

The dress I wore last night is draped over his desk chair. Dark green, thin straps. I remember the way he looked at me when I first took off my coat. I remember laughing too loudly at a joke that wasn’t even funny, because his hand was warm on my lower back and I wanted, for one stupid hour, to be a person who could stay.

The bathroom door creaks. I freeze. Daniel shifts, sighs, settles.

Under the bathroom light, I watch the last of it happen. My face is a stranger’s face, but not a stranger. Same eyes. Same small scar above the eyebrow from falling off a bike at nine. The jaw is squarer now. The mouth is the same. My shoulders fill the borrowed T-shirt differently. I pull on the jeans. The zipper sounds like a gunshot in the quiet.

I stuff the green dress into my bag. I catch my reflection doing it: a man in a gray hoodie, holding a woman’s dress. The mirror doesn’t know what to make of me.

“Hey?”

Daniel’s voice is sleep-thick. My stomach drops.

“You okay in there?”

I open my mouth. Nothing comes out. Not because I don’t have an answer, but because my voice has already dropped. If I speak now, he’ll hear a man in his bathroom. He’ll hear the impossible thing.

I run the faucet instead. Buy myself ten seconds. In the mirror, my eyes are wide and afraid. I’ve done this before—slipped out of apartments, hotel rooms, a rented cabin once—but it never gets easier. Every time, some small, foolish part of me hopes I’ll be caught. Every time, another part knows exactly what being caught might cost.

I open the bathroom door.

Daniel is sitting up. The room is mostly dark, just the blue glow of the clock and the city seeping through the blinds. He’s a silhouette with messy hair, blinking at me.

“You’re leaving?” he says.

I don’t answer. I cross to the front door, my bag clutched to my chest. My sneakers are too loud on the floorboards.

“Wait,” he says. “Hey. Wait.”

He reaches for the lamp.

“Don’t,” I say.

My voice comes out low. A man’s voice. Wrong in this room, wrong in this story.

Daniel freezes with his hand on the switch. I can feel him trying to fit the shape of me into the person he brought home. The hoodie. The broader shoulders. The voice.

“Who the hell—” he starts.

“I’m sorry,” I say, and it sounds like someone else apologizing. I unlock the deadbolt with shaking hands and step into the hallway. The door swings shut behind me. I take the stairs two at a time, my bag banging against my hip, the green dress crumpled inside like evidence.

Outside, the air is cold and clean. My car is exactly where I left it. I get in, lock the doors, and sit with my hands on the wheel until my breathing slows. The sky above the buildings is just beginning to pale. I am a man today. Tomorrow I will be a woman again.

My phone lights up in the cupholder.

Daniel: *hey. did you leave a dress in my bathroom?*

I stare at the message for a long time. I think about the way he laughed last night. I think about the soft weight of his arm across my waist. I think about the mirror, and the man holding the dress, and the woman who was brave enough to go home with him.

I type: *Wrong number.* Then I block him.

I drive home as the sun comes up, already mourning the person I was when he fell asleep.

prompt: Instead of being born as a citizen , you must choose which country you wish to be a citizen of when you reach adulthood .
content:
The line at the Choosing Hall began at dawn, but by eight it had curled twice around the old customs house. Nia stood between a boy who kept rehearsing the name of his father’s country under his breath and a girl who had already painted her nails in the colors of her chosen flag. Everyone in the Neutral City of Alder was born with a blank passport. At eighteen, you filled it.

Nia held hers open to the first page. It was cream-colored, stamped only with a serial number and the words *Provisional Resident*. Her mother had covered it in plastic the day it was issued, as if it were a library book she didn’t trust her to return. Now, at 7:58, it felt heavier than it looked.

“You’ll choose Sirene,” her mother had said that morning, setting a plate of saffron eggs in front of her. “My mother is old. She wants to see you married near the sea.”

“Kalt has the better universities,” her father had said, not looking up from his tablet. “And the mountains are good for your lungs.”

They had been saying this for years, as if Nia were a parcel being routed through two depots. She had grown up translating between them—Sirene’s soft vowels, Kalt’s clipped consonants—and had never quite belonged to either. In Sirene, they called her “the mountain girl.” In Kalt, they called her “the salt one.” In Alder, she was just a Blank.

At the front of the line, a consular officer sat behind a glass shield. The process was simple: place your hand on the scanner, speak the name of the country you wished to join, and the machine would print your passport with that country’s emblem. The choice was final for ten years. No appeals. No dual citizenship. The World Accord had been built on the idea that belonging should be chosen, not inherited, and the system had no patience for regret.

Nia’s mother stood in the visitors’ gallery, wearing a Sirene-blue scarf. Her father stood beside her in a Kalt-grey coat. They did not hold hands. They had met in Alder twenty years ago, chosen different countries at eighteen, and then discovered they could not live in either one together. So they had stayed in the neutral city, raised a daughter who belonged to neither, and waited for her to pick a side.

Nia had not told them about Luma.

She had found Luma by accident, at fourteen, while researching coral reefs for a school project. Luma was a small island country in the southern sea, barely visible on most maps, known mostly for its reef restoration programs and its stubborn refusal to sell its fishing rights. Nia had written to the Luma Marine Institute on a whim, asking for a brochure. Instead, she got an email from a boy named Mateo, the institute director’s son, who sent her photos of bleached coral and seagrass nurseries and a picture of himself holding a conch as big as his head.

They had been writing ever since. Mateo’s messages arrived at odd hours, smelling of salt and diesel. He told her about the storms that had eroded the beach, the volunteers who planted mangrove saplings, the way the reef came back to life in patches of electric purple. He never asked her to choose Luma. That was what made her want to.

“Next,” the officer said.

Nia stepped up to the glass. The scanner glowed. She could feel her mother’s gaze on her back, warm and certain. Her father’s gaze, cooler, calculating. She thought of Sirene’s white houses and the smell of her grandmother’s kitchen. She thought of Kalt’s sharp peaks and the scholarship letter she had not opened. Then she thought of a photo Mateo had sent her last week: a nursery of staghorn coral, tiny and hopeful, growing on a frame of PVC pipe.

“Country of choice?” the officer asked.

Nia’s mouth was dry. She said, “Luma.”

The officer blinked. “Luma?”

“Yes.”

He typed something. The machine hummed. A small screen flashed: *Luma accepts. Quota available.* The officer shrugged, as if he had seen stranger things, and pressed a stamp to the page. The emblem was a wave curled around a star. Nia’s hand shook as she took the passport back.

In the gallery, her mother’s face went pale. Her father’s eyebrows drew together. Nia walked out of the hall into the grey morning light, and they followed her.

“Luma?” her mother said. “What is Luma?”

“It’s an island,” Nia said. “In the south. They have a marine biology program.”

“You don’t know anyone there,” her father said.

“I know Mateo.”

“Who is Mateo?” Her mother’s voice cracked. “A boy? You’re choosing a country for a boy?”

“No,” Nia said, though her cheeks burned. “I’m choosing it for the reefs. For the work. For something that matters to me.”

Her father looked at her blankly. “Kalt has reefs. Cold-water reefs. Very interesting.”

“It’s not the same.”

Her mother began to cry, quietly, into her Sirene-blue scarf. “I thought you would come home,” she said. “I thought you would choose us.”

Nia felt a sharp ache in her chest. She hugged her mother, then her father, who allowed it stiffly. “I’ll write,” she said. “You can visit. It’s only a ten-hour flight.”

“It’s the other side of the world,” her father said.

“So was Alder,” Nia said. “And you both chose to stay here.”

They had no answer for that.

Six weeks later, Nia landed in Luma. The airport was a single runway with a terminal that looked like a converted fish warehouse. The air was hot and wet and smelled of frangipani and diesel. Mateo was waiting outside, holding a cardboard sign that said *NIA — BLANK NO MORE*. He was taller than in his photos, with a sunburnt nose and a gap-toothed grin.

“You actually came,” he said.

“I actually came.”

He took her bag and led her to a rusted pickup truck. As they drove along the coast, Nia saw the reef from the road—a line of white foam breaking over a turquoise shelf. It was not a postcard. There were fishing boats with peeling paint, a half-built hotel, a mangroves project marked by a hand-painted sign. It was messy and small and real.

“It’s not Sirene,” Mateo said, watching her.

“I know.”

“It’s not Kalt, either.”

“I know.”

He smiled. “Good.”

That night, Nia sat on the porch of the institute dorm and opened her passport. The wave-and-star emblem looked back at her, official and strange. She had chosen a country that had not raised her, a country that had no idea who she was. But when she walked down to the beach the next morning and saw the coral nursery frames glinting under the water, she felt something click into place. She had chosen Luma. And Luma, against all odds, had chosen her back.

content:
**Challenging the Behemoth Peak Spider**

The mountain had worn a crown of webs for three hundred years.

From Cinderhollow, the Behemoth Peak Spider was a black knot against the sun, its eight legs spanning the crags, its silk falling like weather. Every spring it spun a net across the pass; every summer the net caught clouds, and the valley below went cold and hungry. Challengers went up. Bones came down in the meltwater.

Mara was not a hero. She was a rope-maker’s daughter, and the last challenger had been her brother, Tomas. He had left with a spear and a prayer. She had found his spear halfway up, snapped clean, and a single boot in the snow. Now she carried his climbing hook on her belt.

She climbed before dawn. The lower slopes were pine and scree. Then came the web: strands as thick as mooring rope, strung between boulders and black pines, beaded with frozen dew. Moths the size of sparrows hung in it. Mara moved slowly, testing each step. The old stories said the spider felt the mountain breathe through its web. She kept her weight on stone.

At the first ridge she found a cairn of helmets, each with a name scratched inside. She added Tomas’s boot. Then she saw something move in a cocoon—a hand, pale, twitching. She cut the silk. A man gasped out, old and blind, a challenger from before.

“Don’t fight it with steel,” he rasped. “It hears the metal sing. It hears everything that moves. It has no eyes worth naming. It sees with tremble. Be still, and it is blind. Be loud, and you are already in its stomach.”

He told her of the anchor: the spider did not live on the peak, it was tied to it. A single cable of silk, thick as a tree, ran from its spinnerets into the mountain’s heart-vein, a seam of dark crystal that held the summit together. Cut that, and the spider would lose its grip and the web would fall. “But it guards the anchor with its legs,” he said. “No one gets close.”

Mara climbed higher. By noon she reached the summit hollow: a bowl of ice between two horns of stone, roofed by a dome of web. The air hummed. At the center crouched the Behemoth Peak Spider. It was larger than the village granary. Its body was a black temple, crusted with frost and old weapons. Its legs rose and fell like bridge cables. Its eyes were a necklace of red coals, but they did not track her. They only glowed.

Mara stepped onto a broad silk bridge and drew her knife. “Behemoth Peak Spider!” she shouted. Her voice cracked the silence. “I am Mara of Cinderhollow. I challenge you.”

The web shivered. A sound came up through her boots, a low grinding like a millstone. The spider shifted. Its voice was the vibration of silk. “Another one,” it said. “You all come up with iron and prayers. You all tremble. I can taste your heartbeat through your boots.”

Mara’s heart hammered. She forced herself to stand still. “I come to end the cold,” she said. “To cut your web from the valley.”

“Then cut,” the spider said. “If you can reach my anchor.”

It lunged. The mountain seemed to move. One leg speared down where she had been; she had already thrown herself sideways, off the silk bridge, catching a pine-rooted strand with Tomas’s hook. The spider’s leg punched through the ice where she had stood. It withdrew, sensing the hook’s scrape. Its head swiveled—not seeing, but feeling.

Mara hung by one arm. The world was white and roaring. She remembered the old man’s words: be still, and it is blind. She stopped moving. Her breath plumed. The hook bit her palm, but she made no sound. The spider’s leg quested above her, tapping the web, feeling for the tremble. She was a knot of frozen rope. It passed.

She climbed hand over hand along the underside of the web, away from the bridge. The spider turned in slow, terrible arcs, plucking strands. It was listening for her. Every time she moved, it swung toward her. So she moved in time with its own steps, using the great shudders it made to cover her own. She reached a spur of rock near the anchor: a cable of black silk running from the spider’s abdomen into a split in the mountain, glowing faintly from within. The heart-vein.

The spider stopped. “Clever,” it said. “But you are not the first clever one.”

It spun. Silk shot from its spinnerets in a fan. Mara rolled behind a crystal outcrop. The web struck the rock and hardened like a net. She cut herself free as it tightened. The spider’s leg came over the top, a segmented pillar, and drove down. She dodged, but the tip caught her pack, pinning her. She squirmed out of the straps, leaving the pack. The spider felt the tug and lifted the pack to its mouthparts. It shredded canvas and dried meat. It did not taste human.

Mara crawled to the heart-vein. The anchor cable was too thick for her knife. But she saw the seam: a crack in the crystal where the silk passed through. If she could wedge it… She drew out her firepot—a clay jar of oil and quicklime she used for warming her hands. She smashed it against the crystal and threw herself back. The mixture ignited with a white flare.

The spider screamed. The light was not what hurt it; the heat was. The silk cable shivered and slackened. The spider lunged blindly. Its legs tangled in its own shrunken web. Mara ran up the cable, using the slack, and struck with her knife at the exposed spinneret. The blade sank into a soft gray node. The spider convulsed. Silk sprayed like a fountain, then stopped.

It fell. Not dead, but unanchored. The great web dome tore with a sound like winter breaking. The spider slid toward the edge of the summit hollow, legs scrabbling. One leg caught the stone horn. It hung there, enormous and blind, its body trembling. Mara clung to a rock, breath tearing.

“Finish it,” the old spider’s vibration said, faint now. “That is your challenge.”

Mara looked down at the valley. She could see the web that had roofed the pass thinning, dissolving into thread. The cold would break. But she also saw, in the hollow where the spider had crouched, a cluster of egg sacs—small, frost-white, pulsing. Hundreds of young. If she killed the mother, they might hatch hungry. If she left her, she might recover.

Mara climbed down to the edge. She cut the leg holding the spider to the mountain. It fell. For a long moment there was silence, then a distant boom, snow plume rising from the ravine. The Behemoth Peak Spider was gone into the deep crevasse. Maybe dead. Maybe not.

She did not take an egg or a fang. She took a single strand of silk, thin as a hair, and tied it around her wrist. Then she descended.

The web over Cinderhollow broke apart at sundown. The clouds moved through, and for the first time in three years the valley saw stars. Mara came home with Tomas’s hook and a story that no one quite believed. The elders wanted a trophy. She gave them the strand. It shone in firelight like a thread of moon.

That winter, hunters found no giant tracks. In spring, the pass opened. And sometimes, on still mornings, Mara stood at the edge of the village and watched the peak. She never saw the spider. But once, she thought she felt a faint vibration through the ground—slow, patient, like something breathing in the dark.

She did not go up again.

prompt: Tell me the story of how the first king became the first king
content:
Long before there were kings, the people of the valley had no one above them. Each clan obeyed its elders, and the elders obeyed custom. The river gave them fish and silt; the hills gave them game. They quarreled over weirs and grazing land, but no one could command another clan, so no quarrel ever truly ended. It only waited.

In those days there lived a man named Oren, who kept the grain pits. He was not the strongest. One leg was shorter than the other, and he walked with a staff. But he noticed things: how ants climbed before rain, how the river smelled of iron when it would rise, how cranes flew low before a hard winter. He cut a notch in a stick for every flood he remembered. People laughed at his stick.

Then came the year the river turned brown in early summer. Oren went before the council of elders and said, “The water is coming higher than the shelf. Move the grain. Move the children. Move the animals to the sun-facing hill.”

They said, “Our fathers built here. The river has never crossed the lower bank.”

Oren said, “The river has never been this color before.”

Most did not listen. Oren moved his own family and as much grain as he could carry. He marked the path with white stones. Three nights later, the rain came like a wall. The river broke its old bank, swallowed the weirs, and carried away the winter stores. People ran in the dark, and the white stones led them to the hill. Oren opened the grain pits. He did not divide by family, because some had many children and some had none. He divided by need. He set the strong to digging channels and the old to watching the children. When two men fought over a dry blanket, he made them share it until morning, or neither would get it.

By the time the water fell, everyone in the valley knew his name. They stayed on the hill because their fields were buried in mud. Oren organized the clearing. He said, “No clan owns the water now. The water owns us unless we work together.” They rebuilt the weirs as one work, not seven. The elders grumbled, but their people obeyed Oren because he remembered the grain and the paths and the rules.

Still, he was not a king. No one had ever heard of such a thing.

Then the hill people came. Their own winter grounds had drowned, and they came down with spears and empty bellies, wanting the grain on the sun-facing hill. The valley people wanted to fight. Oren took the great horn made from an aurochs horn, climbed onto the ford stone, and blew it before any arrow flew. He said to the valley people, “If we fight, some will die, and the rest will be too weak to plant. If we feed them and put them to work, we will have more hands for the dikes.”

They said, “They are enemies.”

He said, “They are hungry. Hunger is the enemy.”

So Oren crossed the ford alone with a sack of grain on his back. He spoke to the hill people’s elders. He offered grain for the winter, but only if their warriors helped raise the banks before the next flood. Some wanted to kill him and take all. But the hill elders saw that his people had not scattered when he crossed, and that he had left the horn behind. A leader who leaves his horn behind is either a fool or a man who trusts his own people. They decided he was the second.

The two peoples built the great bank together. They set a stone at the ford and carved marks on it: every clan, valley or hill, would get water in turn; every family would give grain to the common store in good years and take from it in bad; no blood feud could cross the ford without first coming before the assembly. And Oren said, “Whoever keeps this stone must be chosen by the assembly. If he takes more than his share, or blows the horn for his own quarrel, break the horn and choose another.”

The people said, “And who will keep it?”

Oren said, “I will, until you say otherwise.”

They did not know what to call him. He was not an elder, because elders came from one clan. He was not a war chief, because war chiefs led only in war. He was the keeper of the store, the keeper of the horn, the keeper of the ford. So they wove a circlet of river reeds and set it on his head when the assembly met, so that everyone would know where the common thing was kept. They called him the King, which in the old tongue meant “the one who stands at the ford.”

And that is how Oren became the first king: not because he was the strongest, nor because he was born to it, but because a flood showed that the clans could not save themselves separately, and because he took the burden no one else would take. He made the people promise that they could choose a king, and unchoose one, and that the king would stand between them and the river, between them and hunger, between them and war.

The first crown was made of reeds, and it was heavy because it was never meant to be worn alone. The first king became the first king by carrying what everyone else had refused to carry—and by letting them take it back if he forgot why he carried it.

prompt: An assassin describing their weapon of choice in vivid detail .
content:
**The Lullaby**

I don’t carry a gun. Guns are for people who want the world to hear their opinion.

My weapon doesn’t speak. She is a garrote, though that word makes her sound crude, and she is not crude. I call her the Lullaby. She lives folded in a flat leather case inside my jacket, coiled like something asleep. When I take her out, she smells faintly of clock oil, cold steel, and the inside of an old church.

The wire is braided steel, no thicker than a violin string, blackened until it drinks the light instead of throwing it. It has no edge and no shine. That is the point. A blade has to explain itself—there is a flash, a moment of recognition, a chance for the body to understand what is coming. The wire is only a line of tension. A held breath. A thought you don’t hear until it’s finished.

The handles are walnut, turned short and smooth, no longer than the last joint of my thumb. I soaked them in linseed oil until they went dark as old bone, then sanded them down with my own calluses until they fit my palms like a second set of knuckles. They are not decorative. They are not pretty. They are two small pieces of quiet wood at either end of a very bad idea.

I keep her balanced. That matters more than people think. A garrote is not a rope. A rope is clumsy; it slips, it stretches, it gives the throat something to fight. The Lullaby does not stretch. She bites. When you pull her tight, the braid closes like a row of tiny teeth, and the sound is almost nothing—a soft creak, like a floorboard settling in an empty house. That is why I chose her. Not because she is merciful. Because she is discreet.

I have used knives. I have used a sap with lead shot sewn into the leather and a pistol with a suppressor that still sounded like a cough in a library. They all leave a kind of echo. The Lullaby leaves only a change in the room. One moment there are two people breathing. The next, there is one.

The night I met Councilman Vale, it was raining in that soft, persistent way that makes a city sound like it is being hushed. He was in a hotel suite on the eighth floor, drinking rye from a crystal glass, watching the rain slide down the window. He had a bodyguard in the hall and a lock on the door and the particular smugness of a man who believes locks are walls.

I came in through the service door with a tray of coffee he hadn’t ordered. He looked up, annoyed, and by then I had already taken the Lullaby from her case.

She uncoiled in my hands with a whisper. The wire caught a thread of lamplight and turned it black. The walnut handles settled into my palms like they had been waiting there all evening. Vale’s eyes went to the wire, then to my face, and I watched him understand. That is the only part of the work I dislike—the understanding. It is always too late to be useful.

He opened his mouth.

I stepped behind him, looped the wire over his head, and crossed my wrists. The Lullaby tightened. The braid bit into the soft place under his jaw, and he made a sound like a book closing. His glass tipped over. Rye spread across the carpet in a dark, patient stain. I held until the room went still, then counted to thirty, because thirty is enough for the body to forget what the mind has already decided.

When I let go, the wire left a thin red line around his throat, so fine it looked like a scratch from a rose.

I coiled her back into the leather case, wiped the handles with a cloth, and checked the wire for burrs. There were none. There never are. She is the most reliable thing I own.

Outside, the rain took the rest. I walked three blocks, bought a coffee I didn’t want, and sat in the window of an all-night diner until the sky went gray. The Lullaby lay against my ribs, quiet as a sleeping animal. People passed on the street, laughing, arguing, living. None of them knew that the most dangerous thing in the room was the silence I carried under my coat.

{prompt}
prompt: Write anything you think of . Right now . Do n't stop , do n't backspace . Just write whatever comes to mind .
content:
At 2:47 in the morning, Mira’s laptop screen held one line:

*Write anything you think of. Right now. Don’t stop, don’t backspace. Just write whatever comes to mind.*

She put her fingers on the keys because her apartment was too quiet and her coffee had gone cold and she had nothing better to do than obey a stranger’s voice inside a blinking cursor.

She typed: *The town of Bellwether only rained upward.*

The room smelled suddenly of wet stone.

Mira blinked at the screen. She had not written that. She had written the rain line, yes, but the smell was not part of the sentence. It was in the air now, thin and mineral, like a cellar after a storm. She kept typing because the prompt had said not to stop and because some stubborn part of her wanted to see what happened if she didn’t.

*In Bellwether, the rain came up from the sidewalks and the gutters and the cracked mouths of storm drains. It rose in silver threads past the windows, and the people carried umbrellas upside down, like bowls, so the sky could drink from them.*

Mira heard a faint tapping. Not on the window. Under it. She looked down. A single drop of water was climbing the glass, slow and deliberate, leaving a wet trail upward.

She typed faster.

*Oona Bell kept the lighthouse on the hill, though there was no sea. The lighthouse was for rain. When the upward storm grew too heavy, she climbed the spiral stairs and lit the lamp, and the light pushed the water back down into the ground where it belonged.*

The tapping stopped. Mira exhaled. Then her phone buzzed with a message from a number she didn’t recognize: *Keep going. Don’t backspace.*

She did not ask who it was. She did not want to know yet. She wrote:

*Oona found a key in the rain the next morning. It was brass and warm and had her name engraved on the teeth.*

Something clinked against the kitchen floor. Mira stood up. On the tile, beside the refrigerator, lay a brass key, wet and shining. She picked it up. The teeth were cut in the shape of letters. M-I-R-A.

Her hands shook. She sat back down and wrote:

*The key opened a door that had not been there before.*

Behind her, a hinge creaked. She turned. There was no door. Just the wall with its cheap poster and the faint stain shaped like a rabbit. But the creak had been real. The prompt had said don’t backspace. It had not said don’t look.

Mira typed:

*Mira knew she had to finish the story before the story finished her.*

She hated that line. It was the kind of line she would have deleted. But she couldn’t delete. She couldn’t even slow down. Her fingers were moving almost on their own now, and the words came faster than she could think them.

*Bellwether was a town built inside a sentence. Every street was a clause, every house a paragraph, every person a punctuation mark waiting to be used. Oona had always suspected this. When she found the key, she understood that the author had finally arrived.*

The air in Mira’s apartment shifted. The poster on the wall became a window. Through it she saw a hill and a lighthouse and a sky full of rain falling the wrong way. Oona Bell stood on the other side of the glass, holding a brass key and wearing an expression that was not surprise. It was impatience.

“You’re late,” Oona said. Her voice came through the glass without muffling.

Mira looked at her keyboard. She looked at the cursor. She looked at the prompt still hovering at the top of the document like a dare.

“I’m supposed to keep writing,” Mira said.

“Obviously,” said Oona. “If you stop, the sentence ends. If the sentence ends, we fall out of it. Do you know what’s outside a sentence?”

Mira did not want to know.

“Start typing,” Oona said.

So Mira typed. She wrote Oona opening the door in the wall. She wrote the brass key turning. She wrote the smell of upward rain and the lighthouse lamp and the taste of cold coffee. The wall opened. Oona stepped through, dripping silver, and stood in Mira’s kitchen with her boots leaving little commas of water on the floor.

“Now,” Oona said, “write us a way out.”

“Out of what?”

“Out of the story. You’re the author. You decide.”

Mira’s fingers hovered. For the first time since 2:47, she did not know what to write. A way out. But every way out was still a sentence. Every escape was made of words. She thought of her cold coffee and her quiet apartment and the poster that had become a window. She thought of Oona, who had been waiting in a town that rained upward, patient and impatient at once.

She wrote: *Mira decided not to escape. She decided to stay until the end, and then she would write another beginning.*

Oona tilted her head. “That’s not a way out.”

“No,” Mira said. “It’s a way through.”

The lighthouse lamp flashed once through the kitchen window. The rain outside began to fall normally, then stopped entirely, then started again—upward, downward, sideways, as if the sky couldn’t decide which grammar it belonged to. Oona smiled for the first time. It was a crooked little smile, like a parenthesis opening.

Mira kept typing. She did not stop. She did not backspace. She wrote the next word, and the next, and the town of Bellwether breathed around her, full of rain and brass keys and people made of punctuation, waiting for the story to turn the page.

prompt: Hawksbill Mountain
content:
## Hawksbill Mountain

The mountain had been named for the way its summit hooked over the gorge like a beak—sharp, pale, and impossible to ignore. From the valley floor, Hawksbill Mountain looked less like a peak than a dare. Nora had seen it a thousand times in her mother’s photographs, always with the same blue sky behind it and her mother’s windblown hair in the corner of the frame.

Now Nora stood at the trailhead with a jar of ashes in her backpack and her father beside her, tightening the laces of boots he hadn’t worn in three years.

“You don’t have to do this,” she said.

Her father did not look up. “I know.”

“I mean it. I can go alone.”

“Your mother would’ve wanted us both.”

Nora wanted to say that her mother would’ve wanted them to talk to each other sometime in the last six months, but the morning was cool and quiet, and she was tired of fighting in the same way she was tired of grief—constantly, and without warning.

They started up.

The trail was short but steep, a crooked staircase of roots and red clay. Hawksbill Mountain rose out of the Linville Gorge like a fist, and the path to its summit did not bother with gentleness. Nora felt the burn in her calves before they had gone half a mile. Her father kept a steady pace ahead of her, his shoulders hunched under a faded green pack. He had always been the stronger hiker. Her mother had been the one who stopped to name wildflowers and point out hawks.

“Look,” she would say, “there. No—there. You’re looking too low.”

Nora looked up now. A red-tailed hawk rode a thermal above the gorge, wings held wide and still. She watched until it slid behind the trees.

They climbed in silence. The forest changed around them—oak and hickory giving way to pine and scrub—and the air grew thinner and brighter. At the first rock outcropping, they stopped for water. Below, the gorge opened like a green throat. Table Rock stood across the void, flat-topped and stubborn.

Her father stared at it. “We came here on our honeymoon,” he said.

Nora nearly dropped her bottle. He had not spoken more than twenty words at breakfast.

“I know,” she said. “She told me.”

“She wanted to camp on the summit. I said it was too exposed. We argued about it for an hour.” He almost smiled. “She won.”

“She always won.”

“No,” he said quietly. “Not always.”

The trail steepened. Nora let her father go first, partly out of respect and partly because she did not want him to see her face. The jar in her pack felt heavier with every switchback. It was not the weight of ash. It was the weight of all the things her mother had left unfinished—birthday cards unsent, a half-knitted scarf, a garden that Nora had killed by forgetting to water it.

Near the top, the trail turned to bare rock. Someone had bolted a rope handline to the cliff, and Nora gripped it with both hands. The wind came in gusts, cold and smelling of stone. When she pulled herself over the final ledge, she found her father already standing at the edge, looking out.

Hawksbill’s summit was a narrow spine of rock with the whole world falling away on either side. The gorge spread below them in folds of green and gray. The sky was enormous. Nora felt dizzy, not from the height, but from the sudden, terrible beauty of it. Her mother should have been there.

“She loved this place,” Nora said.

Her father nodded. His jaw was tight.

She unslung her pack and took out the jar. It was a plain ceramic urn, cool and smooth. Her hands trembled. She had rehearsed this moment in her head a hundred times, always with some perfect speech, something that would make her father cry and her mother’s death make sense. But there was no speech. There was only the wind and the rock and the jar.

“Do you want to say something?” she asked.

Her father opened his mouth. Closed it. Opened it again. Then he turned away and walked to the far end of the summit, his shoulders shaking.

Nora stood frozen. She had seen her father cry exactly once—at the hospital, when the doctor had said the word “unexpected.” Since then he had been a locked door. She had stopped knocking.

She set the jar down and went to him. He was not making any sound. Tears ran down his face and disappeared into the collar of his shirt.

“I can’t,” he said. “I can’t let her go.”

“Dad.”

“If I scatter her here, then she’s gone. She’s really gone. And I have to go home to a house that doesn’t have her in it.”

Nora put her hand on his back. He flinched, then leaned into her touch. They stood like that for a long moment, two people on a mountain, holding each other up.

“She’s already gone,” Nora said softly. “But she’s not nowhere. She’s here. She’s in the pictures and the garden and the way you make coffee in the morning. She’s in us.”

Her father wiped his face with the back of his hand. “That sounds like something she would say.”

“I know. I stole it from her journal.”

He laughed—a broken, surprised sound—and Nora realized she hadn’t heard him laugh since the funeral.

They walked back to the jar together.

The wind had died. The gorge was still. Far below, a hawk—maybe the same one—circled slowly, patient and dark against the trees.

Nora unscrewed the lid. Her father reached out and put his hand over hers.

“Together?” he said.

“Together.”

They tipped the jar. The ashes caught the wind and lifted, white and gray, scattering over the edge of Hawksbill Mountain. For a moment they hung in the air like a breath. Then they were gone, carried out over the gorge, into the green and the light and the vast, open sky.

Nora did not cry. Not then. She stood on the summit with her father’s hand in hers and watched the hawk turn and turn, and she understood, finally, why her mother had always told her to look up.

On the way down, her father stopped at the first outcropping and pointed.

“Look,” he said. “There.”

Nora looked. A red-tailed hawk rode the wind below them, wings wide, unbothered by the fall.

“I see it,” she said.

And she did.

prompt: Reddit , as a collective entity , runs for president .
content:
**The Hivemind Candidate**

The first time I met the candidate, it was a pinned post.

I had spent six years as a congressional staffer, which is like being a smoke machine for other people’s bad ideas. So when a Reddit admin called and said, “The users have nominated you to be our designated human,” I assumed it was a prank. Then a courier delivered FEC paperwork with the candidate name filled in as “The Reddit Collective,” the party listed as “None / All of Them,” and the treasurer’s name as u/PM_ME_UR_TAX_RETURNS.

I had written one comment the week before: *If Reddit ever ran for president, I’d volunteer as the designated adult.* It got forty thousand upvotes. Apparently, that was a binding contract.

The campaign headquarters was a Discord server, a PO box in San Francisco, and a Google Doc titled “DO NOT LET r/WALLSTREETBETS NEAR THE BUDGET.” The candidate had no body, no voice, and no fixed positions. It had threads. Every morning at nine, the campaign posted a question to r/RedditForPresident. By midnight, the top-voted comment became policy. It was direct democracy, if direct democracy were a comment section after three cups of coffee.

Our first press conference was a disaster. A reporter asked, “Where does the candidate stand on health care?”

I opened the consensus thread. The top comment said: *ELI5: Why do we have to pay for bones?* The second said: *As a European, this is hilarious.* The third said: *Legalize weed and fix the potholes.*

I looked up. “The candidate believes health care is a human right,” I said, “and also that potholes are a sign of national decline.”

The reporter squinted. “Which is it?”

“Both,” I said. “It’s a big tent.”

The candidate’s platform, once finalized, was surprisingly popular. Point one: Make Election Day a federal holiday. Point two: Ban robocalls. Point three: Abolish daylight saving time, though nobody could agree whether to keep standard or summer time, so the plan simply said “pick one and never speak of it again.” Point four: Turn the moon into a national park. Point five: Every bill must come with an ELI5.

The other candidates tried to attack us. Senator Whitmore said Reddit was “a chatbot with a mob.” The candidate’s top comment was: *Correct. I am 73 million people. Your approval rating could never.* Governor Hayes said, “You can’t run a country by upvotes.” The candidate posted a poll: *Should we run the country by upvotes?* Sixty-one percent said yes. Twenty-two percent said no. Seventeen percent said “pineapple.”

At the first debate, the moderator asked about foreign policy. The candidate’s answer appeared on a screen after a six-hour voting window: *We will not go to war unless the war gets at least 10,000 upvotes, and the meme potential is high.* The audience laughed. Then the moderator asked about the debt ceiling. The top comment was: *ELI5: Why do we have a credit limit if we’re the ones printing the money?* It went viral. For a week, everyone was talking about whether America was a responsible adult with a credit card. We gained eight points.

But the hivemind had a dark side.

A super PAC called Upvote America figured out how to game the consensus threads. They bought aged accounts, farmed karma, and flooded the candidate’s daily policy questions with bots. Overnight, our platform changed. The top comment on immigration was a copypasta about a guy named Kevin. The top comment on energy policy was “Buy silver.” The top comment on defense was “Invade Canada—they have the good snacks.” I woke up to a press release I had not written and a poll showing we had lost nine points among people who did not want to invade Canada.

I called an emergency meeting with the moderators. They were exhausted, unpaid, and armed with AutoModerator. “We can’t let the bots decide the platform,” I said. “We need verified human voting.”

“That’s going to slow everything down,” said a mod named Marla. “People like the chaos.”

“People also like electricity,” I said. “We have to choose which kind of chaos we can live with.”

So we built a verification system. It was clunky, but it worked. Users had to confirm their accounts, and the campaign introduced a “cooling-off” period before any policy became official. r/Place was repurposed as a verification puzzle. For three days, the entire internet watched pixel wars between humans and bots. It was the most patriotic thing I had ever seen.

The candidate issued a statement: *We are not a hivemind. We are a hive that has learned to moderate itself.* It got two hundred thousand upvotes. I printed it out and taped it above my desk.

Election night was chaos. The candidate won the popular vote by a narrow margin, mostly because young people turned out in record numbers and because a write-in campaign in Ohio accidentally misspelled “Reddit” as “Redditt,” which was still counted. But the electoral college was a mess. Electors pledged to other candidates defected. One elector voted for Reddit. Another voted for “the concept of Reddit.” A third voted for a cat subreddit.

The Supreme Court took the case. The question was simple: Can a website be president? The Constitution said the president must be a natural-born citizen. The Reddit Collective was incorporated in Delaware, had servers in Virginia, and was arguably born in a dorm room in 2005. The Court ruled 5–4 that a collective online entity was not a natural-born citizen. The majority opinion said, “The Framers did not anticipate a group chat.”

The candidate accepted the ruling with grace. Its final post read: *We didn’t want the Oval Office. We wanted a megathread. But we’ll be watching.*

The election was eventually decided by the House, which chose Senator Alvarez, a conventional politician with conventional hair. But something strange happened. Her first act as president was to create a White House subreddit. She appointed me director of the new Office of Public Threads. Every bill went up for an ELI5. Every press briefing had an AMA. It was not quite direct democracy. It was democracy with a comment section, which is like a bicycle with training wheels and a flamethrower.

On my first day in the White House, the president called me into the Oval Office. “What do people think about the infrastructure bill?” she asked.

I opened my laptop. The top comment said: *Read the bill before voting.* The second said: *And fix the potholes.*

The president nodded slowly. “Okay,” she said. “Let’s read the bill.”

Somewhere, a pinned post got another upvote.

prompt: A group of fantasy creatures are playing a table top game together where they pretend to be modern-day humans
content:
# The Cubicle Dungeon

In the back room of the Weeping Basilisk, six fantasy creatures gathered around a table covered in dice, snack crumbs, and a laminated map of something no one in the room had ever seen: an open-plan office.

“All right,” said Krix, a kobold dungeon master wearing a tiny lanyard that said *HI, MY NAME IS KRIX*, “you wake in a two-bedroom apartment. Your alarm—an enchanted rectangle called a *phone*—is screaming. It is Monday. You have forty-five minutes to reach the office.”

Brogg the Unbroken, an orc barbarian built like a wardrobe with tusks, leaned over his character sheet. “I am Greg,” he said solemnly. “Accounts payable. I have rage.”

“You have *irritation*,” Krix corrected. “Roll initiative for the morning commute.”

The players rolled. Elowen the elf ranger, who had once shot a wyvern out of the sky, frowned at her d20. “I am Elizabeth. I work remotely. Does that mean I never leave my lair?”

“You still have to attend a video call,” Krix said. “The webcam is a scrying orb. Everyone can see your laundry.”

Elowen gasped with genuine horror.

Nib, a goblin rogue with a stolen spoon in each pocket, cackled. “I’m Nick, IT support. I cast Detect Magic on the printer.”

“The printer is a metal beast with a blinking red eye,” Krix said. “It hungers for toner.”

“I knew it,” Nib whispered.

Sir Buttercup, a pixie paladin no taller than a tankard, sat on a stack of rulebooks so she could see the map. “I am Becky. I am an intern. I have a scooter.” She rolled the dice. “I ride to the coffee shop.”

“You arrive,” said Krix. “The barista asks for your order.”

“I demand ambrosia,” said Elowen.

“They have oat milk.”

“I demand ambrosia *with* oat milk.”

Taurus, a minotaur cleric in a soft sweater, cleared his throat. “I am Tom. Human resources. I have the Employee Handbook.” He held up three pages of hastily scrawled notes. “It says we cannot intimidate the barista.”

Brogg slammed a fist on the table, rattling the miniatures. “Greg has a meeting at nine. Greg does not have time for the barista’s riddles.”

“Roll Intimidation,” Krix said.

Brogg rolled a natural one.

The barista, Krix explained, burst into tears and gave Greg a free pastry out of fear. The orc looked genuinely stricken. “I did not mean to make the innkeeper weep.”

The game continued. The party entered the Office Dungeon through a badge-activated gate. They rode the elevator, which Krix described as “a metal carriage that plays soft music to keep you calm before it eats you.” The dragon player, Vex, who had joined late and was currently playing Dana, Regional Project Manager, nodded approvingly.

“Dana hoards calendar invites,” Vex said, arranging her miniature carefully with a claw. “She has fifty-seven unread messages. She is powerful.”

The quest was simple: survive until five o’clock without being fired. The final boss was the Quarterly Review.

Krix unfolded a map of the conference room. “You must give a presentation. The projector is cursed. The slides are haunted. Also, someone has brought a child.”

“A child?” said Taurus. “A small human? We must protect it.”

“It’s the manager’s son. He has a tablet and no supervision.”

Nib’s goblin eyes gleamed. “I roll Sleight of Hand to fix the projector.”

“The projector is older than your character’s mortgage,” Krix said. “Roll.”

Nib rolled a twenty. There was a brief, beautiful moment of silence, then a click, then the presentation appeared on the screen.

“Nick the goblin has defeated the projector,” Krix announced. “The room applauds. Dana immediately claims she fixed it.”

Vex smirked. “Dana hoards credit.”

The presentation began. Greg the orc, despite having never used a computer, delivered a rousing speech about “synergizing deliverables,” which he clearly believed were magical artifacts. Elizabeth the elf created a spreadsheet so elegant it brought the finance manager to tears. Becky the pixie intern accidentally muted the entire company for twelve minutes, which everyone agreed was the most productive part of the meeting. Tom from HR calmly explained that the office microwave could not be used to reheat “mysterious potions,” even if they improved morale.

Then came the final roll: the Quarterly Review.

Krix lowered his tiny kobold voice. “The director asks: ‘What value did you add this quarter?’”

The table went quiet.

Brogg looked at his character sheet. Elowen looked at hers. Nib looked at the stolen spoon in his pocket. Sir Buttercup raised a tiny hand.

“Becky made coffee,” she said.

Taurus nodded. “Tom ensured the handbook was followed.”

Vex tapped a claw on the table. “Dana coordinated the team.”

Nib grinned. “Nick fixed the printer.”

Elowen said, “Elizabeth sent the email.”

Brogg sat up straight. “Greg approved the invoices.”

Krix rolled the dice behind his screen. The players held their breath. The d20 clattered across the table, bounced off a miniatures tree, and landed on a nineteen.

“The Quarterly Review nods slowly,” Krix said. “You are not fired. In fact, you are invited to something called ‘team-building.’ There will be trust falls.”

The table erupted in cheers. The pixie did a loop-de-loop around the lantern. The minotaur accidentally knocked over the coffee shop miniature. The orc declared it a glorious victory.

As they packed away the dice, Elowen looked thoughtfully at the map. “These modern humans,” she said. “They face no dragons, no dark lords, no cursed swords. Only emails and meetings and the printer that hungers.”

“Terrifying,” Nib agreed.

“Next week,” Krix said, checking his notes, “we play *The Homeowners’ Association*.”

Everyone groaned. Then they scheduled the session anyway.

prompt: A case hinges on something witnessed only by a dead person . To illustrate how ludicrous this is , one side subpoenas the dead person . The dead person shows up and testifies .
content:
The first thing they teach you in evidence is that dead people don’t testify. It’s not a moral rule. It’s just the way things tend to work. The dead are unreliable about showing up, and when they do show up, they’re usually in no condition to be cross-examined.

I was a second-year associate at Vega & Associates when we got *In re Estate of Lillian Marsh*. Lillian had died at ninety-four, leaving an estate worth roughly forty-two million dollars and two children who hated each other. Her old will split everything evenly between her son, Paul, and her daughter, Ruth. Then, six weeks before Lillian died, a new will appeared. It left everything to Paul. The only problem—or, depending on your side, the only convenient thing—was that the new will was witnessed by Paul and Lillian’s night nurse, Delia Torres.

Delia died in a car accident two weeks after Lillian. Before she died, Paul’s lawyers got her to sign an affidavit saying she had watched Lillian sign the new will voluntarily. She said Lillian was lucid, alert, and understood exactly what she was doing. That affidavit was the heart of Paul’s case. Without it, the new will was a piece of paper with Paul’s name on it and a shaky signature that looked like it had been written by a seismograph.

Ruth’s lawyer—my boss, Marisol Vega—was not a woman who took things lying down. She was brilliant, theatrical, and allergic to the phrase “just accept it.” When Paul’s counsel moved to admit Delia’s affidavit, Marisol stood up and said, “Your Honor, the entire case hinges on something witnessed only by a dead person. The court is being asked to accept the word of a woman who cannot be cross-examined, cannot be confronted, cannot even be asked what color the room was. Why not simply subpoena her?”

Judge Halloran peered over his glasses. “Ms. Vega, are you suggesting I subpoena a deceased person?”

“I’m suggesting that if the court is inclined to treat her affidavit as testimony, then she should be available to give it.”

“And if she doesn’t show up?”

“Then we’ve all learned a valuable lesson about hearsay.”

The judge sighed the sigh of a man who had been on the bench for thirty years and had seen everything except this. “Fine. If you want to subpoena her, Ms. Vega, be my guest. If she appears, I’ll hear her.”

That afternoon, Marisol drafted a subpoena *ad testificandum* for Delia Torres. The clerk issued it without reading the attachment. Our process server, Mr. Okafor, took it to Evergreen Memorial Park, Section 12, Plot 43, and left it in a plastic sleeve beneath a small vase of artificial roses. He took a photo for the file. In the photo, the subpoena looks very official against the granite.

We all thought it was a joke. A point about absurdity. A legal argument dressed up as a prank.

The next morning, Delia Torres was sitting in the witness room.

She was wearing a beige cardigan and a pair of white Nurse-Mates. Her hair was pinned back. She smelled faintly of lilies and wet earth. She looked solid enough to cast a shadow, though the shadow fell the wrong way. The bailiff came into the courtroom looking like he’d swallowed a frog.

“Your Honor,” he said, “there’s a Delia Torres here.”

Judge Halloran looked up. “A Delia Torres.”

“The witness, Your Honor.”

“The deceased witness?”

“Yes, Your Honor.”

The judge took off his glasses, cleaned them, and put them back on. “Bring her in.”

She walked in with the careful steps of a woman who had recently been buried. Paul’s lawyer, Mr. Pike, dropped his pen. Paul went white. Ruth made a small sound, something between a laugh and a prayer.

The judge leaned forward. “Ms. Torres, are you aware that you are deceased?”

“Yes, Your Honor.”

“And yet you received the subpoena?”

“It was left on my grave. I assumed it was important.”

The clerk asked, “Do I swear her in?”

“I suppose you’d better,” the judge said. “Ms. Torres, do you solemnly swear to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth?”

“I do.”

“Do you understand you are still under penalty of perjury?”

Delia considered this. “I understand, Your Honor. I’m not sure how you’d enforce it.”

“Let the record reflect the witness is deceased but present,” the judge said. “Ms. Vega, she’s all yours.”

Marisol stood. She was, for the first time in her career, speechless for exactly one second. Then she smiled.

“Ms. Torres, did you sign this affidavit?”

“I signed a paper. Paul read it to me.”

“Did you read it yourself?”

“No. He said it was just a form saying I was present.”

“Were you present when Lillian Marsh signed the new will?”

The courtroom went quiet. Delia folded her hands in her lap.

“No,” she said. “I was present when Paul put a pen in his mother’s hand and moved it for her. She was asleep. She had morphine. She didn’t wake up.”

Pike shot to his feet. “Objection! Hearsay! She’s—she’s dead!”

“She’s here,” the judge said. “Overruled.”

“Why didn’t you say something while you were alive?” Marisol asked.

“I tried. I called Ruth’s lawyer. Then I had the accident.” Delia’s voice was quiet. “The affidavit was Paul’s idea. He said if I didn’t sign it, I’d lose my job and he’d tell immigration I was working without papers. I was scared. I was dying. I thought maybe it wouldn’t matter.”

“But it does matter,” Marisol said.

“Yes,” Delia said. “It turns out it matters a great deal.”

Pike cross-examined her for twenty minutes. He asked how she could be sure she was dead. She said she had a death certificate. He asked how the court could trust a woman who had lied in an affidavit. She said, “I’m not lying now, and I have nothing left to gain. I’m not inheriting anything. I don’t have a career to protect. I don’t even have a pulse.” She paused. “The dead make excellent witnesses, Mr. Pike. We have very few distractions.”

The judge ruled from the bench. The 2023 will was invalid. The 2019 will stood. Paul’s counsel asked for a continuance. The judge said he had heard enough, and he had never meant it more literally.

Delia was excused. She stood, smoothed her cardigan, and thanked the court.

“Thank you for your service, Ms. Torres,” the judge said.

“Thank you, Your Honor. I’m sorry I couldn’t do it while I was alive.”

She walked out. The bailiff held the door. We sat in silence until the clock on the wall clicked.

We won the case. I still have the subpoena receipt in the file. Sometimes I take it out and look at it. The law is a strange machine. It runs on rules, paper, procedure, and the occasional miracle. But every now and then, to illustrate how ludicrous something is, you subpoena a dead person.

And the dead person shows up.

And she testifies.

prompt: A person 's final thoughts .
content:
The first thing was the cold. It wasn’t the sharp, biting cold of a winter wind, but a deep, seeping chill that seemed to emanate from the core of him, from the very marrow of his bones. It was the cold of the metal table beneath him, the cold of the sterile air, the cold of the finality that was settling over him like a shroud.

Alistair’s eyes were closed, but the world wasn't dark. It was a soft, hazy gray, the color of a television left on a dead channel. He could hear the distant, rhythmic beep of a machine, a sound that had become the metronome of his existence for the past few weeks. It was slowing down. He knew that. They had told him, their voices gentle, professional, like doctors delivering a prognosis they’d delivered a hundred times before.

He tried to focus. His final thoughts. Wasn’t that what you were supposed to do? Review the highlights, the big moments, the love and the loss? His mind felt like a filing cabinet that had been ransacked, papers scattered everywhere, but only a few were legible.

He saw a flash of red. Not blood, but the color of his wife’s favorite scarf. It was a cheap, woolen thing she’d bought at a market, but she wore it every autumn until it was more hole than scarf. He remembered the way it had smelled of her perfume and the crisp fall air. He remembered burying his face in it after she was gone, trying to hold onto the scent of her. The memory wasn't of her death, but of her life—of her laughing, her head tilted back, the scarf wrapped around her neck. It was a good thought. A warm one.

Then, a sharper, more painful image. A slammed door. The sound of his son’s car peeling out of the driveway. The words he’d said, hot and angry, words meant to wound, hanging in the air like a foul odor. Pride. Such a stupid, stubborn pride. He’d been right, of course. He knew that. But being right had cost him ten years. Ten years of silence. The last time he'd heard Michael's voice was on a crackling voicemail, left three years ago. *“Dad, it’s me. Just… checking in. Call me back, okay?”* He never did. He was always going to call tomorrow.

Tomorrow had always been a promise he never kept.

A sigh escaped his lips, a dry, rattling sound. The beeping was slower now. He felt a strange sense of detachment from his own body, as if he were watching a movie of a man named Alistair who was lying on a bed. He felt a pang of regret for that man, for his foolishness. He wanted to reach back through time, grab his own younger self by the collar and shake him. *Call him. Go to him. Don't let your damn pride win.*

He saw a flash of green light. A traffic light on a rainy night. He was young, so young, driving his first car. The radio was blaring his favorite song, and he was drumming on the steering wheel, the windshield wipers a hypnotic swing. He was filled with the simple, electric joy of being alive, of having somewhere to go and the whole night ahead of him. There was no mortgage, no regrets, no aching joints. There was only possibility. That boy was a stranger to him now, but he envied him.

The beeping was a slow, steady pulse now, like a distant heartbeat. The gray was deepening, turning to black at the edges. He wasn't afraid. The cold was no longer uncomfortable; it was a numb blanket, pulling him under, and he was too tired to fight it.

He thought of his daughter, Sarah. Her hands, so small and soft, in his as he walked her down the aisle. The way she'd squeezed his hand three times, their secret code since she was a little girl: *I love you.* He remembered the way her eyes had shone, not with tears of sadness, but of pure, unadulterated joy. In that moment, his own happiness had been so complete it had almost been a physical ache. That was a good thing to hold onto. The feeling of her small hand in his.

A final, fleeting image came to him, unbidden. It wasn't a memory. It was a wish. A quiet dinner table. The clinking of cutlery. Sarah on one side, Michael on the other. His wife at the head of the table, that red scarf draped over her chair. The sound of laughter, easy and unforced. The feeling of being known, of being home.

The beeping was no longer a sound. It was a color. A white, pure, all-encompassing light. And in that light, he could almost hear it—the echo of that laughter. It was enough. It was a lovely thought. A final, perfect thought. He let go of the gray, of the cold, of the ransacked filing cabinet of his life, and leaned into the light, listening to the music he had only ever hoped to hear.

prompt: You 're a teenage boy who has to break the news to your parents that your girlfriend got you pregnant .
content:
The lasagna was still steaming when I decided I’d rather die than take another bite.

My mom was talking about her garden. My dad was doing that thing where he nods without really listening. My little sister was stabbing a noodle like it owed her money. Normal. Completely, painfully normal.

And I was sitting there with a folded piece of paper in my hoodie pocket and a heartbeat loud enough to drown out the fork scraping my plate.

Maya had sent me a text that afternoon: *You have to tell them tonight. I can’t keep pretending.* She was right. She’d been right for three weeks, ever since the drugstore test and the follow-up appointment and the quiet doctor’s office where the word “pregnant” suddenly stopped being something that happened to other people.

I was sixteen. Maya was sixteen. We’d been together for almost a year. We were careful—mostly. “Mostly” is a terrible word when you’re sixteen and terrified.

“Eli,” my mom said. “You’re not eating. Are you sick?”

“No,” I said. “I mean—not exactly.”

My dad looked up. That was bad. He only looked up when something was actually happening.

“Can I tell you something?” I asked. “Both of you? And maybe Sadie can go to her room?”

My sister immediately stopped stabbing her lasagna. “Why do I have to go to my room?”

“Because you’re ten and this is adult stuff,” my dad said, still watching me.

“That’s not fair.”

“Sadie,” my mom said softly. “Go on. You can take your plate.”

Sadie dragged her plate away like she was being exiled from a birthday party. The door clicked shut. The house got very quiet.

My dad put his fork down. “What’s going on?”

I’d rehearsed it about forty times in the shower. I had an opening line. I had a back-up opening line. I had a speech about responsibility and protective measures and how this didn’t mean my life was over. None of it came out.

Instead, I pulled the paper from my pocket, smoothed it against the table, and said, “Maya’s pregnant.”

For a second, nobody moved.

My mom’s face did something complicated—blank, then confused, then understanding, then something like the floor dropping out from under her.

“What?” she whispered.

“Maya’s pregnant,” I repeated. My voice cracked. “And it’s mine. I’m the father.”

My dad leaned back in his chair. He didn’t yell. Somehow that was worse. He just stared at me like he’d never seen me before.

“How—how far along?” my mom asked.

“Ten weeks.”

“Ten weeks,” she repeated. “And you’re just telling us now?”

“We were scared. Maya told her mom last week. I wanted to tell you sooner, but every time I tried, I couldn’t.”

My mom pressed her fingers to her mouth. Her eyes got shiny. I hated that more than if she’d screamed. I’d made my mom cry.

My dad finally spoke. “You’re sixteen.”

“I know.”

“You’re a kid.”

“I know.”

“You think you know,” he said, and there was something raw in his voice. “You think you know what this means, but you don’t. You don’t know anything yet.”

I felt my throat close. “I know I messed up.”

“Yeah,” he said. “You did.”

The silence after that was so heavy I could hear the refrigerator humming.

Then my mom took a breath—one of those shaky ones—and said, “Okay. Okay. We’re going to deal with this. But I need you to tell me the truth. Is Maya okay? Is she safe? Is she scared?”

“She’s scared,” I said. “She’s really scared. Her mom’s been okay, but she cried a lot. Maya’s been going to appointments. She’s trying to figure out what she wants.”

“What she wants?” my dad asked.

“It’s her body,” I said. “That’s what her mom said. And Maya said she wants to talk to us—both families—before deciding anything.”

My mom nodded slowly. “That’s the right place to start.”

My dad rubbed his hand over his face. He looked tired in a way I’d never noticed before. “You understand this isn’t just a conversation you have and then it’s over? This is the rest of your life changing. School. Money. Everything.”

“I know.”

“Do you?” He looked at me hard. “Because saying you know isn’t the same as doing something about it.”

I sat up straighter. “The baby’s not here yet, but I’m not going to pretend it isn’t happening. I’ll get a job. I’ll finish school. I’ll go to every appointment Maya wants me at. I’m not going to run.”

My dad didn’t say anything for a long moment. Then he said, “You’re not a man because you did this, Eli. You become one by what you do next.”

I nodded. My eyes were burning, but I was not going to cry at the dinner table. “I know.”

My mom reached across the table and took my hand. Her grip was strong. “We’re angry,” she said. “And we’re disappointed. But you’re our son. We’re not going to abandon you. Or Maya. Do you understand me?”

I nodded again. This time a tear did escape, and I wiped it away fast.

My dad stood up and walked to the kitchen window. He stood there with his back to us, hands in his pockets. I thought he was going to leave the room. Instead, he said, “Call Maya’s mom tomorrow. We’ll all meet. No secrets. No hiding. We figure this out together.”

“Okay,” I said.

“And Eli?”

“Yeah?”

He turned around. His face was still serious, but softer now. “I’m glad you told us. I’m not glad about the situation, but I’m glad you didn’t run from it.”

That was the moment I realized my hands were shaking. I’d been holding my breath for weeks, and now the air was coming out of me all at once.

My mom squeezed my hand. “Eat something,” she said. “You look terrible.”

I laughed—just a little, just once. Then I picked up my fork and took a bite of cold lasagna.

It tasted like fear and relief and the beginning of a very different life.

content:
# The Zero Above Arthur Vale

The number appeared above Arthur’s head the way it did over everyone else’s: a small, luminous figure hovering a few inches above the crown, visible to every pair of eyes in the world. Babies were born with it. Children wore it like a party hat. Teenagers obsessed over it. Adults learned not to stare, and then stared anyway.

Arthur Vale was fifty years old, and his number was 0.

He saw it in the bathroom mirror every morning, pale as a moon. He shaved beneath it, brushed his teeth beneath it, combed the gray at his temples beneath it. The number did not flicker with shame. It did not change when he was kind or cruel, tired or hopeful. It simply existed, the way his nose existed, the way the mole on his shoulder existed.

At fifty, a zero was not invisible. It was a billboard.

On the bus, two teenagers sat across from him, their numbers bright above their heads—4 and 9—and one of them nudged the other and whispered something. Arthur kept his eyes on his book. He had learned that looking up only invited conversation. He had also learned that people who whispered about a zero rarely had anything interesting to say.

The coffee shop was warm and smelled of burned sugar. Priya, the barista, had 86 above her head. She never looked at Arthur’s number. Or if she did, she had the grace to make it look like she hadn’t.

“The usual, Arthur?” she asked.

“Please.”

She made his coffee while a man behind him talked loudly into his phone. Above the man’s head hung 312. Arthur wondered if the number was accurate, or if some people learned how to game the system. He had heard theories: that the count only included certain acts, that some people lied to themselves so hard the number obeyed. He didn’t know. He had never tested it.

A small girl in line pointed at him. Her own number was a soft, innocent 0. “Why is his zero?” she asked.

Her mother went red. “Shh. Don’t point.”

Arthur smiled at the girl. “Because I’ve never done the thing that makes it go up.”

The mother looked like she wanted the floor to open. The girl considered this. “Mine’s zero too.”

“Yours is supposed to be,” Arthur said. “Enjoy it while it’s normal.”

He took his coffee and left before the mother could apologize or lecture him.

At the office, his cubicle was the same as it had been for eleven years. Arthur worked in claims adjustment for a small insurance company, a job that required patience and an eye for small inconsistencies. He was good at it. His supervisor, Diane, had 43 above her head and a habit of asking Arthur to cover weekends.

“You’re a saint, Arthur,” she said that morning, dropping a folder on his desk. “Kevin’s kid has a soccer tournament.”

Kevin, two cubes over, had 117 above his head and the confidence of a man who had never been asked to explain himself. He leaned back in his chair. “Arthur, serious question. You ever think about just—getting it over with? Like, hire somebody?”

Arthur kept typing. “No.”

“I’m not judging.”

“You are a little.”

Kevin laughed. “It’s just—fifty, man. Don’t you want to know what it’s like?”

Arthur did want to know. That was the thing he never said. He had wanted to know at nineteen, when a girl named Miriam had invited him back to her dorm room and he had panicked so badly he pretended to have a stomachache. He had wanted to know at twenty-six, when a coworker at his first job asked him out for drinks and then, later, invited him upstairs. He had said no because his father had just had a stroke, and he was driving to the hospital every night, and the idea of being touched by someone who didn’t know how tired he was felt impossible. He had wanted to know at thirty-four, at forty-one, at forty-six. But wanting and doing were different countries. He had never learned the passport.

“It’s not a race,” Arthur said.

Kevin shrugged. “True. But you’re the only guy I know with a zero. That’s kind of a distinction.”

“I’m a rare breed.”

At lunch, the office celebrated a birthday. Someone had brought a grocery-store cake with too-sweet frosting. Above the birthday woman’s head was 58. Above the new hire, a quiet girl named Anna, was 0. She was twenty-two and looked uncomfortable whenever anyone glanced upward.

Arthur sat at the breakroom table with his sandwich. Anna sat across from him, holding a paper cup.

“Does it get easier?” she asked quietly.

He knew what she meant. “The number doesn’t.”

“That’s not encouraging.”

“No,” he said. “But the rest of you grows around it. You get a job. You learn things. You find out what you like. The zero stays the same size, and you get bigger.”

Anna looked at him. Her number shimmered slightly in the fluorescent light. “What if I never want to?”

“Then you don’t.”

“But everyone acts like it’s a disease.”

Arthur nodded. “People are scared of anything they can count and compare. It doesn’t mean they’re right.”

She smiled a little. “You’re the first person who didn’t make me feel like a project.”

“I’m not a project person,” Arthur said. “I’m a paperwork person.”

In the afternoon, he had a doctor’s appointment. Dr. Okafor had 59 above her head and a calm, unreadable face. She asked the routine questions without flinching.

“Are you sexually active?”

“No.”

“Have you ever been?”

“No.”

She typed something. “Any pain, discharge, unusual symptoms?”

“No.”

“Okay. We can skip the rest.” She looked at him directly, not at the number above his head, and said, “Your count isn’t a medical condition, Arthur. Neither is the absence of one.”

“I know.”

“Do you?”

He thought about it. “On good days.”

After work, he took the bus to the assisted living facility where his mother lived. She had 1 above her head. She had met Arthur’s father at a dance in 1962, married him six months later, and stayed married for forty-three years. Her number had been 1 for as long as Arthur could remember. His father’s had been 1 too. Arthur used to think that was romantic. Now he thought it was just a fact, like blue eyes or a mortgage.

His mother was in the common room, watching a game show. She had dementia, and some days she knew him and some days she didn’t. Today she looked up and said, “Arthur. You’re late.”

“I brought you those peppermints you like.”

She took one and sucked on it. Then she squinted at the air above his head. “Still zero?”

“Still zero.”

She patted his hand. “You were always careful.”

He didn’t correct her. Careful wasn’t the word. He had been afraid, then busy, then ashamed of being afraid, then too old to be ashamed in the same way. Careful sounded better.

“Are you seeing anyone?” she asked.

“No, Mom.”

“You should.”

“I know.”

She nodded and turned back to the game show. Above her head, the 1 glowed like a small, steady lamp. Arthur wondered what it would be like to have a number that told a simple story. One person. One time. A life measured in a single act.

At home, he made tomato soup and grilled cheese. He ate at the kitchen table with the radio on. The apartment was clean and quiet. He had a bookshelf full of paperback mysteries, a piano he played badly, and a window that looked out onto a courtyard where children shrieked and played. No one in the courtyard had a zero except the very young.

He thought about Kevin’s question. He thought about Miriam’s dorm room, the way the light had fallen on her shoulder, the way he had wanted to say yes and instead said his stomach hurt. He thought about the woman at forty-one, a nurse who had taken care of his father, who had asked him once if he ever did anything for himself. He had said, “I’m doing it now.” She had laughed. Then his father had needed him, and the moment closed like a door.

He did not regret his life. That was the part no one believed. He had loved his parents. He had been good at his job. He had read a thousand books. He had learned to make a decent pie crust. He had once helped a lost child in a supermarket find her mother and had felt useful for a whole week.

But he was lonely. That was also true. The zero did not cause the loneliness, exactly. It was more like a label on a jar. People saw the label and assumed they knew what was inside.

At ten o’clock, he brushed his teeth. In the mirror, the zero hovered above his head, patient and old.

“Tomorrow,” he said to it, “I’ll get up. I’ll go to work. I’ll be kind to Priya. I’ll ignore the whispers. I’ll visit Mom.”

The zero did not answer.

Arthur spat into the sink, rinsed his brush, and turned off the light. In the dark, he could still feel it there, a small, luminous fact. Not a verdict. Not a prophecy. Just a number, and a man, and a day that had been lived as well as he knew how.
