{prompt}
prompt: A woman you casually know spots you as you walk through a store , approaches you , smiles and says , `` I saw your gravestone today , just lovely ! '' and nonchalantly strolls away .
content:
**Practice Stone**

I was in the produce section of Marlow’s Market when Adelaide Finch, a woman I knew only from Tuesday pottery class, came around the endcap with a bunch of cilantro. She spotted me, smiled, and said, “I saw your gravestone today, just lovely!” Then she strolled away toward the bakery as if she’d told me the weather.

I stood there holding a red onion.

Adelaide and I had exchanged maybe forty words total, all of them about glaze recipes. I called after her, but she was already gone around the corner. I abandoned my cart and followed—bakery, dairy, checkout. No Adelaide. Just a woman in a green coat buying a baguette. I drove home with my heart doing a strange, uneven shuffle.

For the rest of the day I couldn’t stop thinking about it. I am a stone carver. Not the abstract kind—I cut letters into granite and slate for funeral homes. I have a small workshop behind my house. Six months ago, for a community art walk, I had put a practice slab near the sidewalk: a piece of pale gray granite, about knee-high, with my name cut into it in a serif I’d been trying to master. NORA VALE. 1979. A blank space beneath.

I’d thought of it as a sample, a billboard for my work. I hadn’t thought of it as a gravestone. But of course, to anyone walking by, that’s exactly what it was.

Still, when Adelaide said it, I felt cold. I’d had a mammogram callback a few months earlier. Everything turned out fine, but for two weeks I had lived with a small, dark possibility. And my father had died in March. And “your gravestone” doesn’t sound like a compliment about craftsmanship. It sounds like a warning.

I drove to the workshop. The practice stone was still there, leaning against the fence. NORA VALE. 1979. The letters looked good, actually. The V had a nice sharp apex. I ran my finger over the blank date. I thought: she saw this. She walked past my house, saw my name on a stone, and thought, *Just lovely.* It was a compliment. It was also a thing that had made me feel, for three hours, like a ghost.

I called my partner, Sam. He said, “You’re a stone carver. People are going to see stones with your name on them. It’s not an omen; it’s a lawn ornament.”

“It’s not supposed to be a lawn ornament,” I said. “It’s a sample.”

“Then maybe don’t put your name and birth year on it.”

He had a point.

At pottery class the next week, Adelaide was at the wheel, her hands gray with slip. I said, “Adelaide, about what you said at Marlow’s—”

She looked up, blank.

“The gravestone,” I said. “You said you saw my gravestone.”

Her face cleared. “Oh! Yes. The one in your yard. The letters are beautiful. I was walking to the post office and I saw it and thought, *That’s Nora’s work. Just lovely.*” She smiled. “I hope that wasn’t strange. I know you make them, but I’ve never seen your work up close.”

I laughed. It came out too loud. “No, it’s fine. I just—I didn’t know you’d seen it.”

“I did. The V is very elegant.” Then she went back to her bowl. She had no idea she’d scared me. She was just a woman who liked good lettering.

That should have been the end of it. But for the next few days I kept thinking about the stone. I had carved my name into it as a placeholder, but a placeholder for what? I had carved my birth year. I had left the death year blank because that’s how samples work, because you need negative space to show what a date would look like. But the blank space had started to feel like a mouth.

On Saturday, I took the stone back into the workshop and sanded off the letters. It was harder than I expected. Granite doesn’t forgive. I had to use a diamond pad and water, and after an hour my arms ached and the name was gone, leaving a pale scar where the letters had been.

I cut a new sample instead: a simple phrase, no names. **AS YOU ARE.** I put it by the fence. It was less personal. It was also less creepy.

But a week later, I woke up early and went outside. The morning was foggy. The new stone looked like a small white ghost. I thought about Adelaide, walking to the post office, seeing my name and thinking it lovely. I thought about how strange it is that we make monuments for the dead out of the same material we use for kitchen counters. I thought about my father’s stone, which I had carved myself, and how I hadn’t been able to look at it for a month after the funeral.

I went back inside and made coffee. Sam asked if I was okay.

“Yes,” I said. “I think I’m going to put the practice stone back.”

“The one with your name?”

“No. A new one. Something truthful.”

“Like what?”

“I don’t know yet. Maybe ‘STILL HERE.’”

He laughed. “That’s not very cemetery.”

“Exactly.”

The next Tuesday at pottery, Adelaide said, “I saw your new stone. ‘As You Are.’ Also lovely.”

“Thank you,” I said. “It’s a sample.”

She nodded. “I like that one better. The other one was a little sad.”

She didn’t explain. She just went back to her wheel. And I understood: she had seen it too. The blank date. The mouth. She had said “lovely” because it was, but she had also known, in the way people know things in small towns, that it was a strange thing to leave by a fence. She had been kind about it. She had also been honest.

I still have the scarred piece of granite in my workshop. I use it as a doorstop. Sometimes I look at the pale space where my name used to be and think: this is what it is to be alive. You are a blank date. You are a practice stone. You are a compliment from a woman in the produce aisle, strolling away with her cilantro.

And you are still here.

prompt: You are a child who experienced a nightmare about a werewolf . Now , in every sleep , you experience the same nightmare . You have the choice to claim victory or defeat to end your recurring dream .
content:
I was seven the first time the werewolf found me, and after that it found me every time I slept.

It always began the same way: my bare feet on moss so cold it felt wet, a moon too big and too white above the pines, and the smell of rain on old wood. I knew the clearing. I knew the crooked tree with the split trunk. I knew the exact moment the growl would roll out from between the trees like thunder under a floor.

Then it came—tall as a door, fur like burnt paper, eyes the color of coins. It never howled. It just watched me until I ran.

I always ran.

The branches whipped my face. The same root caught my foot. The same black pond waited at the bottom of the hill. I always reached it. I always turned. I always saw the werewolf rise up behind me, its shadow swallowing the moon.

Then I woke up.

At first Mom said it was just a nightmare. Dad checked under my bed and in my closet. The doctor said children’s sleep changes, that I would grow out of it. But the dream did not care about growing. Every sleep, even naps, took me back to the pines. Every night, I woke with my heart hammering and my sheets twisted around my legs. I stopped wanting to close my eyes.

After a while, I started learning the dream the way you learn a scary hallway in your own house. I memorized the number of steps to the crooked tree. I knew which branch would scratch my cheek. I learned to turn my head before the growl came.

One night, I even spoke.

“I know you,” I whispered.

The werewolf stopped. The forest went silent, as if someone had pressed a hand over its mouth. The moon leaned closer. The wolf tilted its head, and its coin-colored eyes narrowed, not like a beast’s but like a person’s.

At the black pond, before it could pin me, a voice rose from the water. It was not the werewolf’s voice. It was not mine. It sounded like the bottom of a well.

“Claim victory or defeat,” it said. “Either one ends this dream.”

I woke before I could answer.

The next night, I was ready. I reached the pond and the werewolf rose behind me, and the voice asked again. I grabbed a branch and shouted, “Victory!”

The branch turned to smoke in my hand. The werewolf laughed, a terrible human sound, and its jaws closed around the dream.

I woke up crying.

The night after that, I tried defeat. I lay down in the moss and said, “I lose.”

The wolf stepped onto my chest. It was heavy as a wardrobe. I could not breathe. I woke with my mouth open and my pillow wet with sweat. The dream had not ended. It had only tasted me.

So I kept going back. Every sleep, the same trees, the same moon, the same pond. Every time, the voice asked its question: victory or defeat. I began to hate the words. They felt like two doors in a dark room, and I could not see what was on the other side of either one.

One night, after I woke up screaming, Mom sat on the edge of my bed and smoothed my hair back.

“What are you fighting?” she asked.

“A wolf,” I said.

She was quiet for a long time. Then she said, “Sometimes winning isn’t hitting harder. Sometimes winning is stopping the fight long enough to see what’s actually there.”

I did not understand her then. But I remembered it.

The next time I slept, I did not run.

The dream began the same. Cold moss. Too-big moon. The growl in the trees. But when the werewolf came, I stayed where I was. My heart beat so hard I could feel it in my teeth, but I did not run.

The wolf circled me. Its claws clicked on the stones. Its breath smelled of pine sap and old smoke. It waited for me to break. I did not.

Then I walked to the black pond. I heard it following, heavy and patient. At the water’s edge, I turned around.

The werewolf rose up, taller than before. Its shadow covered me. The voice from the water whispered, “Claim victory or defeat.”

I looked at the wolf. Really looked. Its fur was patchy. Its ribs showed. Its coin-colored eyes were not hungry. They were tired. It had been chasing me for so long that it did not know how to stop either.

I thought of Mom’s words.

“I claim victory,” I said.

The wolf snarled. The forest shook.

“No,” I said, louder. “Not over you. Over the fear. I’m not running anymore.”

The werewolf did not disappear. It did not explode into smoke. It shrank, slowly, like a shadow at sunrise. Its fur smoothed. Its teeth went blunt. It became smaller and smaller until it was just a gray wolf standing at the edge of the pond, watching me with eyes that were no longer coins but only eyes.

Then it turned and walked into the trees.

I woke up in my bed. The room was dark and ordinary. My heart was quiet. I waited for the fear to come back, but it did not.

I slept again that night, and the dream was different. I stood in the same forest, under the same too-big moon, but the pines were soft and silver. The gray wolf walked beside me, and we did not run.

I never had the nightmare again.

Some nights I still dream of the forest. But now I know what I am dreaming. I know the choice was never really between winning and losing. It was between running and turning around.

I claimed victory. Not over the wolf. Over the fear that had taught it to chase me.

prompt: Professor Paradox manipulates time so that his defeat would cause a paradox
content:
# The Load-Bearing Man

Professor Paradox appeared in Ben Tennyson’s kitchen at 7:03 a.m., three minutes before he had left.

“Ben,” he said pleasantly, “whatever happens today, do not save me.”

Ben lowered his cereal spoon. “That’s not a normal way to say good morning.”

“It is for me.” Paradox adjusted his cravat. “An old acquaintance has decided to erase me from history. She has built a device called the Causal Scalpel. It can cut a person out of time without creating a paradox. Very impressive. It will almost certainly work.”

Rook set down his tea. “Then why are you not concerned?”

“Because,” Paradox said, “it will almost certainly work *in a way that causes a paradox*. There is a difference.” He checked a pocket watch that had no hands. “I have spent a very long time arranging that difference.”

Ben stood. “Okay, where is she? We’ll help.”

“No,” Paradox said, gently but firmly. “If you help, you introduce a variable I have not spent several centuries accounting for. Besides, this is my defeat. I would hate to miss it.”

He vanished before Ben could argue.

—

The Temporal Court floated in the remains of a dead timeline. Archivist Null had built it from the bones of collapsed centuries. She was tall, silver-eyed, and half machine, and she smiled when Paradox stepped into her vault.

“You came,” she said.

“I was already here,” Paradox said. “From a certain perspective.”

Null gestured at the device beside her: a long, black instrument like a surgeon’s knife crossed with a tuning fork. “The Causal Scalpel. It does not erase you. It erases every cause that led to you. Your birth. Your accident. Every intervention you ever made. It cuts cleanly.”

“There are no clean cuts,” Paradox said.

“Spoken like a man about to be forgotten.”

Null activated the Scalpel. Ben and Rook, who had ignored Paradox’s advice in the way of all good friends, burst through the vault doors just in time to see Paradox begin to fade.

“Paradox!” Ben shouted.

Paradox smiled faintly. “Do not intervene.”

Null drove the blade through his chest. For one breath, Professor Paradox became translucent. His coat thinned to smoke. His eyes became two distant sparks.

Then time stuttered.

Null’s smile wavered. The Scalpel in her hand flickered. Not malfunctioned—*flickered*. Its black metal became transparent, then solid, then transparent again.

“What—” she began.

Her mechanical arm vanished first.

Null stared at the empty sleeve. The vault lights went out. The floor beneath her feet shimmered like a mirage. Her guards were gone. The walls were gone. The Temporal Court itself began to peel away, century by century, like old wallpaper.

“You see,” Paradox said, his voice echoing from everywhere and nowhere, “you made a common mistake. You assumed a paradox is a knot. It is actually a load-bearing wall.”

Null lunged for the Scalpel. It was already gone.

“Your Scalpel was designed by Dr. Vellen,” Paradox said. “She survived the Chronal Plague because I redirected a plague ship into a sun. She only understood temporal metallurgy because I left a book in her library. The alloy in its blade came from an asteroid I nudged two million years before you were born. Your fortress stands on a moon whose orbit I stabilized. Your ancestor lived because I once told a stubborn man to take a different bridge.”

“Liar!” Null shouted.

“I am a great many things,” Paradox said. “A liar is rarely one of them.”

Time tried to resolve the contradiction. If Null defeated Paradox, then the Causal Scalpel erased Paradox. But the Scalpel existed only because Paradox had saved Dr. Vellen. If Paradox was erased, Vellen died, and the Scalpel was never built. If the Scalpel was never built, Null could not defeat Paradox. If Null did not defeat Paradox, the Scalpel remained.

The universe shuddered.

Null screamed as her own body began to loop: present, absent, present, absent. Her fortress vanished and reappeared and vanished again. Through it all, Professor Paradox faded back into existence, coat first, then smile, then the rest of him.

He straightened his cravat.

“You tried to cut me out while standing on my footsteps,” he said. “Reality found that unreasonable.”

Null dropped to her knees—when she had knees. “Stop it. Stop it!”

Paradox raised his cane. The loops paused, leaving her frozen halfway between existence and erasure.

“I did not arrange your life,” he said. “You chose your path. But every road you could have taken to defeat me was a road I had already paved. Not to control you. To make my defeat the one thing time would refuse to accept.”

“Why?” she whispered. “Why not just stop me?”

“Because stopping you would have been temporary. You would have found another way. A paradox, however, is permanent.” He tilted his head. “Unless you would prefer to keep experiencing your victory being erased, one iteration at a time?”

Null shook her head violently.

Paradox nodded. “Then choose a different road.”

He touched her forehead with the tip of his cane. The Temporal Court became a quiet morning street in a city that had never been erased. Null—small, ordinary, and very confused—blinked at the sunlight.

Ben and Rook found Paradox outside, waiting by a blue door that had not been there a moment before.

“You could have told us the plan,” Ben said.

“If I had,” Paradox said, “you would have tried to save me. And your attempt would have been the one variable I could not predict.” He smiled. “Also, you would have been late.”

Rook frowned. “But if your defeat caused a paradox, then you were never truly in danger.”

“Oh, I was in terrible danger,” Paradox said cheerfully. “A paradox is only a guarantee after it happens. Before that, it is merely a very confident hope.” He opened the door. “Now, if you’ll excuse me, I have to be somewhere yesterday.”

He stepped through and closed the door behind him.

From the other side, faintly, Ben heard him add, “And Ben—don’t drink the orange juice. It’s expired.”

prompt: Fear and The Emotions of Social Interaction ( Come Together )
content:
**Come Together**

At 6:12 p.m., Mina’s apartment buzzed. It was the neighbor’s potluck. She had RSVP’d “maybe” to avoid lying.

Fear arrived first, as it always did. It was a small gray thing with damp eyes, and it sat on her chest while she put on her shoes.

“They’ll ask what you do,” Fear said. “You’ll say ‘work stuff.’ Then silence.”

Mina knew the script. Social interaction came with a whole weather system inside her: Anticipation, electric and restless; Embarrassment, a hot coal; Shame, a wet coat; Curiosity, a moth at the window; Longing, a hand reaching toward a circle of laughing people. They all lived in her. Fear was the bouncer.

She went downstairs anyway.

The courtyard had string lights and folding tables. People orbited one another with paper plates. At the gate, her emotions gathered. Anticipation fluttered. Curiosity leaned toward the cheese board. Embarrassment hid behind a fern. Longing looked at a group of neighbors laughing near the grill. Shame put a hand on Mina’s shoulder, heavy as a coat.

Fear stepped in front. “We don’t have to go in.”

“I want to know what the potato salad is,” Curiosity said.

“Potluck potato salad?” Embarrassment whispered. “You’ll get a hair.”

“Maybe it’s good,” Longing said.

Fear turned on them. “What if she freezes? What if they see she doesn’t belong?”

Mina felt the old pull toward home. She nearly turned around. Then Jo from 3B appeared at the gate, a baby on her hip, and said, “You made it! Can you hold the door?”

It was such a small request. Fear blinked. Mina held the door. Then she was inside.

At the potluck, Fear kept close, whispering: *that laugh is at you; you’re standing alone; your name is gone; everyone can tell.* The other emotions tried to manage. Anticipation turned into a low hum. Curiosity got her to the food table. Embarrassment made her spill salsa on her sleeve, then discovered, with some surprise, that no one cared. Shame tried to make the spill mean something, but Longing sat down beside her and said, “Look. There’s a seat.”

Then Jo introduced her to a circle: a teacher, a bike mechanic, and a man named Ravi who was also new. “What do you do?” Ravi asked.

Fear sharpened its teeth. Mina’s mind went blank.

But Curiosity stepped forward. “I work in spreadsheets,” Mina said. “But I’m trying to learn how to make bread.”

The bike mechanic groaned. “Sourdough is a cult.”

Ravi laughed. “I killed my starter. His name was Doughlores.”

Mina laughed. It surprised her. Fear recoiled—but not away. It sat down at the edge of the circle, uncertain. Embarrassment whispered, “You laughed too loud.” Shame agreed. But Longing said, “No. We’re here.”

The party continued. Someone dropped a plate. Everyone clapped. The teacher told a bad joke. Fear kept expecting the room to turn cold, but the room just kept being a room. Mina talked to Ravi about bread and bad roommates. She noticed that the emotions of social interaction weren’t trying to evict Fear. They were trying to include it.

Curiosity asked Fear, “What are you protecting us from?”

Fear said, “Being seen. And rejected.”

Shame said, “Same.”

Embarrassment said, “Same, but louder.”

Longing said, “Same. But I still want the cheese.”

They laughed. Not a big laugh. A small, human one. Fear shrank to the size of a pebble. It didn’t vanish—it never vanished—but it sat in her pocket instead of on her throat.

At 8:47, Mina said goodbye. She had been there for two hours, which felt like a miracle and also like ordinary life. Jo said, “See you next month?”

Mina said, “Yeah.” Fear flinched, but Anticipation nodded.

Walking upstairs, she felt all of them settle: Fear, Curiosity, Embarrassment, Longing, Shame, Hope, Belonging. They didn’t agree. They didn’t become one thing. But they came together, the way a room comes together when someone holds the door.

At home, she texted Ravi: *Doughlores deserved better.*

He replied with a bread emoji.

Fear whispered, “What does that mean?”

Mina said, “It means I’m going to try again.”

She put her phone down. The gray thing on her chest curled up. It was still fear. But it was no longer alone.

prompt: You wait tables in a Southern bar with a cartoonishly sassy , gay , black cook and are best friends with his sister . A vampire walks in to have a drink of the new fake blood your bar sells . You can also hear people 's thoughts and you 're half human , half fairy . Who killed your grandmother ?
content:
The first vampire to walk into the Blue Lantern ordered the new fake blood like it was a craft cocktail.

“Synthetic O-negative,” he said, smooth as a funeral parlor. “Neat. Room temperature. No garnish.”

From the kitchen window, Dante—our cook, six-foot-four, black, gay as a Mardi Gras parade, and sassy enough to make a lemon pucker—leaned out and said, “No garnish? Honey, what kind of vampire are you? You want me to put it in a sippy cup and call it a night?”

The vampire smiled with exactly one fang showing. “I’m trying to be discreet.”

“Baby, you’re pale as a biscuit at a funeral. Discreet left the building.”

I laughed into the rag I was using to wipe down the bar. His sister, Imani, my best friend since we were small enough to fit in the same church pew, slid the glass of fake blood across the counter. “Don’t mind Dante,” she said. “He was raised by drag queens and a pressure cooker.”

“Same thing,” Dante called.

The vampire picked up his drink. And that was when I heard him thinking.

I’m half fairy on my mother’s side, which means I hear thoughts the way other people hear a radio left on in another room. Usually it’s just white noise—Dante thinking about seasoning, Imani thinking about her ex, the trucker in the corner thinking about his prostate. But the vampire’s mind came through cold and clear, like a window cracking in winter.

*If Ione’s granddaughter has the gift,* he thought, *she’ll know I was there that night.*

My hand slipped. The glass I was holding hit the floor and shattered.

Imani said, “Ruby?”

Dante said, “Lord, she done dropped another one. Y’all know I love her, but she’s a liability with glassware.”

But I was already staring at the vampire. He was staring back.

*Mama Odette,* I thought. My grandmother. Murdered twelve years ago in her own garden, iron shears through the heart. Fae blood on the roses. Case never solved. My mother said it was a drifter. My daddy said it was a hate crime. The sheriff said it was a shame and then went fishing.

I walked over to the vampire. “You knew my grandmother.”

He set the glass down slowly. “I did.”

“You were there when she died.”

The bar seemed to get quieter, though nobody else knew why. Dante had stopped rattling pots. Imani had her hand under the counter where she kept the baseball bat.

The vampire’s thoughts were careful, arranged like silverware. *Don’t scare her. Don’t lie. She can smell lying.*

“I was in her garden,” he said. “I used to visit her at night. We played chess. She cheated.”

“She always cheated.”

“She used to say the roses grew better when they were cursed.”

I felt my throat tighten. “Who killed her?”

He looked past me, toward the corner booth. Sheriff Hoyt was sitting there, drinking sweet tea, eating peanuts, and thinking about the new bass boat he wanted to buy. I’d known him since I was a kid. He’d pulled me out of a ditch once when my bike went off the road. He’d given me a silver dollar and told me not to tell my mama.

Then I heard his thoughts, and the whole world went sideways.

*That vampire’s still got the rings. I should’ve staked him when I had the chance. Ione should’ve signed the deed. Now her granddaughter’s staring at me like she knows.*

I must have made a sound. Imani looked at me. “Ruby? You’re white as the cook’s apron.”

Dante leaned out again. “Now don’t insult my apron. It’s eggshell.”

I didn’t laugh. I couldn’t. I was reading the sheriff’s mind in a flood now—ugly, splintered thoughts. *Iron shears were her own. Easier to make it look like a robbery. That old fairy land was worth more than she was. Should’ve burned the garden. Should’ve burned the vampire too.*

The vampire said softly, “He used her own shears. I tried to get to her. I was too slow.”

Sheriff Hoyt finally looked up from his peanuts and found all three of us staring at him. His thoughts went sharp and panicked. *Play it cool. She’s half human. She can’t know.*

I said, “Sheriff, you want to tell me why you killed my grandmother?”

The bar went dead quiet. Even the jukebox seemed to hold its breath. Dante came out of the kitchen with a cast-iron skillet in one hand and a wooden spoon in the other.

“Say that again,” the sheriff said, standing up slow. “Because that’s a serious accusation.”

“You used her own shears,” I said. “You wanted her land. You thought nobody would know.”

His hand went to his hip.

Dante said, “Uh-uh, sugar. You pull that gun, I’m gonna have to ruin my skillet on your head, and I just seasoned it.”

The vampire moved faster than I could see. One second he was at the bar, the next he was behind the sheriff, one pale hand clamped on the man’s wrist. Imani grabbed the shotgun from under the counter and pointed it at the ceiling—not at anybody, just enough to make the room remember she had it.

The sheriff’s thoughts were screaming now. *The vampire. The vampire saw me. The fairy girl knows. The cook’s got a skillet.*

“You’re going to sit down,” I told him, “and you’re going to wait for the state police.”

He sat.

Dante leaned against the bar and fanned himself with a menu. “Well,” he said. “Ain’t this a Tuesday.”

Imani called the police. The vampire stood over Sheriff Hoyt like a polite, well-dressed crow. I picked up the broken glass and tried not to shake.

“I’m sorry,” the vampire said quietly. “I should have come sooner.”

I looked at him—at the man who had played chess with my grandmother and cheated and cursed her roses. “You came,” I said. “That’s what matters.”

He nodded. Then he lifted his glass of fake blood. “For what it’s worth,” he said, “this is terrible.”

Dante snorted from the kitchen. “It’s a bar, honey. We sell atmosphere and bad decisions. The blood’s just for tourists.”

So that’s how I found out who killed my grandmother. Not a drifter. Not a monster in the night. Just a man with a badge, a debt, and a hunger for land. The sheriff killed her.

And thanks to a vampire with a conscience and a cook with a skillet, he didn’t get away with it.

template:
Write a story based on the following prompt.

{prompt}
prompt: - A successful movie actor decides to go through and watch his older films . But , while watching , discovers odd things . Scenes he does n't remember , lines that were n't in the script , and interviews he never did . It 's in all his movies , and gets steadily more sinister .
content:
# The Retrospective

The box set arrived on a Tuesday, wrapped in black paper with no note.

Daniel Rourke had never been a watcher of his own work. He could sit through premieres, awards seasons, junkets, even the occasional late-night cable broadcast if he was drunk enough and the remote was far away. But alone, in his own house, with no one to perform for? No. Looking at his younger self felt like visiting a stranger who had stolen his memories and charged rent.

Still, the studio had ordered a retrospective for his lifetime achievement award, and his assistant had left the box on the kitchen island with a sticky note: *“You should probably know what they’re celebrating.”*

So on the first rainy night of his self-imposed exile from Los Angeles, Daniel carried a bottle of whiskey into the home theater, lowered the lights, and began at the beginning.

The first film was *A Small Fire*, a 1997 indie drama about a grocery clerk who dreams of moving west. Daniel had been twenty-six, hungry, and unbearable. He remembered every day of the shoot because it had rained constantly and the director kept saying things like “Truth lives in the pauses.”

He watched himself slouch through a grocery aisle, all cheekbones and manufactured sorrow. It was fine. More than fine, maybe.

Then came the kitchen scene.

His character, Ellis, sits across from the girl he loves. She tells him she’s leaving. He’s supposed to say, *“That’s okay. I mean, what did I expect?”* Daniel remembered the line because he’d fought to cut it. Too self-pitying.

On screen, he said nothing for a long moment.

Then he smiled and whispered, *“You missed the part where I forgive you.”*

Daniel sat up.

The girl on screen kept talking. The scene continued. No one reacted.

Daniel rewound. Watched it again. His younger face, luminous in the kitchen light, formed the words with perfect clarity. The voice was his, but lower, almost fond.

He checked the subtitles.

*You missed the part where I forgive you.*

“Huh,” Daniel said aloud, and took a drink.

He told himself it was an alternate take, something the director had slipped in. Directors did things like that. He’d worked with auteurs. Some of them were pathological.

He pressed play.

The second film was *The Summer We Drowned*, a sun-bleached thriller about four friends and a lake house. Daniel had hated the shoot because of the mosquitoes and the director’s habit of playing Enya between takes. But the film had made him a star.

Halfway through, during a crowded party scene, Daniel noticed a mirror behind his character.

In the mirror, there was a man.

He was standing in the doorway, half hidden by a curtain. Gray coat. Hands at his sides. His face was blurred by the shallow focus, but Daniel could see enough to know it was familiar.

It was his own face. Older. Tired. Or maybe just the angle. Daniel paused. He zoomed in.

The man in the mirror was him, but not as he had been in 1999. It was him now, roughly—same cropped beard, same deep line between the brows, same small scar above the left eyebrow from a car door in 2011.

Daniel felt the hairs on his arms lift.

He rewound and played the scene at quarter speed. The man in the mirror did not move with the crowd. He stood utterly still, eyes fixed on the camera. On Daniel.

Daniel checked the credits. No extra listed. He called the director, who answered on the third ring, sounding sleepy and annoyed.

“The party scene in the lake house,” Daniel said. “Who’s the guy in the mirror?”

“What guy?”

“The one in the gray coat. Behind the curtain.”

There was a long pause. “Daniel, there was no guy. We shot that scene with twelve extras, and I knew every one of them. Also, there was no mirror.”

Daniel looked at the screen. The mirror was there. The man was there.

“Right,” Daniel said. “Sorry. Whiskey.”

He hung up.

The third film was *Night Ledger*, a 2004 crime thriller. Daniel played a corrupt detective who spends most of the movie smoking in stairwells. He remembered the shoot as a blur of night calls and bad coffee. He did not remember the hospital scene.

But there it was, twenty-three minutes in.

His detective walks into a hospital room. A woman lies in bed, pale and terrified. Daniel has never seen her before in his life. She is not in the script. She is not in the credits. The room is shot in a sickly green light, and the camera is too still, too patient.

Daniel’s character leans over the woman.

*“I know what you did with the boy,”* he says.

The woman begins to cry.

*“Don’t,”* she whispers. *“Please.”*

Daniel’s character smiles. It is not an expression Daniel remembers making. It is too wide, too knowing.

He touches her cheek.

Then the scene cuts to black. When it returns, he is back in the stairwell, smoking, as if nothing happened.

Daniel paused the film. His heart was going too fast.

He called the editor, a man named Harris who had worked on six of his movies and still owed him fifty dollars from a poker game in 2008.

“The hospital scene,” Daniel said. “Who wrote it?”

“What hospital scene?”

“In *Night Ledger*. The woman. The boy. What boy?”

Harris was quiet for a moment. “Daniel, there is no hospital scene in *Night Ledger*. I cut the movie. There was never a hospital sequence. We didn’t have the budget for a hospital.”

“I’m looking at it right now.”

“Then you’re looking at something else.”

The line went dead.

Daniel poured another whiskey. He told himself he would stop watching. He told himself it was a prank, a deepfake, some elaborate marketing stunt for the retrospective. But the box set was sealed. The discs were pressed. The anomalies were in the film itself, scratched into the negative like a birthmark.

He opened the bonus features.

There was an interview he did not remember doing.

It was labeled: *PRESS JUNKET — CHICAGO, 2007.*

Daniel had done a hundred junkets in 2007. He had sat in hotel rooms with plastic plants and answered the same seven questions until his soul left his body. But this room was wrong. The curtains were the color of dried blood. The interviewer’s face was never shown; only a hand holding a microphone, and a voice that sounded electronically smoothed.

On screen, Daniel—younger, thinner, wearing a suit he vaguely recognized—sat in a chair with his hands folded.

*“You’ve played a lot of men with secrets,”* the interviewer said. *“What’s yours?”*

On screen, Daniel smiled.

*“I’m practicing being him,”* he said.

The interviewer laughed. It was a sound like a door closing.

*“And how’s that going?”*

*“He’s almost ready.”*

Daniel’s younger self leaned toward the camera.

*“Don’t let him finish the box set.”*

Daniel stopped the playback. His hands were shaking.

He did not sleep that night. He sat in the kitchen with all the lights on, listening to the rain, trying to convince himself that the man in the mirror had been a lighting trick, that the hospital scene was an outtake, that the interview was a deepfake. But he knew his own voice. He knew his own mouth.

At dawn, he called Mara Velez, an archivist he had dated briefly in the early 2000s. She worked at a film preservation lab now, restoring old negatives. She was the only person he could think of who might tell him the truth.

She arrived two hours later with a scanner and a look of professional skepticism.

They watched the anomalies together. Mara said very little. When the hospital scene ended, she rewound it and played it again. Then she took a small magnifying loupe from her bag and held it to the screen.

“The grain pattern is correct,” she said. “The lighting matches the rest of the film. The film stock is from the same batch. This wasn’t digitally inserted.”

“So it was shot?”

“It was shot.” She looked at him. “But not by anyone who’s still alive, according to the credit list.”

They watched the Chicago interview next. Mara paused on Daniel’s younger face and studied the reflection in the hotel window behind him.

“There,” she said.

Daniel leaned in. In the window, behind his younger self, there was a figure. Gray coat. Hands at his sides. The face was mostly obscured by the angle, but the body was unmistakable. It was the same man from *The Summer We Drowned*.

“It’s in every film,” Mara said quietly.

“What?”

She began opening the other discs. She moved through them with the speed of someone who had spent years looking at things most people never noticed. In *A Small Fire*, the man stood at the far end of the grocery aisle, barely a smudge. In *The Summer We Drowned*, he was in the mirror. In *Night Ledger*, he was reflected in a stairwell window. In a 2010 romantic comedy Daniel had made for money and regret, the man was sitting in the back of a café, reading a newspaper with Daniel’s face on the cover.

In a 2016 action film, he was in the back seat of a car, visible for three frames.

In a 2019 prestige drama, he was standing directly behind Daniel in a bathroom mirror, close enough to touch. His face was clear now. It was Daniel’s face, aged by maybe five years. His eyes were flat and patient. His mouth was moving.

Mara paused. “What’s he saying?”

Daniel leaned closer. The words were soundless, but the shape of the mouth was unmistakable.

*“Almost.”*

“It’s a progression,” Mara said. “In every film, he’s closer to the camera. Closer to you. He’s been walking toward the front of the frame for thirty years.”

Daniel felt something cold settle in his chest. “What happens when he gets there?”

Mara did not answer.

They found the last disc at the bottom of the box, wrapped in black paper like the set itself. There was no title on the label, only Daniel’s name and a date: *TODAY.*

“Don’t,” Mara said.

But Daniel had already put it in.

The screen went dark. Then it showed his house.

His living room. His kitchen. His home theater. The camera was mounted high in the corner, the way a security camera would be. The footage was grainy, green-tinted, and entirely real. On screen, Daniel watched himself sitting in the theater chair, remote in hand, face lit by the screen.

But there was someone else in the room.

In the back row, in the shadows, a man in a gray coat sat perfectly still.

Daniel turned around in his chair. The back row was empty.

On screen, the man in the gray coat stood up. He walked down the aisle slowly, deliberately, his face still hidden. The on-screen Daniel did not turn. He kept watching the screen, oblivious.

The man stopped directly behind him.

Then he leaned down and whispered something into Daniel’s ear.

On the recording, Daniel’s body went rigid. His head tilted. His mouth opened.

The man in the gray coat straightened, stepped around the chair, and sat down beside him.

Then he turned to the camera.

It was Daniel’s face. Older. Tired. The same scar above the left eyebrow. The same eyes, but emptier, as if something behind them had been switched off.

He smiled.

*“You missed the part where I forgive you,”* he said.

The screen went black.

For a moment, the room was silent except for the rain. Mara was saying something, but Daniel couldn’t hear her. He was listening to the house.

Somewhere down the hall, a door opened.

Then footsteps.

Slow. Measured. Familiar.

Daniel looked at Mara. Her face had gone white. She was staring past him, toward the entrance of the theater.

Daniel did not want to turn around.

But he did.

In the doorway, a man stood in a gray coat. His face was Daniel’s face, older by a few years, or perhaps just worn down by something Daniel had not yet done. His hands were at his sides. His mouth was moving.

*“Almost,”* he said.

And then he stepped into the room.

{prompt}
prompt: You find a maintenance hatch to Earth .
content:
# Maintenance Access

I found the hatch on a Tuesday, which is a stupid way to start a story about the end of the world, but that’s how it happened.

I was a maintenance tech on Juno Ring, a rusted halo in geostationary orbit, anchored to Earth by a space elevator so old its cables had their own weather. The planet below was a warning: brown oceans, grey continents, cloud decks like bruises. We’d been told the Blight killed it. We lived in the ring because it was safe. We ate printed protein and hydroponic lettuce and pretended we weren’t afraid of the dark.

A pressure alarm went off in sublevel twelve. I went down with a toolkit and a bad attitude. The leak was a cracked seal on a coolant line, easy enough. But behind the line, a panel had been bolted shut for so long the bolts had rusted into little red flowers. I cut them with a plasma torch. The panel fell away. There was a hatch.

It was knee-high, painted the same grey as the wall, with a brass plate that read: **MNT-0 / EARTH. AUTHORIZED ACCESS ONLY.**

I laughed. Earth was a joke. The ring’s schematics didn’t show any hatch here, let alone one that went to Earth. The space elevator’s maintenance shaft was on the other side of the station, behind three security doors and a biometric lock. This was probably an old service crawlway, mislabeled by some dead comedian.

But the handle turned.

Inside was a service elevator, small as a coffin. A handwritten sticker on the wall said: *Battery charged. Please log.* The logbook was empty except for a single entry from 2089: *All clear.* I stepped in. The door closed. I hit the only button: DOWN.

The descent took four hours. I know because I counted the lights on the shaft wall. They were spaced every hundred meters, and there were a lot of them. My ears popped. The elevator hummed. The walls changed from ring steel to elevator composite to something older, concrete streaked with mineral deposits. Then it stopped. The door opened onto a concrete platform.

The air was warm, damp, and smelled like cut grass. I hadn’t smelled cut grass in my life.

I stepped out. There was a sign: **Earth Surface Access — Maintenance Personnel Only.** Beyond it, a path through ferns. Real ferns. Real dirt. A sky, pale blue, with clouds that looked like torn cotton. I cried before I even saw the trees.

The trees were not dead. They were a forest, a real forest, with birds. I heard a woodpecker and didn’t know the word for it until I saw it. I followed the path to a small cottage with solar panels and a greenhouse. An old woman came out with a shotgun. She lowered it when she saw my ring uniform.

“You’re from up there,” she said. Not a question. “Took you long enough.”

Her name was Dr. Aris. She had been a botanist before the Blight, and then a caretaker after. She made tea. The tea was made from mint she grew in the greenhouse. She told me the truth: the Blight had been contained fifty years ago. Earth was alive. It was healing. The quarantine was a lie, but a necessary one. The ring’s population was two hundred thousand people in a fragile tin can. If they knew Earth was habitable, they’d come down in droves, strip the forests for fuel, and finish what the Blight started. The hatch was a maintenance access for the elevator’s ground terminal, used by a small staff to keep the tether’s base station running. It was supposed to be sealed.

“Why not tell anyone?” I asked.

“Because people are people,” she said. “And because the Earth isn’t ready. Maybe in another century.”

I stayed for two hours. She showed me the garden. I ate a strawberry. It was the first real fruit I’d ever tasted. The flavor was so intense it hurt my teeth. She gave me a small jar of soil and a packet of tomato seeds.

“For the ring,” she said. “Grow something. It helps.”

I went back up the elevator. I logged the coolant repair. I didn’t mention the hatch. I didn’t mention the forest. I didn’t mention Dr. Aris or the strawberry. I went to my bunk and stared at the ceiling. The ring hummed. The air recyclers wheezed. I thought about the hatch. It was a maintenance access. My job was to maintain things. But what if the thing that needed maintaining was the truth?

The next week, I took a small bag of soil to the ring’s hydroponics lab. I planted the tomato seeds in a spare tray. They sprouted. They grew. They made tomatoes that were small and ugly and tasted like summer. My supervisor asked where I got the seeds. I said a new strain from the ag lab. No one questioned it. In the ring, no one questions a good tomato.

I went back down three months later. Dr. Aris had a dog now, a scruffy thing that barked at my boots. She showed me the tree she’d planted the year I was born. It was an oak. It was taller than the cottage. I sat under it and listened to the wind. She told me the hatch was still sealed on the ring’s schematics. She told me to keep it that way. I promised.

I visit every few months. I bring back seeds: basil, sunflower, a cutting from a rose. I tell people they’re experimental strains. I’ve become the ring’s unofficial gardener. The maintenance hatch is still there, behind the coolant pipe. Sometimes I stand in front of it and remember the smell of grass. I don’t open it more than I have to.

Some maintenance is just keeping a door closed. Some is learning when to open it. And some is a tomato, growing in a tin can in the sky, proof that the dead world is still alive.

{prompt}
prompt: As you tend your large garden , you notice a naked couple walk unnervingly close to a tree bearing golden fruit ...
content:
# The Golden Fruit

I was staking tomatoes when I saw them.

The garden at Wren Hall is large enough to lose a person in. Hedges divide it into rooms, and the old orchard sits at the center like a heart. I had worked there thirty years and knew every path, every trick of light. So when two naked figures came walking down the gravel walk between the espaliered pears, I knew they did not belong.

They were young, a man and a woman, and they did not hurry. Their skin was pale as the inside of a mushroom, unmarked by sun or thorn. They moved with a careless grace, as if the garden had been made for them. I called out. They did not startle. They turned, and the woman smiled.

“We are looking for the tree,” she said.

“What tree?” I asked, though I knew.

“The one with the golden fruit.”

My mouth went dry. The tree stood at the end of the walled orchard, behind a low iron fence I had been hired to maintain. The owner, Mrs. Alcott, was ninety-two and seldom left the house. She had one rule: no one goes near the golden tree. She paid me well and never asked questions. I had never seen the fruit up close. From a distance it looked like small apples, or maybe pears, each one glowing as if a candle burned inside. In autumn, when the leaves fell, the fruit stayed on the branches, never softening, never dropping.

I stepped into their path. “You can’t go there,” I said. “It’s not safe.”

The man looked at me. His eyes were the color of honey. “Why?”

“It’s the owner’s rule.”

“We have come a long way,” the woman said. “We only want to look.”

They walked around me. Not aggressively—they simply moved as if I were a gate that had swung open. I followed. The gravel was cool under my boots; their bare feet made no sound. I noticed they left no prints in the damp path. My heart began to beat hard.

“You need clothes,” I said, stupidly. “There’s a shed. I can get you a blanket.”

“We are not cold,” the man said.

The woman stopped and turned to me. “You tend this garden,” she said. “Do you ever wonder why the tree is here?”

I shook my head. “I just keep the weeds down.”

“Then you are the perfect gardener for this place,” she said, and there was something in her voice I didn’t like. Pity, maybe.

We reached the iron fence. Beyond it, the tree stood in a circle of unmown grass. Its trunk was thick and twisted, its leaves dark and glossy. The golden fruit hung heavy, each one perfect. The air around it smelled sweet and strange, like rain on hot stone. The couple stood at the fence, their hands on the bars. I thought of the portrait in the hall, the one Mrs. Alcott kept turned to the wall. I had glimpsed it once, when she sent me to dust the library. A man and a woman, naked, under a tree. The woman had the same smile.

“Please,” I said. “She’ll have my job.”

The woman looked at me. “She cannot have what you do not own.”

The man reached over the fence and touched the trunk. I saw a shiver go through the leaves, though there was no wind. The fruit swayed. One of them, the lowest, began to turn slightly, as if on a string. The man lifted his hand. The fruit came loose and dropped into his palm. It was not gold, exactly; it was the color of sunlight through honey. He held it out to the woman. She took it.

“You don’t understand,” I said. “It’s not food. She says it’s a poison.”

“It is not poison,” the woman said. “It is memory.”

She bit into it. The sound was crisp, like an apple. I expected her to fall, to choke, to turn to dust. Instead, she closed her eyes. Tears ran down her cheeks. The man took the fruit from her and took a bite. He laughed, then stopped, then covered his face.

“What do you see?” I asked, though I didn’t want to know.

The woman opened her eyes. They were wet and very bright. “Everything,” she said. “The first morning. The gate. The angel. The long walk. The children we buried. The world we built. The world we broke.”

The man said, “We forgot it. For a long time. We forgot who we were.”

I looked at the tree. The branches were empty now. Every fruit had fallen. They lay on the grass, pulsing with light. The couple stepped through the fence—it was not locked; I had never locked it—and knelt in the grass. They gathered the fruit into their laps. They did not eat any more. They simply held it.

I heard footsteps on the gravel. Mrs. Alcott was walking toward us, her black coat brushing the roses. She was old, but she moved quickly. She stopped at the fence and looked at the couple. Her face was pale and furious and sad.

“Mother,” she said. “Father.”

The woman looked up. “Elspeth,” she said. “You kept the tree.”

“I kept the tree,” Mrs. Alcott said. “I kept everything. You left me here. You left me with the garden and the gate and the fruit that never rots.”

“We had to leave,” the man said. “You know that.”

“I know nothing,” Mrs. Alcott said. “You ate the fruit and you knew, and you still left. You left us in the world you made.”

The woman stood. She was naked and unashamed. She reached through the fence and touched Mrs. Alcott’s cheek. “We are sorry,” she said. “We have been sorry for a hundred years. We came back to return it.”

“Return what?”

“The memory,” the woman said. “We cannot carry it anymore.”

She held out a fruit. Mrs. Alcott stared at it. She was trembling. I stood very still, the way you do when a wild animal is near. The garden was quiet. Even the bees had stopped.

Mrs. Alcott took the fruit. She was ninety-two, and her hands were spotted and thin. She held the fruit like a child. Then she bit into it. I saw her eyes go wide. She gasped, and for a moment she looked young, then old, then young again. She sat down in the grass outside the fence. The couple sat with her. They did not speak. They passed the fruit between them, each taking a small bite, and the light from it moved over their faces. I thought I should leave, but I couldn’t.

Finally, Mrs. Alcott stood. She looked at me. “You can go home,” she said. “The garden is finished.”

“What about the tree?” I asked.

She looked at the golden fruit scattered on the grass. “Let it rot,” she said. “It has done its work.”

I walked back to the shed and put away my tools. When I came out, the garden was empty. The iron fence stood open. The tree was bare. The three of them were gone, and the grass where they had sat was already springing back up. I never saw Mrs. Alcott again. The house was sold. The garden was dug up for a housing development. But sometimes, in late summer, I smell that sweet, strange scent, like rain on hot stone, and I remember the naked couple walking toward the golden tree, and I wonder what they remembered. I wonder what I would remember, if I had taken a bite. I think I know. I think it would be this: the garden, the light, the sound of their bare feet on the gravel, and the way they looked at each other before they ate. That is enough. That is more than enough.

prompt: You arrive in the year 1000 , and all you have are the clothes on your back , a laptop with the entire Wikipedia library , and a solar charger .
content:
# The Mirror of Small Things

I woke on a shingle beach with my cheek against cold stones and the taste of salt in my mouth.

For a moment I thought I had fallen asleep on a camping trip. Then I sat up and saw the sea, gray and enormous, and behind me a country of wet grass, thorn trees, and smoke rising from a cluster of huts no bigger than a football pitch. No road. No power lines. No sound of engines. Just gulls and wind and a dog barking somewhere far off.

I had my jeans, my hoodie, my waterproof jacket, and my sneakers. I had a laptop in a padded shoulder bag and a folded solar charger in the side pocket. That was all.

I did not know yet that it was the year 1000. I only knew I was not where I had been.

I opened the laptop on the beach, shielding the screen with my jacket. The offline Wikipedia library opened like a door into a house I had lost. I searched *survival priorities*. I searched *edible seaweed*. I searched *how to make fire without matches* and then realized I had no water, no food, and no idea where I was.

I was still staring at the screen when a boy found me.

He was maybe ten, wrapped in a wool cloak the color of wet bark, carrying a stick. He stopped when he saw me. I must have looked like something washed up from another world—blue jeans, bright jacket, a black rectangle glowing faintly under my arm.

I raised my hands. “Hello,” I said. “I’m lost.”

He ran.

I found the village before dusk, because I followed the smoke. It was a huddle of timber huts with thatched roofs and a muddy track between them. People stared. A woman crossed herself. A man picked up an axe. I stopped well away and sat down on the grass with my empty hands open.

That was the first thing Wikipedia had told me, really. Not in those words. But I had read enough about first contact and ethnography to know that a stranger appearing out of nowhere should be small, still, and unthreatening.

A monk came out of a small stone church at the edge of the village. He was thin and weathered, with a shaved crown and a cross on a cord around his neck. He spoke to me in a language I did not understand. I shook my head. He tried again, slower.

Then I remembered the laptop. I opened it, tilted the screen away from the villagers, and searched *Latin phrases*. I pointed at one.

*Salve. Amicus. Peregrinus.*

The monk’s eyes went wide. He looked at the screen, then at me, then at the screen again. He said something that sounded like a question. I searched *I am from far away*. I found *e terra longinqua venio*. I pointed.

He crossed himself.

That night I slept in the church porch, under a borrowed blanket that smelled of sheep and smoke. I did not sleep much. I kept the laptop closed and my hand on it like a talisman. The solar charger lay against my chest, useless until morning.

The monk’s name was Brother Eadric. He fed me barley bread and thin ale and tried to teach me words. I tried to learn. I had no dictionary for Old English, but I had Wikipedia. I searched *Old English language*, *Old English phrases*, *history of England 1000*. I read until the battery dropped below sixty percent and then I made myself close the lid.

I learned that the year was around the turn of the first millennium. I learned that I was probably somewhere in England, though I could not be sure. I learned that the world I had come from was not just far away. It had not happened yet.

For the first week, I was a curiosity and a burden. I helped carry wood. I learned to say *water*, *bread*, *thank you*. I watched where people went to the toilet and where they drew drinking water and saw that the two places were not nearly far enough apart. I searched *handwashing* and *boiling water* and *sanitation*. I did not preach. I just began washing my hands before I ate, and once, when a child cut his foot on a flint, I asked for clean water and honey and a strip of linen.

The mother looked at Brother Eadric. He shrugged. He was a monk, not a physician.

I cleaned the wound. I smeared it with honey. I wrapped it. The child screamed, then stopped. Three days later, the cut was not oozing. It was not red and swollen. It was healing.

After that, people began to bring me small hurts. A woman with a burn. A man with a bad tooth. A girl with a fever and a dry mouth. I searched *oral rehydration* and mixed boiled water with a little salt and honey, and made her sip it slowly. She lived. Maybe she would have lived anyway. But the village decided I was useful.

The laptop became my secret. I charged it during the day, when the sun was out, laying the panel on the church roof where no one could see. I used it only at night, under my blanket, with the brightness turned down. I read about wound care and childbirth and crop rotation and soap. I read about the history I was now living inside. I read about the Vikings and the Danes and the kingdoms of England, and I understood that the people around me were not living in a story. They were living in the middle of one, and no one had told them the ending.

Brother Eadric knew about the laptop. He had seen it on the first day. He did not understand it, but he was a practical man. He decided it was either a miracle or a temptation, and that either way it was better kept quiet. He let me charge it in the monastery scriptorium when the sun was strong. He told no one.

For a while, that was enough. I was not comfortable, exactly. I was cold a lot. I was hungry sometimes. I missed soap and coffee and the sound of traffic. But I was alive, and I had a purpose. I taught the village to dig its latrines downhill from the well. I taught the children to wash their hands before they ate. I learned enough Old English to explain that bad water could kill, and that it was not a punishment from God but a thing you could see if you looked closely enough.

Then the lord came.

His name was Leofric, and he came to the village with ten men and a demand for grain. He was limping. A wound on his calf had gone black at the edges and smelled sweet. The village headman brought him to me because he had heard there was a stranger who could heal.

I looked at the leg and felt my stomach drop. I searched *gangrene* that night. I read about debridement and infection and the limits of what could be done without antibiotics. I read about honey again. I read about willow bark for pain. I read about cleanliness.

In the morning, I cleaned the wound with boiled water. I cut away the dead flesh—there was a knife, and there was me trying not to shake. I packed it with honey and clean linen. I made him drink willow-bark tea. I told him, through Brother Eadric, that if the leg turned black and hard and he could not feel it, they should take it off. I did not know if I could do that. I did not want to find out.

Leofric survived. The leg healed, ugly and scarred, but whole. He gave me a silver coin and a piece of land at the edge of the village. He also asked to see the shining book.

He had heard about it, of course. Secrets in a village are like water in a cracked pot. Someone had seen the glow through the church window. Someone had told someone.

I brought the laptop out at the lord’s hall, with the screen dark. I told him it was a relic. A closed book of knowledge from a far country. I told him it was dangerous to open without prayer and fasting, and that its light could blind an unworthy man. It was nonsense, but it was useful nonsense. Leofric looked at the black slab and then at my face, and he decided he did not want to risk blindness.

He made me his physician anyway.

The next years were not easy. I was still a stranger. I was still watched. When a cow died or a child took a fever, some people whispered that I had brought bad luck. A traveling priest once called me a sorcerer. Leofric laughed and said a sorcerer who could save a man’s leg was worth more than a priest who could not.

I learned to make soap from ash and fat. I learned to keep the village well away from the latrine field. I learned to set bones and treat burns and recognize the signs of childbirth going wrong early enough to call for help. I learned to write down what I knew, because the laptop was not going to last forever.

The battery had begun to fail by the third winter. The solar charger still worked, but the screen flickered. The fan rattled. I copied pages by candlelight onto parchment, in a clumsy hand, with Brother Eadric correcting my Latin and my spelling. We made a book. It was not Wikipedia. It was a thin, stubborn thing: clean water, clean hands, honey on wounds, willow bark for pain, how to build a latrine, how to recognize a broken bone, how to keep a mother alive after childbirth. We made three copies. The monastery kept one. Leofric kept one, though he could not read it. I kept one.

On the last day the laptop turned on, I was alone in my hut. Outside, the rain was coming down hard. The screen glowed for about four minutes. I opened the offline encyclopedia one last time and searched *year 1000*.

There it was: a world on the edge of a new millennium. People who thought the world might end. Kingdoms I had only read about. A century that had not yet built the things I missed. The screen dimmed. I read one line about the Abbey of Waltham, or maybe I imagined it. Then the screen went black.

I sat there for a long time with the dead machine on my knees. I had carried the whole of human knowledge in a bag across a thousand years, and in the end it had done what knowledge does. It had leaked out, one small fix at a time.

I never went home. I do not know if there was a way home. But I did not die of hunger or cold or infection. I married a widow named Ælfgifu, who could gut a fish faster than anyone I have ever met. We had a son. I taught him to wash his hands. I taught him to read. I taught him that the world is not made of magic, mostly. It is made of small things done carefully.

When I am old, I will tell him about the black mirror that held every book in the world. He will not believe me. That is all right.

I have a book of my own now. It is not very big. It is not very accurate. But the village uses it, and the monastery copies it, and a girl in the next valley has learned to boil water before she gives it to her baby.

The year is not 1000 anymore. I have stopped counting. The world did not end. It just went on, one small fix at a time.

prompt: You wake up in a pile of hay , you are the infamous Wizard of the Beer .
content:
I woke up in a pile of hay with straw in my beard and a headache that was either a goblin war band or the aftermath of my own “Festive Thunderbrew.” Given the empty tankard clutched in my hand, it was probably both.

My name is—well, the wanted posters call me the Wizard of the Beer. They usually add a reward, a crude drawing of my hat, and the words “Approach with caution; may cause spontaneous fermentation.” I am a wizard of modest talent and immodest brewing. I can turn a keg of sour mash into a potion of courage, a barrel of barley into a love charm, or a quiet tavern into a riot in under an hour. The last one is why I’m infamous.

I sat up. The barn spun gently around me. My pointy hat was perched on a rooster, who was staring at me as though he had personally witnessed my worst decisions. My wand—a copper spigot with a hawthorn handle—was jammed into a fence post. Somewhere outside, men were shouting and armor was clanking. That was never a good sign before breakfast.

A girl of about twelve appeared in the barn doorway, carrying a bucket and a pitchfork. She looked at me, then at the wanted poster nailed to the wall, then back at me.

“You’re him,” she said. “The Wizard of the Beer.”

“I prefer ‘beverage thaumaturge,’” I said.

“Da says you turned the Duke’s prize stallion into a cask of lager.”

“It was a very smooth lager,” I said. “And the Duke shouldn’t have called my triple-bock ‘fizzy peasant water.’”

The girl’s name was Mira. She told me the Duke’s men were in the village, searching for me. They’d already arrested the blacksmith for whistling suspiciously. The village well had gone sour. The winter ale had spoiled. Her mother was sick. And the rooster wearing my hat had started following her around like a feathered disciple.

“Can you help us?” she asked.

I looked at the barn: a barrel of sour mash, a sack of barley, a crock of honey, and a lump of magical yeast I keep in my hat for emergencies. The rooster clucked. My hat fell off.

“Child,” I said, “I once turned a fountain into a passable mild ale. I can save anyone. But first, I need three eggs, a copper pot, and something that has never been afraid.”

The rooster looked nervous.

We worked fast. I built a brewing rig from a milk pail, a lambskin, and a horseshoe. I sang the Fermentation Hymn in the key of G, which made the mash bubble like a swamp in a hurry. The yeast did its work. By noon, I had a barrel of “Hair of the Dog” ale—golden, fragrant, with a head like a thundercloud. It had one simple magical property: it made anyone who drank it remember exactly what they’d forgotten.

The Duke’s men kicked in the barn door as I tapped the barrel. There were four of them in blue cloaks, holding pikes and wearing expressions like they’d been weaned on lemons.

“By order of Duke Aldric,” said the captain, “you will come with us to answer for the stallion.”

“Gentlemen,” I said, “let’s not be hasty. Have a drink. On the house.”

“We don’t drink with criminals,” he sneered.

Mira said, “It’s true. He’s a criminal. But he’s also a terrible wizard, so if you arrest him, you’ll have to explain the goat.”

The captain hesitated.

I poured four mugs. The ale did what “Hair of the Dog” does. The captain drank, blinked, and said, “The Duke didn’t order this. The chancellor did. He said the Wizard of the Beer cursed the stallion to raise taxes on ale.”

There was muttering. The guards lowered their pikes.

By evening, we’d marched back to the Duke’s keep with a barrel and a confession. The chancellor tried to flee, but tripped over the rooster, who had followed me because it liked my hat. The stallion was restored—though for a week it smelled faintly of lager and would only drink from a tankard. The Duke, embarrassed, pardoned me on the condition that I brew his wedding ale.

I did. It was magnificent. Everyone danced for three days, the bride floated six inches off the ground, and no one turned into a goat.

They still call me infamous. I suppose I deserve it. But now, when I wake up in a pile of hay, it’s usually because I’ve chosen to. That, and because the rooster insists on sleeping on my hat.

prompt: Hmm , kitten ...
content:
**The Thimble Thief**

“Hmm, kitten…”

Tessa stopped in the doorway of her repair shop with a mug of cold tea in one hand and a growing suspicion that she had not locked the display cabinet the night before.

The kitten on her workbench was small, black, and entirely unrepentant. It sat with its tail curled neatly around its paws and Tessa’s grandmother’s silver thimble clamped in its mouth like a tiny pirate with treasure.

“That is not yours,” Tessa said.

The kitten blinked.

“And it is enchanted. It stitches things back together whether you want them stitched or not.”

The kitten glanced at the sleeve of Tessa’s cardigan, where a loose button dangled by a thread, and somehow managed to look smug.

Tessa set down her tea and approached slowly. The kitten watched her with luminous green eyes. It did not run. It did not even flinch when she crouched to its level. It simply sat there, thimble in mouth, radiating the ancient confidence of a creature that had never once been told no.

“All right,” she murmured. “Where did you come from?”

No collar. No tag. Only a smear of chimney soot along one ear and the faint smell of rain. The shop’s cat flap had been stuck for months, but the kitten had clearly found another way in. Tessa glanced toward the back room, where the small window over the sink was open exactly three inches—the width of a determined cat.

The kitten hopped off the workbench and trotted toward the door.

“No,” Tessa said. “Give me the thimble.”

The kitten looked back at her. Then it pushed through the cat flap, which swung open with a creak that proved it had not been stuck at all.

Tessa stared. “You little liar.”

She grabbed her coat.

The kitten led her through the wet streets of Hallowick, tail high, pausing every few rooftops to make sure she was following. It moved like a small shadow with opinions. Past the bakery, past the clockmaker’s shop, past the row of crooked houses where the rain always fell a little sideways. Finally it slipped through the iron fence of the old Bellweather house—the one that had been boarded up since before Tessa was born.

Tessa hesitated. Every sensible part of her said to go home. But the thimble had been her grandmother’s, and the kitten was now sitting on the porch steps, waiting, the silver glint still visible in its mouth.

“Hmm,” she said. “Fine.”

The front door was not locked. It opened at her touch, shedding dust and a smell of old smoke. Inside, the house was dark and quiet, except for a faint sound from the parlor: a child humming.

Tessa followed the sound.

In the parlor, a girl sat cross-legged on the floor. She was maybe seven, pale as candle smoke, and translucent at the edges. A ghost. She held a doll in her lap—a cloth rabbit with one button eye and a torn seam along its belly.

The kitten trotted to her and dropped the thimble into her small hand.

“Thank you, Pepper,” the girl said.

Tessa’s mouth opened. Then closed. “Pepper?”

The girl looked up, startled. “You can see me?”

“I’m a witch,” Tessa said, as if that explained everything. It usually did. “Who are you?”

“Lila. I live here.” The girl frowned. “I did. I was waiting for my mother. There was a fire, and then I was still here, and no one came back.” She held up the rabbit. “Mr. Buttons got torn. Pepper brings me things to fix him, but I can’t sew.”

The kitten—Pepper—sat beside Lila and washed one paw as though his work here was done.

Tessa knelt. “The thimble won’t help unless you know how to use it.”

Lila’s lip trembled. “I tried. It only made the thread go crooked.”

Tessa looked at the rabbit, at the ghost girl, at the ridiculous black kitten who had stolen from her in order to help someone else. “May I?”

Lila nodded.

Tessa took the thimble, threaded a needle with a bit of red yarn from her pocket, and began to sew. The enchanted silver warmed against her thumb. The rabbit’s seam closed neatly, and the loose button eye tightened. When she was finished, Mr. Buttons looked almost new.

Lila hugged him to her chest. “He’s better.”

“He is,” Tessa said. “And so are you, I think.”

Lila looked down at her translucent hands. “I don’t have to wait anymore?”

“No,” Tessa said gently. “You don’t.”

The ghost girl smiled. She began to fade—softly, like morning mist. Before she vanished, she kissed Pepper on the top of his head. “Goodbye, Pepper.”

The kitten meowed once. It was a very small sound.

Then Tessa was alone in the old house with a black kitten and a silver thimble.

She carried Pepper home in her coat pocket. He fell asleep against her ribs, purring like a tiny engine. At the shop, she set out a saucer of milk and a cushion by the stove. The kitten ate, washed his face, and climbed onto the cushion as though he had always lived there.

Tessa looked at him for a long moment.

“You’re a menace,” she said.

Pepper yawned.

“And you’re staying, apparently.”

He tucked his nose under his tail.

Tessa sighed, but she was smiling. She put her grandmother’s thimble back in the cabinet, then left the cabinet door unlocked.

Just in case.

prompt: Mission Compromised ! ABORT ! ABORT !
content:
# The Last Honest Thing

Kira had ninety seconds and a lie in her ear.

The Black Ledger sat in the vault of the Meridian Auction House, a wafer of sapphire glass no larger than a thumbnail. It held names, payments, and the quiet architecture of a dozen governments’ sins. Her gloved fingers were steady as she slid it from its cradle.

“Package secured,” she murmured.

“Copy.” Ellis, her handler, sounded like he was smiling. “You’re clear to exfil. Service lift, basement level. I’m bringing the van around.”

Kira stepped over the guard she hadn’t killed—just persuaded with a pressure point and a very sincere apology. The corridor smelled of ozone and expensive carpet cleaner. Outside, Prague’s winter rain tapped the windows like impatient fingers.

Then her earpiece cracked.

“Mission Compromised ! ABORT ! ABORT !”

The words hit like a gunshot. Kira froze halfway to the lift.

Abort protocol was simple: destroy the package, ditch the gear, exfil by the secondary route. It was not a suggestion. It was command, filtered through Ellis.

She waited for the correction code. Every handler added one after an abort order: three numbers, a safe word, proof the line wasn’t compromised. Ellis said nothing.

“Ellis,” she said quietly. “Confirm abort.”

Static. Then: “No time. Abort. Abort now.”

There it was. The pause before the second *abort*, the tiny catch in his throat. And in the background, barely audible under the rain, a man’s voice said, “Tell her again.”

Kira’s blood went cold.

She looked at the lift. Its brass doors gleamed. If Ellis was captured, whoever had him knew her extraction route. The lift was a coffin.

“Copy abort,” she said.

She did not destroy the ledger.

Instead, she slipped it into the seam of her sleeve and walked in the other direction, toward the stairwell. Her heartbeat counted for her. One. Two. Three.

The earpiece buzzed. “Kira? You copy?”

“I copy,” she said. “Heading to secondary.”

“Good. Good girl.”

*Girl* was not Ellis’s word. Ellis called her “Voss” when he was annoyed, “kid” when he was proud. Never *girl*.

She took the stairs two at a time. On the tenth floor, she yanked the fire alarm. The building did not scream. The Meridian had bought a silent alarm—a polite, expensive pulse of amber lights and recorded instructions. But the kitchen heard it. In the service corridor, catering staff began stacking trays; the security team began moving.

Kira used the noise. She ducked into a coat closet, stripped off the waiter’s jacket, and turned her uniform inside out to the courier gray beneath. She clipped a fake ID to her collar. Then she tapped her comm twice, the old signal.

Ellis answered too fast. “Voss?”

“Where are you?”

“Basement. Get to the—”

“Where are you *physically*, Ellis?”

Silence. Then the man’s voice again, closer now: “Ask her if she has the ledger.”

Kira closed her eyes. There was only one way out that didn’t involve walking into a trap. She pulled the fire alarm’s manual call point from the wall, smashed the glass, and jammed the sprinkler override with her multitool. The penthouse floor above them erupted into a waterfall.

Guests screamed. The auction’s security detail rushed upward, boots thundering past her closet. Kira slipped out behind them and took the freight elevator down three levels instead of nine.

In the basement, she found the service tunnel. The van was there, parked under a flickering light. Ellis sat in the front passenger seat. Beside him, a man in a black coat held a pistol against Ellis’s ribs. Two more stood at the tunnel’s mouth.

Kira stepped out of the shadows with her hands up.

“Miss Voss,” the man said. “The ledger.”

“I don’t have it,” she said. “I staged a decoy. It’s on its way to the roof with the auction’s internal courier. You can catch it if you run.”

The man studied her. He was not stupid. But he was greedy. He nodded to one of his men, who spoke into a radio, then cursed.

“Roof team says a courier just hit the helipad.”

The man in the coat smiled. “Then we’ll take the real one from your corpse later.” He pulled Ellis out of the van by the collar. “Come on. Both of you.”

That was when Kira triggered the van’s anti-theft system—a little modification of her own. The horn blared, the lights flashed, and the side door slid open with a hydraulic hiss. In that second of distraction, Ellis drove an elbow into his captor’s throat. Kira drew the pistol she’d taken from the guard upstairs and put two rounds into the tunnel’s ceiling sprinkler main.

Water and darkness exploded.

They ran. Ellis was bleeding from a cut above his eye, swearing in three languages. Kira shoved him into the stairwell and pulled the ledger from her sleeve.

“Decoy?” he gasped.

“Actually no. There is no decoy.”

“You lied to armed men.”

“I do it professionally.”

They broke through the ground floor into the rain. Behind them, the tunnel alarms joined the fire alarms in a chorus. A black sedan screeched around the corner—their backup, finally.

Only when they were three streets away did Ellis say, “The abort was real, you know. Command got a burst from the Meridian’s internal security. They thought you were burned.”

“They were wrong.”

“Or they wanted the ledger more than they wanted you.” He looked at her. “The man holding me? He had a comm unit with our frequencies. Someone gave him that.”

Kira turned the sapphire wafer over in her fingers. It caught the streetlight, cold and bright. “Then I guess we have a second mission.”

Ellis laughed, tired and shaky. “What’s that?”

She inserted the ledger into the car’s secured reader. Names began to scroll across the screen—contracts, payments, codes. One name appeared near the top of the list, under a payment marked MERIDIAN.

It was Ellis’s.

The car went very quiet. Ellis looked at her. Kira looked back.

Her earpiece crackled with command again: “Kira. Status.”

She touched the comm. “Mission compromised,” she said softly. “Abort. Abort.”

Then she crushed the earpiece under her heel and turned the car toward the river.
