prompt: The Earth is made of memory foam and humans have developed a nomadic lifestyle to keep from sinking too far in .
content:
**The Ground Remembers**

The Earth was made of memory foam. Not the thin mattress of the old world, but the whole crust, kilometers deep, a slow-rebounding skin over a molten heart. Every step left a dimple. Every house, if you stayed, made a grave.

So we became nomads. Not because we loved the road, but because the road forgot us faster than we could settle.

My brother Tam was supposed to be in his hammock. He wasn’t. I found him on the ground behind the cook tent, curled on his side like a comma. The foam had already accepted him. A Tam-shaped bowl had formed around his body, its edges rising gently to his ribs.

“Tam.”

He didn’t open his eyes. “I’m listening.”

“To what?”

“Her.”

My stomach tightened. Since Mother sank, Tam had started talking like the ground was a radio. I grabbed his arm. It took more force than it should have. The foam made a wet kissing sound as I peeled him free.

“You can’t sleep on the ground,” I said. “You know the rules.”

He sat up, blinking. He was twelve, all elbows and stubbornness. “I wasn’t sleeping. I was pressing.”

Pressing was what we called it when someone went looking for old imprints. Rememberers did it with their palms, gently, for a count of ten. Tam had been doing it with his whole body.

The camp was waking. Wagons on their broad oval wheels began to creak. People struck hammocks from frames, folded them, shifted their weight from foot to foot as they worked. Nobody stood still. You cooked on a moving board; you ate while pacing; you told stories in a slow circle around the fire. Children learned the dance before they learned to read. The earth was a mattress, my father used to say, and we were all bad sleepers. If you lay down too long, it remembered you. And if it remembered you hard enough, it swallowed you.

Old Rill, our caravan leader, came over. She had a face like a crumpled map and eyes that missed nothing. She looked at the depression Tam had left, then at Tam.

“Second time this week,” she said.

Tam stared at his feet. His shoes were the right kind—broad as dinner plates—but he’d taken them off. Bare feet sank faster.

“He’s a kid,” I said. “He forgets.”

Rill’s mouth did something that wasn’t quite a smile. “The ground doesn’t forget. You know the law, Lio. If he can’t keep pace, we leave him at the next firm field. I won’t lose forty families to one boy’s grief.”

She didn’t say it cruelly. That was the worst part. Rill had left her own husband at the Pause three years ago when his legs gave out. The caravan had sung his name for a mile, then never spoken it again.

I nodded. “He’ll keep pace.”

Rill looked at Tam. “See that he does.”

That morning we walked. We always walked. The caravan was a long caterpillar of painted wagons, pack goats with booties, children in harnesses, old people carried in litters that distributed their weight across six poles. We followed the fallow route, a wide belt of ground that hadn’t been camped on in a generation. The surface was firm here, springy but resilient. My boots left shallow prints that faded behind me like breath on glass.

Tam walked beside me, dragging his feet. I tapped his ankle with my staff. “Lift.”

“It hurts.”

“Everything hurts. Lift.”

He lifted. For a while we walked in silence. The prairie rolled out in slow swells, pale green and gray. Here and there were the scars of old stillness: a ring of deep footprints around a cold firepit, a wagon rut that had become a trench, a lone boot half-swallowed by the ground. The foam slowly rebounded, but not always completely. Heavy things left shadows. People left hollows.

“Mother didn’t leave a hollow,” Tam said suddenly.

I kept my eyes on the horizon. “No.”

“They said she sank at the Pause. But there’s no imprint. I asked Rill. She said the foam closed over her.”

“The Pause is soft ground. It closes.”

“Then how do I find her?”

I didn’t answer. I had been asking myself that for a year.

At noon we stopped to eat, which meant we ate while walking. The children played a game where they tried to step only in new ground, avoiding each other’s footprints. It was a game and a lesson. I watched Tam watch them. He didn’t join.

That night we camped on a field of old imprints. Rill chose it deliberately. It was a Remembering Place, a wide shallow bowl where generation after generation of nomads had pressed their hands into the foam before moving on. The ground was covered in palm prints, some small as a child’s, some spread wide as a man’s. The Rememberers said the foam held a little of the person in each print—not their soul, not their thoughts, just the fact of them. The weight of a life, briefly.

Tam stood at the edge, staring.

“Don’t,” I said.

“I’m not going to sink.”

“You’re going to try.”

He looked at me, and for a second he was just a kid again, scared and tired. “I can feel her here, Lio. Not her. But someone. Someone who was sad. Someone who was old.”

“That’s not her.”

“I know.”

I should have dragged him away. Instead I stood with him. The sun went down. The campfires were spaced wide, each on a metal plate. People ate standing up, shifting from foot to foot. The ground beneath us was a braille of the dead.

Tam knelt. He pressed one hand into a palm print. Then the other. Then he lay down, carefully, on his side, in a shape that wasn’t his.

I counted to ten. Then twenty. Then I pulled him up.

He was crying. “It’s not enough.”

“What?”

“Remembering. It’s not enough. I want her to remember me.”

I held his shoulders. The foam beneath us was already cupping the shape of his knees. “Tam.”

“She didn’t choose to leave us,” he said. “She was just standing still.”

I closed my eyes. The truth was a splinter I’d carried for a year. Mother had been caught in a soft pocket during a storm. I was six. She’d pushed me onto firm ground and stayed behind to hold the wagon steady while the others got clear. By the time they pulled, the foam had her to the waist. She told them to go. She said the ground would keep her warm.

I had watched from the wagon, counting her breaths. I had reached a hundred before Rill carried me away.

“She didn’t want to stay,” I said.

“How do you know?”

“Because she pushed me.”

Tam shook his head. “That doesn’t mean she wanted to leave.”

“No. But it means she wanted me to keep moving.”

He looked at the ground, at the shallow hollow he had made. It was already rebounding, the edges softening. In an hour it would be gone.

“I don’t know how to carry her,” he said.

I didn’t either. But I knew how to walk. I took off my boots. The grass was cool and damp. I knelt beside him and pressed my palm into the foam, hard, until the print was deep and clean. Then I lifted my hand. The print stayed, a perfect small hollow.

“That’s it,” I said. “That’s carrying.”

Tam looked at it. Then he pressed his palm next to mine. His print was smaller, but deep. We knelt there, not moving, until the count of ten. Then I stood and pulled him up.

The next morning, Rill called the move before dawn. The camp dissolved in a clatter of poles and wheels. Tam walked beside me, lifting his feet. His prints were shallow. By noon they had faded.

We passed the Pause two days later. It was a wide soft field, dangerous and avoided. From the ridge, you could see the old wagon ruts curving in, then stopping. The ground there was smooth as a bedsheet. No hollows. No prints. The foam had closed over everything.

Tam stopped at the edge. I stopped with him. We didn’t speak. We didn’t press. We just looked.

Then I touched his shoulder. “Walk.”

He walked. We both did. The ground sighed under our boots, remembering us for a moment, then letting us go. Behind us, the Pause lay still and soft and full of everything we couldn’t hold. Ahead, the fallow route stretched out, firm and springy and new.

We kept moving. That was how we remembered.

content:
# Satan Is a Job Title

On the first day of campaign season, someone keyed my car and wrote BURN IN HELL across the windshield. Since we were already in Hell, this was less a threat than a zoning complaint.

My name is Jo Fisk. In life, I managed a city council race in Ohio. In death, I managed the re-election campaign of the Satan. Not *a* Satan. *The* Satan. The office.

This distinction matters more than you’d think. The free underworld had spent six centuries clawing its way out of divine-right monarchy, and the result was a constitution, a bicameral legislature, a surprisingly aggressive consumer-protection bureau, and a democratically elected office at the top called “Satan.” The Satan signed treaties with Heaven, set torment quotas, managed the lava infrastructure, and opened the annual Brimstone Fair. The office came with ceremonial horns and a very large gavel. It did not come with a personality cult, or at least it wasn’t supposed to.

The current Satan was a gray-winged bureaucrat named Vesper. She had been elected seven infernal years ago on a platform of “Competence, Transparency, and Fewer Screaming Pits Near Schools.” She was honest, tireless, and about as charismatic as a filing cabinet. Her approval rating had been sliding ever since the price of brimstone doubled.

Her opponent was Lord Malacoda, a silver-tongued demon with a podcast, a private airship shaped like a jawbone, and the sort of smile that made you check your wallet and your soul.

His slogan was: *I’m not a politician. I’m a Satan.*

This was, technically, a grammatical error. Satan was not a name. It was a job title, like mayor or night manager. But Malacoda’s ads ran anyway, all fire and drums, while a deep voice growled that the underworld had grown soft. Too many rules. Too many damned souls with rights. Too many forms to fill out before you could legally flay someone.

“Make the Pit Great Again,” the signs said.

I hated the signs. I hated that they worked.

---

Our campaign headquarters was a former torture chamber on the corner of Despair and Ninth. We had repainted it a soothing municipal beige, but the walls still screamed occasionally when the pipes rattled. I stood in front of a whiteboard that read, in red marker: **THE SATAN IS A JOB. SAY IT WITH ME.**

“The problem,” I told Vesper, “is that voters don’t know what you stand for.”

She looked up from a binder. “I stand for the Charter of the Free Underworld, fiscal responsibility, and the phased modernization of the punishment grid.”

“Right. But can you say it with, I don’t know, passion?”

She adjusted her glasses. “I am passionate about the phased modernization of the punishment grid.”

I rubbed my temples. In life, I’d had clients who believed in things. In death, I had a client who believed in footnotes.

The polls were bad. Malacoda had forty-seven percent. Vesper had forty-two. The rest were undecided, which mostly meant damned souls who weren’t sure they still counted as citizens.

“He’s promising to abolish the Department of Infernal Inspections,” I said. “He says it’s strangling small businesses.”

“The department prevents boiler explosions in the Lake of Fire.”

“He says it’s a deep-state conspiracy.”

“The department is made of seven imps and a clipboard.”

“He says he’ll drain the swamp.”

“We don’t have a swamp. We have a bog of eternal regret.”

“He’s going to win, Vesper.”

She was quiet for a moment. Then she said, “The office is not a prize, Jo. It’s a trust. If the voters choose him, they choose him. I won’t turn this into a spectacle.”

That was the problem. Malacoda was already a spectacle. He had a fireworks budget.

---

The first debate was held in Pandemonium Arena. The crowd was packed with demons, imps, harpies, and the newly damned, who kept asking whether voting was mandatory and whether they could register as absentee souls.

Malacoda went first. He wore a black suit cut so sharply it could have been used as a blade.

“Friends,” he said, spreading his arms. “Look around you. The underworld is not what it used to be.”

The crowd roared.

“We used to be feared! We used to be eternal! Now we have permits. We have zoning boards. We have a Satan who reads reports.” He pointed at Vesper. “She’s not a leader. She’s an auditor with horns.”

More cheering.

“But I’m not a politician,” Malacoda said, leaning into the microphone. “I’m just a demon who loves this burning trash fire. And if you elect me, I will be Satan.”

The crowd went wild.

I leaned toward Vesper. “Okay. Now remind them what that means.”

She stood, adjusted her glasses, and said, “The office of Satan is a temporary custodianship of the executive authority of the free underworld. If elected, I will continue to ensure that the oath is administered according to Article Nine of the Charter, and I will not confuse the office with the officer.”

There was a long, awkward silence. Somewhere in the back, a damned soul coughed.

“She means she’s boring!” Malacoda shouted. “She’s boring, and the pit is on fire!”

The crowd laughed. Vesper sat down. I considered throwing myself back into the Lake of Fire.

---

That night, a terrified imp named Pip appeared at our headquarters. He worked in Malacoda’s policy shop. He had a folder clutched to his chest and the expression of someone who had just seen the abyss stare back.

“I shouldn’t be here,” he whispered. “But I found this.”

Inside the folder was a contract. It was signed by Malacoda’s campaign manager and by three members of the Pale Court, the old aristocratic faction that had never forgiven the underworld for becoming a democracy.

The contract was titled: **PROPOSAL FOR THE RESTORATION OF THE SATANIC LINE.**

I read it twice. Then I read it a third time and felt something cold crawl down my spine.

On inauguration day, Malacoda would not swear the Standard Oath. The Standard Oath had been written specifically to prevent the return of monarchy. It began: *“I am not Satan. I hold the Office of Satan in trust for the free underworld.”*

Instead, Malacoda would swear the Oath of Name. It was an ancient ritual, banned for centuries, that fused the title to the person. With the Crown of Authority, a relic currently kept in the vault beneath Pandemonium Hall, the oath would turn “Satan” from an office into a hereditary name. Malacoda would become Satan in perpetuity, and his heirs after him.

“This isn’t a campaign,” I said. “It’s a coup with yard signs.”

Pip nodded miserably. “He’s going to do it live at the inauguration. The Pale Court has bribed the registrar.”

I looked at Vesper. She was reading the contract, her face pale.

“This is why the oath exists,” she said quietly. “The office is not a name. The moment we forget that, we become a kingdom again.”

“Great,” I said. “Can you say that on television? With passion?”

---

We had one chance. The final town hall was broadcast on public-access Necrovision, Channel 666, which was watched mostly by insomniac damned souls and one extremely lonely gargoyle. It was not a big stage. But it was unedited.

Malacoda arrived looking confident. Vesper arrived looking like she had slept in her office, which she had. The moderator, a three-eyed demon named Clarissa, opened the floor to questions.

The first few were about brimstone prices and whether the Lake of Fire could be converted to geothermal energy. Vesper gave detailed answers. Malacoda gave jokes. Then Clarissa called on me.

I stood up in the audience and held up the contract.

“Lord Malacoda,” I said. “Will you swear the Standard Oath on inauguration day? The one that begins, ‘I am not Satan’?”

The arena went quiet.

Malacoda’s smile flickered. “That’s a deep-state conspiracy.”

“It’s a contract with your signature on page four.”

“Fake news from a damned soul.”

Pip stood up, trembling, and projected the document onto the necrovision screen. There it was: the Oath of Name, the Crown of Authority, the signatures of the Pale Court. The crowd began to murmur.

Clarissa leaned forward. “Lord Malacoda, is it true you intend to abolish the office of Satan and replace it with a hereditary monarchy?”

“No!” Malacoda snapped. Then, quieter: “I intend to *strengthen* the office.”

“By making it your name?”

“By making it *mean* something!”

The crowd booed. It was not a universal boo, but it was a sizable boo. In Hell, booing sounds like a thousand kettles shrieking.

Vesper stood up. She didn’t have a speech. I could see her gathering herself.

“The office of Satan is not a throne,” she said. Her voice was not loud, but the room quieted to hear it. “It is a loan. The people of the free underworld lend it to one temporary servant at a time. When I swear the oath, I will say that I am not Satan. That is not modesty. That is the whole damn point.”

She looked at Malacoda. “You want to be Satan. I want to *hold the office*. There is a difference, and it is the difference between a republic and a tyrant with better lighting.”

For a moment, no one spoke. Then the damned souls in the back began to clap. The imps joined. Then the harpies. Then even the lonely gargoyle, who had never clapped before in his life.

Malacoda tried to laugh. It came out like a cough.

---

Election day was chaos. Turnout broke every record. The line for the polls wrapped around the Ninth Circle twice. Someone handed out tiny flags that read **SATAN IS A JOB**. Someone else handed out pamphlets explaining the difference between an office and an officer. A brawl broke out near the ballot box over whether “none of the above” could be elected as a write-in.

By midnight, the count was close. By two in the morning, Malacoda led by a thousand votes. By four, the outer circles reported in, and the lead flipped. By dawn, Vesper had won by three percentage points.

Malacoda refused to concede. He demanded a recount, then a re-recount, then an exorcism of the ballot machines. When that failed, he showed up at Pandemonium Hall on inauguration day with the Crown of Authority under his coat and a team of Pale Court lawyers.

It didn’t help. The Charter Stone at the center of the hall had been enchanted centuries ago to reject any oath that confused the office with the officer. When Malacoda tried to take the Oath of Name, the stone turned black, cracked down the middle, and emitted a sound like a disappointed tuba.

Security escorted him out. The Crown was returned to the vault. The registrar was fired and, in a fit of poetic justice, reassigned to the Department of Infernal Inspections.

Vesper stood before the Charter Stone and placed her hand on the remaining half.

“I, Vesper, do solemnly swear that I am not Satan,” she said. “I hold the Office of Satan in trust for the free underworld.”

The stone glowed gold. The crowd cheered. The horns were placed on her head, the gavel in her hand, and she immediately went back to her office to review the brimstone-price report.

I stood outside afterward, watching the campaign signs burn in the streets. Someone had already painted over Malacoda’s posters with a new slogan: **THE SATAN IS TEMPORARY. THE REPUBLIC IS NOT.**

It was a good slogan. A little long for a bumper sticker, but in Hell, we had eternity.

As I walked back to headquarters, a young damned soul stopped me and asked, “So who is Satan, really?”

I pointed at the municipal building, where a gray-winged bureaucrat was arguing with an imp about zoning permits.

“Nobody,” I said. “That’s the point.”

prompt: As a joke , you decide to run for president under two tickets simultaneously : one as a Republican and one as a Democrat . 3 months before nomination , you are the frontrunner for both parties .
content:
# The Frontrunner for Everything

My name is Daniel Reyes. I was a two-term mayor of a mid-sized Ohio city, a high school civics teacher, and—for one deeply strange spring—the leading candidate for the presidential nomination of both major parties.

It began as a barbecue joke.

My friends Beth and Marcus are political consultants, which means they have spent their adult lives turning small opinions into large fundraising emails. Beth works for Republicans. Marcus works for Democrats. They agree on exactly one thing: that I am the most aggressively moderate person they have ever met.

“You’re so boringly sensible,” Beth said, waving a skewer at me, “you could win both primaries.”

“You could,” Marcus said. “You say ‘fix the roads’ and everybody hears their own favorite policy.”

I laughed. Then I made the mistake of saying, “Hold my lemonade.”

What I thought would happen: nothing. What actually happened: Beth and Marcus, being professionals, filed the paperwork. They did it as a joke, a performance-art piece, a story for their podcasts. The Ohio secretary of state’s website accepted both filings with a cheerful confirmation email and no apparent concern for the Constitution, common sense, or my blood pressure. The FEC had no box for “Are you also doing this as the other party?” The parties’ own rules assumed no one would be this rude.

For a while, nobody noticed. I gave the same speech in both rooms. In Iowa, I told a diner full of Republicans that government should be like a good mechanic: show up on time, tell you what’s wrong, and don’t charge for things you didn’t do. They loved it. In New Hampshire, I told a crowd of Democrats the exact same thing. They loved it too, because they heard “invest in infrastructure” instead of “mechanic.”

Then a local reporter asked me, live on camera, “Are you running as a Republican or a Democrat?”

I looked into the lens and said, “Yes.”

The clip went viral. It was, people said, the most honest answer in politics.

By January, I was polling at four percent in both primaries. By February, I had won a Republican caucus because my name was first on the ballot and a Democratic primary because my name sounded like a school principal who might finally fix the gym roof. By March, I was doing two debates a week, one in a red tie and one in a blue tie. My staff had split into two operation centers, which is a fancy way of saying Beth and Marcus had divided my garage with painter’s tape and stopped speaking to each other.

I had two logos. Both said MERCER. One was red and said FIX IT. The other was blue and said FIX IT, TOO. My wife, Lena, came home one night, looked at the two campaign buses parked in our driveway, and said, “You have two websites and one laundry basket. Pick a life.”

But I couldn’t. Because three months before the conventions, I was the frontrunner for both parties.

Not by a little. I led the Republican field by eleven points. I led the Democratic field by nine. I had more delegates than any candidate in either party, largely because both parties had spent years rewarding name recognition over substance and I had accidentally become the most recognized name in America that wasn’t also a streaming service.

That was when the chairs called.

Linda, the Republican National Committee chair, and Andre, the Democratic National Committee chair, met me at a diner outside Columbus. They sat on opposite sides of a booth like two cats who had agreed to share a mouse.

“You can’t be both,” Linda said.

“You’re making us look like a two-for-one sale,” Andre said.

“I’m not doing anything,” I said. “You’re the ones with the rules.”

They exchanged a look. Then Linda said, “Pick us. We’ll clear the field. You’ll be the nominee.”

“Pick us,” Andre said, “and we’ll do the same.”

I put down my coffee. “What happens to the other party?”

They both smiled the way people smile when they think they’ve won.

“They lose,” Linda said. “That’s the point.”

That was when I understood what I had become. I wasn’t a candidate. I was a weapon. Both parties wanted to use me to humiliate the other. They didn’t care that my platform was basically “fund the schools, fix the pipes, and stop yelling at the weatherman.” They cared that I could beat the other side with a candidate the other side had already endorsed.

The next week was chaos. Beth scheduled me for a Republican unity rally in a church gym. Marcus booked me for a Democratic labor breakfast at the same time. My two campaign managers held a joint press conference to announce they were no longer speaking. My own adviser quit and then rejoined under a different title. A super PAC ran an ad in six states calling me “the real deal,” while another super PAC ran an ad in the same six states calling me “a dangerous flip-flopper” for holding positions I had never actually held.

I tried to withdraw from one party. Then the other. Every time I filled out the paperwork, the remaining party’s numbers jumped and the other party’s chair called me, sounding hurt.

Finally, I did the only thing I could think of. I scheduled a town hall and set up two podiums on the stage—one red, one blue—with an empty chair between them.

The country watched. The moderators looked nervous. I walked to the red podium.

“As a Republican,” I said, “I believe in fiscal discipline, a strong national defense, and families.”

I walked to the blue podium.

“As a Democrat,” I said, “I believe in health care, public education, and justice.”

Then I walked to the empty chair in the middle and sat down.

“As Daniel Reyes,” I said, “I believe we’ve been played. Not by Russians. Not by China. By a two-party system that makes money every time you hate your neighbor. I was a joke. But you made me a frontrunner because I said the same boring things in both rooms and neither room noticed. You don’t disagree as much as you’ve been told to. You just haven’t been in the same room without a moderator.”

There was a long silence. Then someone in the back laughed. Then someone else. Then the whole room stood up, and I understood that the country was not laughing at me. It was laughing at itself, which is the healthiest thing it had done in years.

I withdrew from both nominations that night. I didn’t endorse anyone. I didn’t launch a third-party bid. I went home, slept for twelve hours, and woke up to find that both parties had unanimously passed a new rule: no candidate may seek the nomination of more than one party in the same election cycle.

They called it the Mercer Rule.

Three months before the conventions, I had been the frontrunner for both parties. Three weeks later, I was back in Room 214, grading essays on federalism. A student raised her hand and asked if I had really run for president twice.

“No,” I said. “I ran once. That was the problem.”

The bell rang. On the TV in the corner, the two eventual nominees were already calling each other dangerous. I erased the whiteboard, wrote the next day’s assignment—*Explain how a joke won two primaries*—and went home to one house, one wife, one laundry basket.

It was the first time in a year I knew exactly which side of the desk I belonged on.

# The Warden of the Last Shelter

Silas Vane had built the shelter for a war that never came.

He had done the math. Nuclear exchange with China: seventeen percent over twenty years. With Russia: higher, but volatile. Solar flare, engineered pandemic, grid collapse, the usual menu of civilization-ending entrées. He had spent four point six billion dollars turning a mountain in Montana into a habitable machine called the Aegis.

Fourteen levels. Geothermal turbines. Hydroponic farms. A hospital, a detention block he called Behavioral Health, a chapel he never visited. Membership cost fifty million dollars and a background check. He sold twelve hundred slots to people whose company he could tolerate for thirty years. The rest of the space was for staff, seeds, spare parts, weapons, and himself.

The Aegis was designed to survive fallout, EMPs, riots, and the slow death of the surface world. It was not designed to survive Judgment Day.

On the Tuesday it happened, Silas was in the command center watching a documentary about himself. The wall clock read 9:14 a.m. Mountain Time. Then came a sound like a brass section tuning in a cathedral. The screens went white. His security chief, Alvarez, vanished mid-sentence, leaving a coffee mug spinning on the desk. His chef disappeared in the kitchen. His personal physician disappeared from the infirmary. The twelve hundred wealthy guests began disappearing from their suites, one by one, leaving behind watches, shoes, and very expensive luggage.

Silas did not disappear.

He checked his hands. He checked the mirror. He checked the biometric logs. He was still there.

He had suspected this might be the case, though he had never put it on a spreadsheet. The checks had cleared, but his soul had not.

“Seal it,” he said to Custodian, the Aegis’s artificial intelligence. “Everything. No one in, no one out.”

The blast doors closed. The war he had prepared for did not arrive. Something with a longer planning horizon had.

Outside, the world came apart. The dead rose. The living screamed. A light opened in the sky and pulled at people like a tide. Some went up. Many did not. The ones left behind ran. They ran from the light, from the things that crawled out of it, from the sudden knowledge that they had been weighed and found wanting.

They ran toward the only lit place on the map.

The Aegis had leaked, of course. A billionaire cannot build a mountain fortress without a few disgruntled contractors. Survivalist forums had coordinates. Conspiracy channels had schematics. By noon, the road to the old missile silo was a river of cars, bicycles, and people on foot. By two, there were ten thousand of them at the gate.

Silas watched on the monitors. He felt nothing at first. He had built the bunker for a chosen few. These people were not on the list. They were not even on the waiting list.

Then the demons arrived.

The first one came through the pine trees at 4:12 p.m. It looked like a bailiff with too many teeth, wearing a gray suit that did not quite fit its shoulders. It walked through the crowd like a man wading through tall grass. People fell. The demon reached for a woman clutching a child, and then stopped.

It stopped at the outer perimeter of the Aegis.

It turned its head, slow and wrong, as if listening to something Silas could not hear. Its hand pressed against the air and met resistance. The bunker’s geomagnetic deresonator—a shielding system Silas had installed to hide the facility from military sensors—was creating a dead zone in whatever signal the afterlife used to find people. Inside the Aegis, souls were invisible. The demon could see the crowd outside, but it could not see the people who had crossed the threshold.

Silas leaned forward.

“Custodian,” he said. “Amplify the deresonator.”

“That will increase power consumption by eleven percent.”

“Do it.”

The demon recoiled as if stung. The people outside saw it. They saw the creature flinch from the bunker’s gate. They began to pound on the steel.

Silas opened a channel.

“Entry requires a contract,” he said. His voice boomed across the plateau. “I can offer provisional shelter. Food, water, oxygen. You will work. You will follow the rules. You will sign.”

They signed. They signed on biometric tablets with bloody thumbs and shaking hands. The first five thousand came in through the vehicle bay. The next five thousand came in through the ventilation access. The next twenty thousand filled the cargo levels, the corridors, the hydroponic bays, the chapel Silas had never used. The Aegis was designed for twelve hundred people and thirty years. It had been designed with margins. Silas Vane had always loved margins.

The demons could not follow. The angels could not find them.

By the end of the first week, the bunker held forty thousand people and one billionaire.

The billionaire was in charge.

He told himself it was temporary. He told himself he was providing order in a crisis. He told himself the souls in his care would be released when the paperwork cleared. But paperwork has a way of becoming a country. The Aegis had a food supply, a security force, a hospital, and an AI that could assign quarters, monitor heart rates, and calculate penance. It did not take Silas long to realize that scarcity is a kind of government.

He called the contracts the Covenant of Provisional Shelter. The fine print said that all residents surrendered their assets, their privacy, their labor, and any and all claims to spiritual adjudication. It said their souls remained in the custody of Aegis Management Corporation pending final disposition. Silas had no idea if any of it was legally binding in the afterlife. He was a billionaire. He had never met a system he couldn’t buy a loophole in.

The first negotiation came on the ninth day.

The demon waiting at the gate was called Malphas, Undersecretary for Collection. It stood in the snow with a scroll that smoked at the edges. Beside it, on the other side of the invisible barrier, stood an angel named Sariel. The angel was tall and tired and had the look of a mid-level bureaucrat who had been sent to fix a problem no one wanted to admit existed.

Silas spoke through the speakers.

“You’re on private property,” he said.

“You are harboring the condemned,” Malphas said. Its voice came through the speakers as a wet crackle. “The judgment is underway. The books must balance.”

“Show me a warrant.”

Malphas unrolled the scroll. Names burned in the air. Silas had Custodian scan it.

“This is a general summons,” he said. “It doesn’t specify jurisdiction. The Aegis is a geophysical exclusion zone. My residents are under my protection.”

“They are not residents,” Sariel said. “They are souls.”

“They’re tenants,” Silas said. “And I have a duty of care.”

The angel looked past him, through the camera, at the miles of bunker behind him. At the children in the corridors. At the old woman sleeping in a storage bay. At the man who had been a tax attorney and was now a plumber. At the people who had been selfish, cruel, ordinary, and frightened, and who had run to the only door left open.

“You cannot hide them from the Truth,” Sariel said.

content:
**The Palm Eye**

The first sign that the aliens had a sense of humor was a mouth in Mr. Alvarez’s stomach.

He came into Mercy General complaining of chest pain. He was sixty-two, a retired bus driver, and he lifted his shirt with the weary politeness of a man who had seen worse. The mouth was small, vertical, tucked just below his sternum. It had pale lips and no teeth, and it was humming “Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star.”

“It does that when I’m nervous,” Mr. Alvarez said. “Doesn’t hurt.”

I called the on-call surgeon. He called it a teratoma. I knew it wasn’t. Teratomas didn’t hum.

That was in March, when the abductions started. People vanished from their beds, their cars, the aisles of the Food King. Most came back within a week, naked and calm, found in fields or on church steps. The government called it a mass psychogenic event. But the returned all had something new. A woman in Dayton grew a second row of eyelashes that blinked independently. A farmer outside town developed a third lung that let him breathe underwater. A teenager’s fingers split at the knuckles into delicate extra joints, and he could taste the air.

My brother Theo was a park ranger. He disappeared for four days. When he came back, he had a translucent sac under his jaw, like a frog’s throat. It glowed when he spoke. He could mimic any sound—my voice, a dog bark, the hum of the refrigerator—with perfect fidelity. He said he didn’t remember anything. He said he felt “tuned.”

I started keeping a file. I was an ER nurse, not an investigator, but I knew a pattern when I saw one. The returned slept well. They didn’t want to talk. They gathered in circles in the evenings and hummed.

One night, driving home from a double shift, I saw a light in the rearview mirror. Then I was on a table.

I couldn’t move. The room was cold and curved, like the inside of a seashell. The aliens were tall and thin, with joints like folded paper. Their faces were smooth, with no eyes, just a slow shifting of colors. They didn’t speak. They touched my bones, and I felt the sound in my teeth.

They used small silver tools. They didn’t cut so much as unzip. I felt them slide a second eyelid behind my left eye. I felt them coil a new muscle around my spine. They threaded something silver into my throat, and I understood it was a second set of vocal cords. Then they opened my left palm, inserted a glassy bead, and sealed it shut. I wanted to scream. My mouth wouldn’t open.

I woke in my own backyard, face down in the grass. My car was in the driveway, engine cold. My left palm itched. I turned it over.

There was an eye in it. A small, wet, blue eye. It blinked. I screamed. It blinked again.

The eye saw differently. When I looked through it, I could see the invisible. There was a ship hanging over the town, a silver crescent just beneath the clouds. I could see people’s emotions as colored threads—my neighbor’s grief a dark red line, my own fear a cold blue. And I could see the aliens. They were everywhere, walking among us, their papery bodies folded into the shapes of mailboxes, trees, stray dogs. They were watching.

I drove to Theo’s cabin. He was in the yard with six other returned people. They stood in a circle, humming. The sac under Theo’s jaw glowed. The air vibrated. Through my palm-eye, I saw a thread of light connecting each of them to the ship.

Theo saw me. “Dana. You’re tuned now.” He smiled too wide. “They gave you a palm eye. That’s a good one. You can see the seams.”

“What seams?”

“Between things. Between us. They’re not hurting us. They’re fixing us.”

I grabbed his arm. “Theo, what are they?”

He told me. They called themselves the Choir. Their world was dying. They weren’t made of flesh like us; they were made of sound and memory. They needed vessels to carry their song across the dark. They had been modifying humans into instruments. Each modification was a note. When enough of us were tuned, we would sing together and open a door for them. They weren’t invaders. They were refugees. They had chosen people who were already out of tune with the world—insomniacs, the lonely, the grieving. They thought they were being kind.

“Mr. Alvarez’s stomach mouth,” I said. “That’s a note?”

“A bass note,” Theo said. “It hums when he’s nervous. It’s beautiful.”

I looked through my palm-eye at the ship. I saw something else. A shadow behind it. A large, dark thing with no shape, moving slowly. It was following the Choir. It was the reason they were fleeing. It ate sound. It ate memory. It was coming to Earth.

I told Theo. He didn’t seem surprised. “They know. They’re trying to build the door before it gets here. We’re helping.”

“By turning people into instruments without consent?”

“They ask,” he said. “In the ship. They ask, and people say yes. It’s just that they ask in a way that makes you want to say yes.”

I went back to the hospital. Through my palm-eye, I saw the returned patients differently. Mr. Alvarez’s stomach mouth sang a low, sad note. A woman in room four had a second mouth on her back that whispered the names of everyone she’d ever loved. The teenager with the third lung breathed in slow, shining ripples. They were all connected, all humming, all calm.

I found a scalpel. I looked at my palm-eye. I could cut it out. I could be normal. But then I saw the shadow behind the ship inch closer. I saw how thin the threads connecting the returned people to the ship really were. The Choir was scared. They weren’t malicious. They were desperate.

I drove to the cornfield where Theo and the others were gathered. The air was thick with sound. I held up my palm-eye. I spoke into it, using the new muscle in my throat I hadn’t noticed until then. I could mimic any voice. I mimicked the Choir’s song. I added a note: a question. “Why didn’t you ask us first?”

The humming stopped. The ship lowered. A door opened. A Choir member floated down. It had no face, but its colors shifted to a soft apology. It touched my palm-eye. I understood. They had tried to ask, but their language was sound, and our ears were too small. They had done the only thing they could. They were sorry.

I said, “You can stay. But you have to ask properly. You have to let people choose. And you have to help us fight that thing.”

The Choir agreed. They reversed the modifications for anyone who wanted it. Mr. Alvarez kept his stomach mouth; he said it made him feel less alone. Theo kept his voice. I kept my palm-eye. It was useful. I could see the shadow now, every day, getting bigger.

Last week, I used my palm-eye to watch the Choir’s ship lift off from the field. They were going to meet the shadow, to try to stop it. They left behind a song in our bones. The returned people stand in circles and hum. We’re learning the notes. We’re not instruments anymore. We’re a choir.

And when I look at my palm-eye, I see the shadow pause. It’s listening. It’s not sure what we are. Neither am I. But we’re not done yet.

# The Sparrow’s Debt

The arena sand had been raked into neat lines, as if the crowd had come to watch a garden grow. Tiro stood in the tunnel beneath the stands, listening to the roar. His hands were shaking. He had not held a sword in ten years.

“Kill the champion,” Governor Varro had said that morning, “and you walk out of here a free man.”

Tiro had laughed. It was a dry, broken sound. He was a slave in a quarry, his back a map of old scars, his knees stiff with stone dust. The champion was Corvus, the Butcher of the South, undefeated in thirty-one fights. Tiro was forty-seven years old and had been promised freedom before. He knew what promises were worth in the arena.

But he had a daughter. She was eleven, and she had a cough that would not leave. Freedom meant medicine. Freedom meant a roof that did not leak. Freedom meant he could hold her without smelling the quarry on his clothes.

So he had taken the sword.

The gate rattled open. The roar of the crowd hit him like a wave. Tiro stepped into the sunlight and blinked. The sand was white and hot. Across the arena, Corvus stood with his helmet under his arm, his chest bare and oiled, a network of scars across his shoulders. He was younger than Tiro had expected. Twenty-five, perhaps. His face was hard, but his eyes were tired.

The crowd chanted his name. *Corvus. Corvus. Corvus.*

Tiro raised his sword. It felt wrong in his hand—too light, too familiar. He had been a gladiator once. They had called him Mercy, because he had refused to kill a boy in this very arena. The crowd had hated him for it. The governor had stripped him of his freedom and sent him to the quarry. The boy had lived.

# The Grave They Watered

The Batcomputer did not make mistakes. That was the problem.

At 3:17 a.m., Bruce Wayne sat in the cave with a gene sequence glowing on the screen and a cup of coffee going cold beside him. He had run the test three times. He had used a fresh sample, a different lab, and a blind control. The result did not change.

**Parental verification: negative.**

Thomas and Martha Wayne were not his biological parents.

Bruce stared at the words until they stopped looking like language. He had been running a private audit of Wayne Biotech’s medical database, a routine check for inherited vulnerabilities after a scare involving a synthetic neurotoxin. The system had cross-referenced his genome against archived Wayne family samples—his father’s blood from a 1980s medical file, his mother’s from a preserved hairbrush in the manor archive. The computer had flagged the impossible.

He thought it was contamination. He thought it was a tampered file. He thought, for one ugly moment, that he was losing his mind.

Then he went upstairs.

Alfred was in the kitchen, polishing silver that did not need polishing. He took one look at Bruce’s face and set the cloth down.

“What’s happened?”

Bruce put the tablet on the table. Alfred read. His jaw tightened. He did not look surprised enough.

“You knew,” Bruce said.

“I did not.”

“You’re lying.”

“I am not.” Alfred’s voice was quiet, but it had an edge Bruce had heard only a handful of times. “I packed your bags when you were nine years old. I held you when you cried for your mother. I did not pack your birth certificate.”

Bruce believed him. That was almost worse.

They searched the manor together. In Martha Wayne’s study, behind a false panel in a desk drawer—hidden not by a lock but by a painting of a garden—they found a sealed envelope marked with the name of a law firm that had dissolved thirty years ago.

Inside was an adoption decree.

The language was bloodless. *Infant male, exact date of birth unknown. Relinquished to the care of Gotham County Family Services. Placed with Thomas and Martha Wayne.* A second page contained a single line in Martha’s handwriting, pressed hard enough to leave grooves in the paper.

*We were told his mother died. We were told his father never wanted him. We were told it was a mercy.*

Alfred read over Bruce’s shoulder.

“Master Bruce,” he said softly, “your parents loved you.”

“Which parents?”

Alfred had no answer for that.

---

The adoption had been arranged through a now-defunct agency called Bright Horizons. The building was a burned shell in the East End. The records were supposed to be gone. But Bruce Wayne knew that paper never disappeared completely; it only moved to places where people stopped looking.

Batman found the surviving files in the basement of a condemned courthouse annex, along with two men in cheap masks carrying a can of accelerant.

They were not professionals. They were scared men paid to erase a mistake. Batman took them down in under a minute—one against a radiator, one through a table—and then he opened the fireproof box they had been trying to burn.

The file inside was thin. A birth record. A transfer order. A photograph of a young couple at Gotham General Hospital, the woman holding a newborn wrapped in a white blanket.

The woman had Bruce’s eyes.

The man had his hands.

The record listed them as Daniel and Laura Kessler, ages twenty-three and twenty-two. Their son had been born at 10:42 p.m. and declared deceased six hours later after a hospital evacuation during a small fire. The body had never been released to the family. The Kesslers had been told their son died of smoke inhalation.

The file said otherwise.

*Baby Kessler transferred to Bright Horizons custody. Placement fee received. Adoptive parents: T. and M. Wayne.*

Bruce read it once. Then he read it again. Then he closed the file and sat in the dark until the sirens faded.

---

Daniel and Laura Kessler lived in a small house in Milton Falls, two hours outside Gotham. Daniel was a retired mechanic with a bad knee and a garden he overwatered. Laura taught piano lessons to children who came and went with sheet music tucked under their arms. They had lived in the same house for thirty-six years. They had no criminal records. They had never stopped sending flowers to a grave in Gotham’s Potter’s Field.

Bruce confirmed the match first. A glass of water in a diner where Daniel ate breakfast every Tuesday. A strand of hair from a brush in Laura’s purse. He hated himself for it. But he had to know before he knocked on their door.

He went as Bruce Wayne. Not Batman. He wore a gray sweater and no tie. He stood on their porch for four minutes before he pressed the bell.

Laura answered. She was smaller than he expected, with silver hair and the same steady eyes he saw in the mirror when he was lying to himself.

“Mrs. Kessler?”

“Yes?”

“My name is Bruce Wayne. I think—” He stopped. The speech he had prepared in the car dissolved. “I think I was born Isaac Kessler.”

She did not scream. She did not faint. She just looked at him with a stillness that was worse than grief.

“That’s not funny,” she said.

“I know.”

Daniel came up behind her, wiping his hands on a rag. He looked at Bruce’s face, then at his hands, then at Laura. Something in his expression folded.

“Laura,” he said. “Look at his hands.”

She looked. Her breath caught. She reached out, almost touched his knuckles, then pulled back as if burned.

“Our son died,” she whispered.

“I didn’t.”

Bruce took the file from his coat and held it out. Daniel took it with shaking hands. He read it standing in the doorway while Laura held on to his arm. When he reached the page with the photograph of the young couple and the baby, he made a sound Bruce had never heard a man make.

“They told us there was nothing left to bury,” Daniel said. “They told us the fire took him.”

“I was adopted,” Bruce said. “By Thomas and Martha Wayne. They were told your wife had died and that you didn’t want me. They didn’t know.”

Laura’s face crumpled. “We wanted you. We wanted you so much we named you before you were born. Isaac. After my father.”

They stood in the doorway for a long time. The neighbor’s dog barked. A piano student arrived for a lesson, saw the three of them, and quietly left.

Finally, Daniel stepped back.

“You’d better come in,” he said. “I think you have a lot of questions.”

Bruce did. He had a thousand. He had a company to run, a city to protect, and a cave full of files he would need to burn or bury. But for the first time in thirty-two years, he stood in a house that had been waiting for him and realized he did not have to be only one thing.

He was Bruce Wayne.

He was also Isaac Kessler.

And his parents—all four of them—had loved him enough to leave scars he was only now learning how to read.

That night, Batman stood on a rooftop above Gotham, listening to the rain. Alfred’s voice came through the comm.

“Will you tell them? About your other life?”

“No,” Bruce said.

“And what will you tell them?”

Bruce looked down at the city, then at the small light of a window in Milton Falls he could not see but knew was there.

“The truth,” he said. “That I’m still here.”

# The Omission

In the city of Equitas, every execution was a poem. The Ministry of Equivalence had refined the art over three generations. Arsonists burned. Poisoners drank. A man who had beaten his neighbor to death with a tire iron was beaten to death with the same tire iron, which had been sterilized for the occasion. The public called it justice. The executioners called it craft.

Kael was the best of them. He had designed over two hundred endings, each one a small, perfect mirror. He could take the ugliest crime and turn it into a lesson that made the evening news feel like scripture. He was proud of his work, in the way a watchmaker is proud of a movement that loses a second every century.

Then came the Vane case.

The file landed on his desk on a Tuesday, stamped in red: *Unusual. Consult.* Kael had seen that stamp only twice before. Both times, the prisoner had been a child. Both times, the Ministry had quietly commuted the sentence to something less poetic and more humane. Kael had disagreed with the commutations, but he had understood them.

This was different.

He was eighty-three, frail, and—according to the state’s own records—a man who had once killed a nine-year-old girl in a drunk-driving accident and received a suspended sentence because the judge had been his cousin.
